Adrenal Glands.description: Mitochondrial homeostasis, governed by the balance between biogenesis and mitophagy, is essential for steroidogenesis in adrenocortical cells [3]. In H295R adrenocortical cells, Ang II led to a significant increase in basal and maximum respiration, ATP production, and proton leak [3], and these findings suggest that hormone stimulation favors mitochondrial activity, thereby enhancing the bioenergetic capacity of adrenocortical cells [3]. Steroid synthesis itself depends on substrate supply and transport, as ID-induced suppression of steroidogenesis was primarily associated with StAR downregulation, which was reversed by iron supplementation [4]. The adrenal gland also produces catecholamines, since Nox4 deletion led to decreased hydrogen peroxide production, diminished dopamine beta-hydroxylase mRNA expression, and reduced norepinephrine levels [5]. Among the adrenal steroids, the strongest sex difference involved Srd5a2, with markedly higher expression in male zona fasciculata [2], and Agtr1a dominated angiotensin II receptor expression in zona glomerulosa without major sex differences [2]. Regulation of adrenal output is shaped by several hormonal and stress signals: aldosterone synthase inhibitors block aldosterone production in the adrenal gland [9], and recent studies have highlighted a dynamic interplay between GDF-15 and the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, suggesting that GDF-15 acts as a sentinel hormone in stress responses [6]. Under chronic stress, chronic exposure may flatten circadian patterns, alter ultradian glucocorticoid pulsatility, suppress downstream reproductive and metabolic axes, and produce heterogeneous effects on DHEA-S, aldosterone, and neurosteroid pathways [1].

papers.title: Adaptive changes in adrenal steroid metabolism under extreme physical and psychological stress: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Chronic exposure to sleep deprivation, insufficient recovery, inadequate energy availability, extreme environmental conditions, repetitive high-intensity exercise, and psychological threat can alter hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis function. Acute activation of the HPA axis is adaptive, whereas prolonged or repetitive activation may contribute to allostatic load, altered daily glucocorticoid exposure, and changes associated with psychological and metabolic maladaptation. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on adrenal steroid metabolism under extreme physical and psychological stress, with emphasis on glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-responsive adrenal androgens, including dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S) and androstenedione. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched through 22 May 2026. Recent human and military studies were prioritized, and earlier seminal work was included when it provided a mechanistic or historical context not captured by recent literature. The review describes how acute stress responses may support substrate mobilization and performance, whereas chronic exposure may flatten circadian patterns, alter ultradian glucocorticoid pulsatility, suppress downstream reproductive and metabolic axes, and produce heterogeneous effects on DHEA-S, aldosterone, and neurosteroid pathways. The strongest clinical and military evidence concerns sleep/circadian disruption, energy deficit, and prolonged military training; evidence for direct nutrient-mediated prevention of HPA-axis maladaptation remains preliminary or indirect. Addressing energy deficit, sleep deprivation and circadian disruption, inadequate recovery, dehydration/heat strain, and clinically relevant nutrient deficiencies may reduce the stressor load that contributes to functional hypercortisolism. Nutritional interventions should focus on correcting deficiencies, maintaining energy, supporting musculoskeletal function, and reducing stress, rather than serving as direct hormonal therapy. Future studies should use standardized steroid sampling, report sex-specific outcomes, and account for energy intake, expenditure, sleep, baseline fitness, and environmental exposures.

papers.title: Single-cell spatial transcriptomic atlas of the mouse adrenal gland reveals sexual dimorphism in steroidogenic enzyme and hormone receptor expression.
papers.abstract: The adrenal cortex shows sexual dimorphism in structure and function. We analysed adrenal glands from 7-week-old male and female BALB/c mice using Visium HD with Cellpose 3 segmentation, comprising 236,077 cells across eleven populations, including four cortical zones. Using curated marker-gene-based zonal annotation, we focused on steroidogenic enzymes and hormone receptors, complementing our companion study based on the same primary dataset. The X-zone was nearly absent in males but prominent in females. Females showed higher Hsd3b1 expression across cortical zones and higher Cyp11b1 expression in outer cortical compartments. The strongest sex difference involved Srd5a2, with markedly higher expression in male zona fasciculata (inner: 77.1% vs. 28.9%), independently supported by RNAscope and immunohistochemistry. Mc2r and Mrap showed discordant spatial distributions, with limited co-expression, suggesting potential MC2R-independent MRAP roles. Agtr1a dominated angiotensin II receptor expression in zona glomerulosa without major sex differences, providing a zone-resolved reference for adrenal sexual dimorphism.

papers.title: Angiotensin II and cAMP signaling pathways regulate mitochondrial biogenesis and activity in human adrenocortical cells.
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial homeostasis, governed by the balance between biogenesis and mitophagy, is essential for steroidogenesis in adrenocortical cells. While the requirement of active mitochondria for steroid synthesis is well-established, the hormonal regulation of genes governing mitochondrial function remains poorly understood. This study investigated whether angiotensin II (Ang II) and the cAMP/PKA pathway modulate the expression of key regulatory factors involved in mitochondrial biogenesis and redox status in the human adrenocortical H295R cell line. Using real-time qPCR and Western blot, we show that Ang II and 8Br-cAMP-a permeant analog of cAMP-modulate NRF-1, Nrf2, UCP2, and ANT1 impacting on mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and respiratory activity. These molecular changes correlated with increased mitochondrial membrane polarization, as confirmed by MitoTracker red staining. Interestingly, Ang II stimulation promoted a time-dependent increase in TFAM levels, a key transcription factor in mitochondria, which correlates with the increase in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) content. The rate of oxygen consumption (OCR) and mitochondrial parameters were determined, with results showing that Ang II led to a significant increase in basal and maximum respiration, ATP production, and proton leak. These findings suggest that hormone stimulation favors mitochondrial activity, thereby enhancing the bioenergetic capacity of adrenocortical cells. Furthermore, treatment with the uncoupler CCCP triggered a retrograde signaling response, upregulating nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes to counteract mitochondrial membrane depolarization. Our findings demonstrate for the first time that hormonal signals directly modulate the mitochondrial genetic program in H295R human adrenocortical cells, optimizing the bioenergetic platform required for efficient steroidogenic function.

papers.title: Iron deficiency impaired StAR-mediated steroidogenesis.
papers.abstract: Iron deficiency (ID) impairs adrenocortical function, yet its underlying mechanism remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that ID suppresses steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR)-mediated adrenocortical steroidogenesis. In dietary ID mice, deferoxamine-treated mice, and H295R cells, mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid hormone production was significantly reduced. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that ID-induced suppression of steroidogenesis was primarily associated with StAR downregulation, which was reversed by iron supplementation. Mechanistically, ID activated the ERK signaling pathway, leading to reduced StAR expression. Pharmacological inhibition of ERK restored both StAR protein levels and steroidogenic output. Collectively, our findings suggest that the ERK-StAR axis represents a potential regulatory pathway associated with ID-induced adrenocortical hypofunction.

papers.title: NADPH oxidase 4 as a source of hydrogen peroxide can regulate norepinephrine levels and vascular contraction.
papers.abstract: The adrenal glands play a pivotal role in maintaining physiological homeostasis, and disturbance in their function can lead to significant clinical disorders, including hypertension, and adrenal insufficiency. Reactive oxygen species (ROS), once considered merely byproducts of cellular metabolism, are now recognized as critical signaling molecules within the adrenal cortex and medulla. Among the major enzymatic sources of ROS are NADPH oxidases (Nox). Dysregulation of Nox-derived ROS has been linked to altered steroidogenesis, oxidative stress- mediated adrenal damage, and tumorigenic processes. We aimed to elucidate the role of Nox4 on adrenal function under healthy conditions. Using Nox4-knockout mouse model, adrenal effects were assessed by histological analysis, real-time PCR, and cathecholamine quantification using HPLC-ECD and LC-MS/MS. Cardiovascular function was evaluated by echocardiography, blood pressure measurements, and ex vivo vascular function analysis. Here, we demonstrated that Nox4 is expressed in the mouse adrenal gland, and its deletion led to decreased hydrogen peroxide production, diminished dopamine beta-hydroxylase mRNA expression, and reduced norepinephrine levels. In chromaffin cells, treatment with hydrogen peroxide stimulated catecholamine release and increased dopamine beta-hydroxylase expression, indicating a regulatory role of hydrogen peroxide in catecholamine synthesis and secretion. Further analysis of the physiological consequences of reduced norepinephrine levels in Nox4 -/- mice revealed decreased alpha-1 adrenergic receptor expression and impaired adrenergic vascular contraction, while cardiac function remained unaffected. In a model of physical activity, Nox4 depletion resulted in smaller adrenal glands and lower urinary norepinephrine concentrations, further explaining diminished physical activity of Nox4 -/- mice. Our findings provide evidence that Nox4-derived H 2 O 2 plays a role in norepinephrine release and norepinephrine-mediated functions. Hence, loss of Nox4 impairs vascular contractility and reduces physical activity performance, highlighting the physiological importance of Nox4 in adrenal function.

papers.title: The Sentinel Hormone GDF-15, Glucocorticoid Homeostasis and Adrenal Disorders.
papers.abstract: Growth and differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15) is a stress-responsive hormone secreted by various cell types in response to cellular stress. To regulate ingestive behaviour, suppress food intake, and induce nausea and vomiting during cellular stress, GDF-15 signals via a brainstem-restricted receptor, GFRAL. Elevated circulating GDF-15 levels serve as a biomarker of cellular stress and are increased in a wide range of diseases. GDF-15 has recently been established as a causal factor in cancer cachexia and GDF15-GFRAL antagonism is being pursued as a therapeutic strategy. Recent studies have highlighted a dynamic interplay between GDF-15 and the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, suggesting that GDF-15 acts as a sentinel hormone in stress responses. Here, we review the canonical role of GDF-15 in stress-related conditions and its potential impact on circadian regulation and HPA axis dysregulation. The review explores the potential activation of the HPA axis by GDF-15 and discuss the hypothesis that downstream glucocorticoid signalling may contribute to some of the cardiovascular, metabolic, immune, and musculoskeletal changes reported for GDF-15. Additionally, the review discusses the potential role of GDF-15 in adrenal insufficiency and its treatment and in adrenocortical carcinoma. In summary, this review aims to elucidate the role of GDF-15 in glucocorticoid homeostasis and adrenal disease in the context of the stress response.

papers.title: Role of NP-59 SPECT/CT in the Management of Mild Autonomous Cortisol Secretion.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives : Recent advancements in medical imaging have provided tools that significantly enhance diagnostic precision and patient care. Among these, NP-59 SPECT/CT imaging has emerged as a promising method for assessing adrenal gland functionality. Current gaps in clinical practice, including the lack of specific diagnostic biomarkers and the paucity of clinical trials demonstrating the efficacy of adrenalectomy in alleviating comorbidities, necessitate the search for other diagnostic methods. Management becomes more challenging when bilateral adrenal adenomas are present. Demonstrating lateralization in cortisol secretion may greatly assist in treatment selection. Unilateral secretion of cortisol indicates autonomy and therefore adrenalectomy should be preferred. The aim of this study was to evaluate the usefulness of NP-59 SPECT/CT in the management of MACS. Methods : We investigated 20 patients with benign bilateral adrenal incidentalomas and MACS between the years 2023 and 2025. The first group (70%) consisted of patients with only hypertension, without additional comorbidities (hypertension only, HO). The second group (30%) consisted of hypertensive patients with additional comorbidities (hypertension with comorbidities, HC). Visualizations of adrenal glands metabolic activity were conducted using the SPECT/CT system after intravenous injection of NP-59. Abdominal SPECT/CT was performed at 3, 5, and 7 days after tracer injection. Lateralization was established when only single adrenal uptake occurred as early as the third day. Results : Six (30%) patients demonstrated lateralization during NP-59 SPECT scintigraphy. All these patients belonged to the HO group and accounted for 43% of it. Conclusions : NP-59 SPECT scintigraphy is valuable in the identification of unilateral cortisol secretion and guiding treatment decisions such as adrenalectomy versus conservative management. Prospective studies are needed to determine its clinical utility.

papers.title: Hypercortisolism: An Under-Recognised Pathway Linked to Multi-System Complications.
papers.abstract: The clinical understanding of hypercortisolism (HC) has evolved from a classic overt syndrome with florid Cushingoid features to a broader spectrum of disease that includes milder presentations, often referred to as mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS). This shift has lowered the threshold for screening and encouraged clinicians to consider HC even in the absence of classic physical findings, particularly in patients presenting with common features, including metabolic, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal and neuropsychiatric comorbidities. Chronic cortisol excess is associated with substantial morbidity and increased mortality through widespread effects on glucose metabolism, lipid homeostasis, cardiovascular function, blood pressure control, bone and muscle health, reproductive function, cognition and mental health. Importantly, many of these complications are frequently seen in patients with MACS, particularly in association with difficult-to-control diabetes and hypertension, emphasising the importance of earlier disease recognition. Recent data suggest that this abnormality may be more common than previously recognised, and its identification can have important implications for patient management. Emerging evidence may also help identify individuals at higher risk through relatively simple screening tests. Recognising this abnormality, particularly in patients with common chronic diseases that are difficult to control, represents a novel and clinically important concept that may lead to more targeted evaluation and management strategies. Cortisol is a hormone secreted by the adrenal gland that works in almost every organ in the body and is essential to life. Cortisol secretion increases during illness and psychological stress and then usually goes back to normal. Its secretion is regulated by signals from the brain through other hormones. Hypercortisolism (HC) is the condition in which there is excess secretion of cortisol that is no longer adequately regulated by these signals. Severe hypercortisolism affects multiple organs and systems leading to a well‐recognized but relatively rare condition call Cushing syndrome. Recent studies have suggested that hypercortisolism is not just the classic Cushing’s syndrome but could have milder presentations, often referred to as mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS). Chronic HC is associated with substantial morbidity and increased mortality through widespread effects on glucose metabolism, lipid homeostasis, cardiovascular function, blood pressure control, bone and muscle health, reproductive function, cognition, and mental health. These complications are frequently seen in patients with MACS, particularly in association with difficult‐to‐control diabetes and hypertension. In such high risk individuals simple screening tests have identified HC in over 20% of that population. The exact cause of this abnormality is unclear, but it may have a significant impact on diabetes and hypertension that is resistant to standard therapy. Fortunately, detection is relatively easy, using well‐established screening tests that can be conducted in most clinical settings. Establishing the cause of this resistance to treatment may make it possible to consider the use of specific and precise therapy that may impact outcomes. Additional studies are needed to confirm the findings so far and help us implement recently established guidelines to recognize and treat HC early.

papers.title: Mechanisms for Mineralocorticoid-Driven Age-Related Hypertension: Potential Therapeutic Role of Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists and Aldosterone Synthase Inhibitors.
papers.abstract: Hypertension prevalence rises dramatically with advancing age, is not well controlled with current therapy, and contributes substantially to cardiovascular, renal, and neurological disorders that are common in the elderly. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is a hormonal pathway with multiorgan involvement critical to controlling blood pressure. The production of the steroid hormone aldosterone and the activation state of its MR (mineralocorticoid receptor) are important clinical targets for hypertension treatment and cardiorenal disease prevention. This review summarizes studies demonstrating that aging is associated with (1) dysregulation of adrenal aldosterone production by autonomous aldosterone-producing adrenal cells and, when comorbid with obesity, by factors released from adipose tissue that promote adrenal aldosterone production; (2) increased expression of the MR due to oxidative stress-activated and inflammation-activated transcription factors; and (3) aldosterone-independent MR activation by oxidative stress-activated Rac1 (Ras-related C3 botulinum toxin substrate 1), angiotensin II signaling, and declining expression of the cortisol-inactivating enzyme 11β-HSD2 (11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2). Together, these data support the concept that elderly individuals are at high risk for mineralocorticoid-driven hypertension and associated cardiovascular, renal, and neurological disease. The review further describes the different classes of agents that inhibit this pathway, including traditional steroidal MR antagonists, newer nonsteroidal MR antagonists, and aldosterone synthase inhibitors, comparing their modes of action. The steroidal MR antagonists and nonsteroidal MR antagonists have different degrees of MR selectivity and potency, yet they all block MR activation by aldosterone, cortisol, and ligand-independent mechanisms. The aldosterone synthase inhibitors block aldosterone production in the adrenal gland and attenuate aldosterone-mediated MR effects. All 3 drug classes raise potassium proportional to the degree of renal MR inhibition. Trials are summarized showing efficacy of the new agents in reducing MR activation, aldosterone production, blood pressure, and adverse cardiorenal outcomes. Head-to-head studies in older individuals are needed to determine the relative efficacy of aldosterone synthase versus MR inhibition for blood pressure control to improve outcomes in the elderly and very old.

papers.title: Immune, metabolic, and steroidogenesis-associated profiles of miR-940, miR-375, and miR-326 in adrenocortical carcinoma.
papers.abstract: Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) has remained a highly aggressive endocrine malignancy characterized by extensive molecular heterogeneity and limited therapeutic options. In the present study, the regulatory significance of hsa-miR-940, hsa-miR-375, and hsa-miR-326, previously identified as central hubs within an ACC competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) network, was comprehensively characterized through integrative transcriptomic, prognostic, and pathway-level analyses using TCGA-ACC tumor samples. Network topology analysis, target prediction, survival modeling, pathway enrichment, protein-protein interaction analysis, therapeutic-response evaluation, and pan-cancer expression characterization were subsequently performed to investigate the biological relevance of these central miRNAs. Distinct network-topology differences were identified between tumor and normal ceRNA networks, with hsa-miR-940 demonstrating increased tumor-associated regulatory centrality, whereas hsa-miR-326 exhibited comparatively higher centrality within normal adrenal networks. Survival analyses further demonstrated that elevated expression of the combined three-miRNA signature was associated with significantly reduced overall survival in patients with ACC (HR = 3.52, p = 1.36E-03). Functional enrichment analyses revealed extensive associations with complement activation, steroidogenic regulation, mitochondrial bioenergetics, extracellular matrix remodeling, immune-associated signaling, lipid metabolism, and apoptosis-related pathways. Protein-protein interaction analysis additionally identified highly interconnected immune- and metabolism-associated hub genes, including CCL2, C3, SERPING1, PPARGC1A, and CFH, within the hsa-miR-940 regulatory network. Cross-cancer analyses further demonstrated substantial context-dependent expression heterogeneity across tumor types. The integrative findings presented in this study support the biological plausibility that hsa-miR-940, hsa-miR-375, and hsa-miR-326 may participate in coordinated regulatory programs associated with ACC progression and endocrine tumor adaptation. Insight box This study explores how three small regulatory molecules, known as microRNAs (miR-940, miR-375, and miR-326), may influence the development and progression of adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC), a rare and aggressive adrenal cancer. By analyzing large-scale gene expression data from tumor and normal adrenal tissues, important differences were identified in immune-related, metabolic, and hormone-associated biological processes linked to these microRNAs. The findings suggest that these molecules may contribute to how ACC tumors grow, adapt, and interact with their surrounding environment. This work demonstrates how integrative computational and biological analyses can help uncover potential biomarkers and future therapeutic targets in rare cancers such as ACC.

papers.title: Controller for Maintaining Hematopoietic Stem Cell Stemness: Genetic Information Transmission.
papers.abstract: Hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) has self-renewal and multilineage differentiation capacities. They sustain lifelong homeostasis and repair of damaged tissues, serving as the core cellular foundation for long-term homeostasis and regenerative repair. Maintaining HSC stemness is essential for normal hematopoiesis; this is not a static property but a dynamically regulated process that directly governs the stable operation of regular hematopoiesis. Recent studies show that HSC quiescence, self-renewal, and lineage differentiation are coordinately controlled by multiple signaling cues. Transcription factor networks, the extracellular matrix, metabolic reprogramming, and epigenetic modifications interact to form a regulatory network that governs stemness maintenance. Under physiological conditions, these factors establish stemness homeostasis; when aberrantly remodeled, they drive diseases such as leukemia and bone marrow failure. This review summarizes the factors that modulate HSC function and stemness during genetic information transmission, and discusses their biological significance. It further elaborates on the regulatory network, compares its distinct patterns in physiological versus pathological states, and explores its translational clinical value. Ultimately, this work aims to provide basic researchers with an integrated conceptual framework and to offer feasible forward-looking strategies for clinical translation.

papers.title: Ambient oxygen disrupts amino acid homeostasis and impairs human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell engraftment.
papers.abstract: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is limited not only by donor cell number and recipient conditioning, but also by loss of stem-cell fitness during collection and processing. Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells normally reside in a physiologically hypoxic marrow environment, yet routine ex vivo handling exposes them to ambient oxygen outside this niche. Although ambient oxygen exposure during ex vivo handling impairs hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) function, the metabolic basis for this effect remains incompletely defined. Using hypoxic handling as a physiologic reference, we examined whether functionally relevant consequences of ambient oxygen exposure remain modifiable in human CD34+ cells during ex vivo handling. Quantitative LC-MS profiling revealed that ambient oxygen exposure rapidly increased intracellular amino acids, including branched-chain amino acids, together with activation of nutrient-sensing pathways. This metabolic shift was associated with increased mTORC1 signaling, attenuation of lysosomal programs, and impaired primary and secondary engraftment. Complementary single-cell analyses supported a coordinated transition toward nutrient-activated states under ambient oxygen, whereas hypoxia preserved relative metabolic restraint. Transient restriction of essential amino acids or branched-chain amino acids during ex vivo handling restored lysosomal programs and improved engraftment of normoxia-handled human CD34+ cells. Pharmacologic LAT1 inhibition similarly improved engraftment. Together, these findings identify disruption of amino acid homeostasis as a previously underappreciated consequence of ambient oxygen exposure during routine ex vivo handling and demonstrate that a functionally relevant component of this injury remains modifiable after exposure to improve human HSPC engraftment.

papers.title: Epigenetic and Metabolic Changes That Drive Trained Immunity in Response to Microbes and Vaccines.
papers.abstract: Trained immunity is a form of innate immune memory in which initial exposure to microbial components or vaccines leads to long-lasting functional reprogramming of innate immune cells through epigenetic and metabolic changes. Unlike adaptive immunity, it does not rely on B or T lymphocytes and provides broad, nonspecific protection against various pathogens. This phenomenon has been observed across a range of immune cells, including monocytes, macrophages, neutrophils, NK cells and even γδ T-cells, as well as at the level of haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs). Key inducers include microbial products (e.g., β-glucan, BCG and MMR vaccines), metabolic byproducts (e.g., mevalonate and lactate) and cytokines such as IL-1β. These agents activate signalling pathways such as the Akt/mTOR/HIF-1α pathway and lead to chromatin remodelling via histone modifications such as H3K4me3 and H3K9me3. Immunometabolism plays a pivotal role, with trained cells shifting toward glycolysis, glutaminolysis and cholesterol synthesis. Lactate and fumarate further link metabolism to epigenetic remodelling. Notably, trained immunity can be protective in infectious diseases and beneficial in noninfectious contexts, such as cancer immunotherapy and autoimmune regulation. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the cellular, epigenetic and metabolic mechanisms underlying trained immunity, highlighting how innate immune cells acquire memory-like properties independent of adaptive immunity. This study also provides insights into the therapeutic potential of leveraging trained immunity for vaccine development, infection control and immunomodulation in noninfectious diseases.

papers.title: Bone Marrow Macrophage STING Signaling is a Direct Nexus Linking Marrow Adipose Expansion to NAD + Depletion and Osteogenic Decline in Skeletal Aging.
papers.abstract: Reversing the destructive remodeling of the bone marrow microenvironment during aging remains a major challenge. Here, we reveal an age-dependent dual role of bone marrow macrophage (BMM) STING signaling during skeletal aging. While BMM STING deficiency is detrimental during early bone development and maturation, it paradoxically confers protection against age-related bone loss from middle age onward. Mechanistically, accumulating bone marrow adipocytes secrete substantial soluble dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (sDPP4). This sDPP4 functions as an extracellular ligand for Toll-like receptor 4 on BMMs, thereby collaborating with endogenous mitochondrial DNA to activate STING signaling. This STING activation concurrently induces a CD38-dependent salvage synthesis pathway. Importantly, this STING-driven upregulation of CD38 not only amplifies bone marrow inflammation but also, through its ecto-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) activity, depletes the precursor nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) required for NAD + salvage synthesis, thereby impairing NMN availability and osteogenic capacity in neighboring bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. Finally, therapeutic intervention combining STING pharmacological inhibition with NMN supplementation effectively attenuated bone loss in preclinical models. Thus, we propose BMM STING signaling as a direct nexus connecting marrow adipose accumulation, innate immune inflammation, and diminished bone formation, and emphasize its targeting potential for managing the aged bone marrow microenvironment.

papers.title: Metabolic processes and microenvironmental regulation in leukemia.
papers.abstract: Leukemia, a heterogeneous group of hematologic malignancies, continues to present significant therapeutic challenges owing to persistent issues, such as relapse, drug resistance, and treatment-related toxicity. While traditional research has primarily focused on genetic drivers, there is increasing recognition of the critical roles played by the bone marrow microenvironment (BMME) and metabolic reprogramming in disease pathogenesis. This review systematically elucidates the dynamic interplay between these 2 hallmarks of leukemia. We detailed how leukemia cells rewire their metabolic networks to sustain uncontrolled proliferation, emphasizing aberrant activation of glucose metabolism and dynamic remodeling of lipid metabolism via de novo synthesis, uptake, and oxidation. Additionally, we highlighted a critical dependency on specific amino acids, such as glutamine and serine. We investigated the use of BMME to create a protective niche for leukemia cells. These include supportive functions provided by bone marrow stromal cells via direct contact and paracrine signaling, the establishment of an immunosuppressive environment characterized by T cell and natural killer cell exhaustion, an increase in regulatory populations, and the driving force of chronic inflammatory signaling. Importantly, these processes are interdependent, and a reciprocal relationship exists wherein metabolic byproducts from leukemia cells remodel the BMME while simultaneously enabling this microenvironment to dictate metabolic phenotypes in leukemia cells. Targeting the intricate axis between metabolism and the microenvironment is a promising frontier for the development of novel and effective combination therapies against leukemia.

papers.title: Elp1 is required for myeloid differentiation and brain repopulation.
papers.abstract: Haematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) transplantation-mediated replacement of microglia-the reconstitution of the central nervous system microglial niche with donor-derived myeloid cells-represents a promising strategy for brain cell therapies 1-7 . However, the cell-intrinsic molecular regulators of HSPC-derived myeloid lineage commitment in the brain have remained largely uncharacterized. This is partially because the scarcity of primary HSPCs has rendered large-scale genetic interrogation intractable. Here we explored whether ex vivo expansion of primary cultured HSPCs (cHSPCs) enables unbiased genetic interrogation of haematopoietic differentiation. We established that cHSPCs can be genetically manipulated and readily differentiate into myeloid cells and repopulate microglia niches of the brain after transplantation. Moreover, primary neonatal astrocytes contained strong signals to induce myeloid specification of cHSPCs in vitro. To identify genes that regulate glia-induced myeloid differentiation, we successfully screened around 20,000 individual genetic perturbations and characterized genes involved in the regulation of cell signalling, cell cycle, mitochondrial function and protein translation. Among these genes was elongator acetyltransferase complex subunit 1 (Elp1), which suppressed the unfolded protein response during myeloid specification and was essential for the generation but not maintenance of myeloid cells. Our work establishes a platform to investigate the molecular mechanisms of brain myeloid biology.

papers.title: Edited HSPCs rescue frataxin deficiency and inflammation-driven multisystemic pathology in Friedreich's ataxia mice.
papers.abstract: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is a multisystemic neurodegenerative disorder caused by GAA repeat expansion in intron 1 of frataxin (FXN), resulting in FXN deficiency and mitochondrial dysfunction. Current therapies do not correct the underlying genetic defect. Here, we demonstrate that ex vivo CRISPR/Cas9 excision of the GAA expansion in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) provides durable, systemic therapy for FRDA. A single infusion of gene-edited Sca1+ HSPCs, mPPL-001, into myeloablative, humanized YG8JR mice resulted in long-term engraftment of donor-derived cells across hematopoietic and FRDA-affected tissues. mPPL-001 increased FXN expression and corrected multiple key pathogenic drivers of FRDA, including mitochondrial stress, microglial and macrophage activation, and inflammatory signaling. These coordinated effects improved motor functions, preserved cerebellar architecture, mitigated cardiac pathology, and promoted survival of insulin-producing β cells in the pancreatic islets of Langerhans. Collectively, these findings establish FXN-edited autologous HSPCs as a one-time, disease-modifying therapy for FRDA and support advancement toward a first-in-human trial.

papers.title: Cells heal themselves: gene-edited hematopoietic stem cells restore frataxin deficiency in multiple organs.
papers.abstract: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is a triplet repeat expansion disorder with multisystem, progressive symptoms caused by reduced frataxin protein levels and compromised mitochondrial function. Restoration of frataxin protein is a focus of clinical trials involving adeno-associated viral vectors, but substantial barriers exist because of the immune response they elicit. In this issue of the JCI, Sivakumar et al. harnessed CRISPR/Cas9 editing of endogenous hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) to excise the frataxin gene (FXN) repeat expansion ex vivo, followed by autologous transplantation. A single, systemic infusion of corrected HSPCs resulted in long-term engraftment and sustained multiorgan benefit in a humanized mouse model of FRDA. This improvement in brain, cardiac, and pancreatic symptoms, mediated by myeloid progeny of the engrafted stem cells, provides strong support for the potential effectiveness of this approach in humans and bypasses the need to correct the FXN deficiency in the affected tissue and cells directly.

papers.title: Lentiviral gene therapy corrects the metabolic and immune abnormalities in purine nucleoside phosphorylase-deficient mice.
papers.abstract: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency impairs purine metabolism leading to severe T cell defects, which can be corrected by allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) transplant, however the associated complications are significant. Therefore, autologous gene therapy is an attractive alternative treatment option. Here, we present a third-generation self-inactivating lentiviral vector expressing the human PNP gene under the control of the elongation factor-1 alpha short promoter (LVV-EFS-PNP), which was delivered ex vivo to HSCs and was tested for its ability to correct the abnormalities in PNP-deficient (Pnp-/-) mice. The LVV-EFS-PNP vector demonstrated effective gene transfer, without jeopardizing hematopoietic colony formation in vitro. In vivo, Pnp-/- mice transplanted with Pnp-/- lineage-negative cells transduced with LVV-EFS-PNP achieved sustained correction of the immune and metabolic abnormalities, including restoration of thymocyte development, T cell proliferation, and T cell-dependent and independent antibody responses. Importantly, genotoxicity assessments demonstrated that LVV-EFS-PNP had a low transformation potential and did not significantly dysregulate gene expression signature linked to vector-induced transformation, similar to other clinically used lentiviruses. These results demonstrate the safety and efficacy of gene therapy using LVV-EFS-PNP in a pre-clinical model of PNP deficiency, providing evidence for a promising new treatment strategy.

papers.title: GPX4-Mediated Inhibition of Ferroptosis by Sodium Selenite Ameliorates Bone Metabolic Disorders in Ovariectomized Mice.
papers.abstract: Postmenopausal osteoporosis (PMOP) and its associated fracture complications have emerged as pressing public health challenges due to rapidly accelerating global population ageing. The functional decline of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) under elevated oxidative stress is a recognised pathogenic cornerstone of PMOP, positioning redox imbalance as a critical therapeutic node. Here, we establish that sodium selenite (Na 2 SeO 3 ) robustly counters oxidative insults in BMSCs, thereby restoring and enhancing their osteogenic lineage commitment. Furthermore, RNA sequencing analysis indicated that ferroptosis may be mechanistically associated with the underlying cellular responses. Ferroptosis is critically mediated by glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a selenoenzyme that functions as its principal enzymatic suppressor. Silencing GPX4 in BMSCs markedly reduced their osteogenic capacity and simultaneously upregulated ferroptotic protein expression. Notably, this impairment was not reversed by Na 2 SeO 3 administration under conditions of GPX4 suppression. These findings suggest that Na 2 SeO 3 enhances osteogenic differentiation primarily by upregulating GPX4 expression, thereby inhibiting ferroptosis. Thus, we have established Na 2 SeO 3 as a potential therapeutic strategy for PMOP by identifying a previously unrecognised molecular axis through which selenium regulates bone metabolic homeostasis.

citations.quote: Transcription factor networks, the extracellular matrix, metabolic reprogramming, and epigenetic modifications interact to form a regulatory network that governs stemness maintenance.

Quantitative LC-MS profiling revealed that ambient oxygen exposure rapidly increased intracellular amino acids, including branched-chain amino acids, together with activation of nutrient-sensing pathways.
Complementary single-cell analyses supported a coordinated transition toward nutrient-activated states under ambient oxygen, whereas hypoxia preserved relative metabolic restraint.
Immunometabolism plays a pivotal role, with trained cells shifting toward glycolysis, glutaminolysis and cholesterol synthesis. Lactate and fumarate further link metabolism to epigenetic remodelling.

We detailed how leukemia cells rewire their metabolic networks to sustain uncontrolled proliferation, emphasizing aberrant activation of glucose metabolism and dynamic remodeling of lipid metabolism via de novo synthesis, uptake, and oxidation. Additionally, we highlighted a critical dependency on specific amino acids, such as glutamine and serine.

Importantly, these processes are interdependent, and a reciprocal relationship exists wherein metabolic byproducts from leukemia cells remodel the BMME while simultaneously enabling this microenvironment to dictate metabolic phenotypes in leukemia cells.

Mechanistically, accumulating bone marrow adipocytes secrete substantial soluble dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (sDPP4). This sDPP4 functions as an extracellular ligand for Toll-like receptor 4 on BMMs, thereby collaborating with endogenous mitochondrial DNA to activate STING signaling.

Importantly, this STING-driven upregulation of CD38 not only amplifies bone marrow inflammation but also, through its ecto-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) activity, depletes the precursor nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) required for NAD + salvage synthesis, thereby impairing NMN availability and osteogenic capacity in neighboring bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells.
These findings suggest that Na 2 SeO 3 enhances osteogenic differentiation primarily by upregulating GPX4 expression, thereby inhibiting ferroptosis.
Transcription factor networks, the extracellular matrix, metabolic reprogramming, and epigenetic modifications interact to form a regulatory network that governs stemness maintenance.

Brain.description: Patients with persistent spinal pain syndrome type 2 underwent [18F]FDG PET/CT brain imaging [9], which showed a distributed pattern of altered glucose metabolism involving frontal, temporal and cerebellar regions [9]. Neurons also draw on lactate, as histone lactylation, an epigenetic modification using lactate as a substrate, becomes prominent post-SCI due to increased neuronal lactate levels [2], and the downstream target secretogranin II was found to exert negative feedback on glycolytic metabolism and lactylation [2]. Mitochondria are central to neuronal energy supply: in dendrites, local, dynamic regulation of ATP levels [5] depends on their positioning, and insulin did not alter mitochondrial membrane potential at rest, but significantly limited activity-evoked mitochondrial depolarization induced by neuronal stimulation [1]. Mitochondrial coenzyme A also matters, since impairment of the mitochondrial CoA pool can weaken a CoA-dependent redox defense without requiring a measurable whole-cell CoA deficit [3]. Insulin acts as a hormonal regulator in the hippocampus, where insulin robustly increased Akt phosphorylation in dentate gyrus tissue when insulin degradation was inhibited, and this response was attenuated by genetic deletion of the insulin receptor in DGCs [1]. Its effects on neuronal energetics are linked to calcium handling rather than ATP, as insulin limited cytosolic Ca 2+ accumulation through an insulin receptor-dependent mechanism [1], while this change had no measurable impact on cytosolic ATP availability [1]. Lipid droplets further influence glial bioenergetics, as oleic acid-induced LDs preserved mitochondrial membrane potential and increased ATP production in BV2 microglia under glucose deprivation and oAβ exposure [6].

papers.title: Insulin regulates activity-dependent mitochondrial depolarization and calcium dynamics in dentate granule cells.
papers.abstract: Systemic insulin resistance is associated with reduced hippocampal energy metabolism and cognitive impairment both in humans and animal models. However, whether insulin rapidly regulates neuronal metabolic stability during activity remains unclear. Here, we examined insulin signaling and queried the corresponding mitochondrial responses in dentate granule cells (DGCs) of adult female mice. This layer of excitatory neurons within the hippocampus plays an essential role in learning and memory. Insulin robustly increased Akt phosphorylation in dentate gyrus tissue when insulin degradation was inhibited, and this response was attenuated by genetic deletion of the insulin receptor in DGCs, consistent with cell-autonomous signaling. We found that insulin did not alter mitochondrial membrane potential at rest, but significantly limited activity-evoked mitochondrial depolarization induced by neuronal stimulation. However, this change had no measurable impact on cytosolic ATP availability and was instead associated with Ca 2+ dynamics. Removing Ca 2+ ions from the extracellular solution, or disrupting mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake, prevented insulin modulation of the mitochondrial membrane potential. Furthermore, insulin limited cytosolic Ca 2+ accumulation through an insulin receptor-dependent mechanism that persisted despite Akt inhibition. Insulin also accelerated the clearance of mitochondrial Ca 2+ transients in active neurons, which occurred without changes in either neuronal excitability or pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphorylation. Together, these findings identify endogenous insulin degradation as a key regulator of hippocampal insulin signaling, and reveal a previously unrecognized interaction between insulin and Ca 2+ signaling in stimulated DGCs. This work also establishes a direct link between central insulin signaling and the maintenance of mitochondrial electrochemical homeostasis in the adult brain. Significance Statement Insulin signaling is known to influence synaptic plasticity, yet its direct effects on neuronal metabolism remain poorly defined. Here, we show that endogenous insulin degradation limits insulin signaling in adult hippocampal tissue. This finding suggests that inhibitors of the insulin degrading enzyme may hold the potential to improve the efficacy of insulin-based interventions aimed at improving learning and memory. Acute insulin signaling does not modify neuronal excitability, or cytosolic ATP availability. Instead, it stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential and reduces calcium accumulation in active dentate granule cells. By identifying an insulin-dependent mechanism that regulates the electrochemical homeostasis of mitochondria in active neurons, this work provides insight into how brain insulin resistance may contribute to cognitive dysfunction in aging and neurometabolic disorders.

papers.title: Glis1 regulates metabolic programming by promoting H3K18 lactylation to alleviate neuronal senescence following spinal cord injury.
papers.abstract: Neuronal senescence is a significant factor impeding spinal cord injury (SCI) repair. Research indicates that Glis1, a Kruppel-like zinc finger transcription factor, is pivotal in reprogramming senescent cells and enhancing genomic stability via lactylation. Histone lactylation, an epigenetic modification using lactate as a substrate, becomes prominent post-SCI due to increased neuronal lactate levels. However, the mechanisms linking neuronal senescence and histone lactylation following SCI remain poorly understood. This study elucidates the roles of Glis1, H3K18 lactylation, and neuronal senescence through comprehensive in vivo and in vitro investigations. The findings reveal a post-SCI rise in neuronal lactate levels, accompanied by cellular senescence. Furthermore, upregulation of Glis1 attenuates senescence and promotes histone lactylation. The downstream target secretogranin II (SCG2), identified via ChIP-seq and RNA-seq, was found to exert negative feedback on glycolytic metabolism and lactylation, thereby suppressing neuronal senescence. These results unveil a novel regulatory mechanism of Glis1 in neuronal senescence following SCI through the p300/H3K18la/SCG2 axis, offering a new therapeutic target for spinal cord repair.

papers.title: Compartmentalized coenzyme A and ferroptosis vulnerability in PKAN and CoPAN.
papers.abstract: Ferroptotic vulnerability may arise from the failure of a local antioxidant defense even when whole-cell metabolite abundance appears preserved. Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) and COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration (CoPAN), two forms of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation caused by defects in coenzyme A (CoA) synthesis, provide a genetically defined setting for examining this possibility. We propose that impairment of the mitochondrial CoA pool can weaken a CoA-dependent redox defense without requiring a measurable whole-cell CoA deficit, while regional iron burden and oxidative demand lower the threshold for ferroptotic death. This model could reconcile apparently preserved bulk CoA with selective neuronal vulnerability. It is testable, remains to be validated directly in patient-derived models, and distinguishes mitochondrial CoA availability from total cellular CoA as the disease-relevant variable.

papers.title: A pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts hippocampal synapse maturation and homeostasis.
papers.abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are critical for activity-dependent synapse maturation and circuit development. De novo missense mutations in AMPAR subunits are linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet how these variants disrupt neuronal function remains unclear. Here, we examine a recurrent pathogenic mutation in the GluA1 subunit (GRIA1 p.A636T) that alters AMPAR function and is associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using GluA1 A636T knock-in mice of either sex, we identify impairments in hippocampal-dependent learning and working memory. Quantitative proteomics combined with bulk RNA-seq revealed age-dependent molecular remodeling in mutant hippocampus. Synaptic protein alterations were present in juvenile and adult mice, whereas a pronounced upregulation of mitochondrial and glial-associated proteins emerged more strongly in adulthood. Transcriptomic analyses showed partial concordance and highlighted divergence between RNA and protein regulation. Consistent with these molecular changes, there were increases in markers of oxidative stress in juvenile and adult mutant animals, whereas altered mitochondria morphology emerged selectively in adult mutants. Electrophysiological recordings demonstrated reduced basal excitatory transmission, persistence of silent synapses in adulthood and exaggerated activity-dependent synaptic potentiation, which were associated with reduced spine size consistent with impaired synapse maturation. Together, these findings indicate that a pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts developmental synapse maturation with secondary metabolic adaptations emerging over time. Significance Statement Mutations in genes encoding AMPA-type glutamate receptors are increasingly linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism and intellectual disability. However, how these mutations disrupt brain function and development remains poorly understood. Using a mouse model carrying a recurrent disease-associated mutation in the GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit, we show that the presence of this mutant subunit protein impairs the normal maturation of excitatory synapses in the hippocampus. Mutant mice retain immature "silent" synapses into adulthood, exhibit abnormal synaptic plasticity, reduced spine size, and deficits in learning and memory. Molecular analyses reveal age-dependent remodeling of synaptic and mitochondrial proteins, suggesting that metabolic changes arise secondary to disrupted synapse development. These findings clarify how pathogenic AMPA receptor variants alter brain function over time.

papers.title: Drosophila dendrites are resilient to adult-onset deficits in mitochondrial dynamics.
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial transport, fusion, and fission are necessary for neuronal development, but the role of mitochondrial dynamics in neuronal maintenance remains unclear. In this work, we employed functional in vivo imaging of neurons in the Drosophila visual system, "horizontal system" (HS) cells, to determine how adult-onset deficits in mitochondrial dynamics affect mitochondrial localization, local regulation of ATP, and dendrite maintenance. In mature HS neurons, inhibition of mitochondrial transport or fusion depleted mitochondria from the dendrite over time but, surprisingly, had no effect on dendrite morphology. Moreover, adult-restricted mitochondrial mislocalization affected neither visual stimulus-driven dendritic calcium responses nor local, dynamic regulation of ATP levels. In contrast, when induced during development, the same perturbations caused mitochondrial mislocalization, loss of dendrite complexity, abrogation of stimulus-locked calcium responses and ATP fluctuations, and age-dependent dendrite degeneration. Thus, although mitochondrial dynamics are necessary during neuronal development, mature dendrites are capable of maintaining form and function in vivo upon mitochondrial depletion.

papers.title: Exercise promotes lipophagy and mitigates cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease through downregulating microglial TMEM9.
papers.abstract: Autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction contributes to lipid droplet (LD) accumulation, which drives pathological progression in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Exercise is reported to restore autophagy-lysosomal function and attenuate cognitive impairment in AD, but its regulation of LD deposition remains unknown. 5×FAD transgenic mice underwent a three-month exercise intervention. Cognitive and emotional behaviors were assessed using the Morris water maze, novel object recognition, and open field test. LD deposition was evaluated by oil red O and BODIPY staining. Proteomic sequencing was performed to identify proteins affected by exercise. Pathological changes were examined by immunofluorescence, western blotting, and transmission electron microscopy. Intracerebroventricular injection of AAV was used to overexpress or knock down microglial TMEM9 to investigate the mechanisms by which physical exercise affects behavior and pathology in AD. In vitro, BV2 cells were cultured and incubated with oligomeric amyloid-β (oAβ), with or without oleic acid to induce LD formation. Chloroquine and rapamycin, which regulate autophagy-lysosomal function, were used to examine the effects of LDs on mitochondrial integrity under glucose deprivation conditions. Lentiviral or plasmid transfection was used to explore the key role of TMEM9 in regulating lipophagy, and the interaction between TMEM9 and ATP6AP1 was detected by co-immunoprecipitation. Clinically, plasma TMEM9 and ATP6AP1 levels in AD patients were measured by ELISA, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to evaluate diagnostic performance. Exercise mitigated cerebral LD deposition through enhanced lipophagy, preserving mitochondrial integrity and attenuating cognitive decline. Mechanistically, exercise suppressed microglial TMEM9 expression, restoring LD degradation. Tmem9 downregulation facilitated LKB1 lysosomal translocation, activating AMPK signaling. In vitro, oleic acid-induced LDs preserved mitochondrial membrane potential and increased ATP production in BV2 microglia under glucose deprivation and oAβ exposure. Tmem9 overexpression exacerbated lipophagy impairment and mitochondrial dysfunction, whereas Tmem9 knockdown enhanced lipophagy and cytoprotection. Aβ clearance was negatively regulated by TMEM9. Clinically, AD patients exhibited characteristic Aβ deposition and glucose hypometabolism, with plasma TMEM9 levels strongly correlating with p-tau217 progression. Plasma TMEM9 and the TMEM9/ATP6AP1 ratio emerged as potential AD diagnostic biomarkers (AUC=0.791 and 0.853, respectively). These findings establish exercise-induced TMEM9 inhibition as a novel therapeutic strategy targeting lipidostasis to combat AD progression.

papers.title: Central relaxin-3/RXFP3 signaling potently drives orexigenic behaviors and attenuates cisplatin-induced anorexia and body weight loss.
papers.abstract: The relaxin-3 neuropeptide system promotes energy balance by increasing feeding behavior. Here, we investigate the behavioral mechanisms mediating the orexigenic effects of relaxin-3 and the therapeutic potential of relaxin-3 to combat metabolic disorders. We show that central and peripheral administration of relaxin-3 increases high-fat diet intake by increasing meal size in obese rats. Furthermore, we deleted relaxin family peptide receptor 3 (RXFP3) neuronally using RXFP3 fl/fl hSyn-Cre+ mice and show that neuronal RXFP3 is required for the orexigenic effects of relaxin-3. In addition, central relaxin-3 administration augmented food motivation for sucrose and hyperphagia in a binge-like eating model. We then evaluated the potential of relaxin-3 to drive food intake in rats receiving acute maladaptive chemotherapy. Pretreatment of central relaxin-3 attenuated cisplatin chemotherapy-induced anorexia and body weight loss. These findings characterize the behavioral mechanisms by which the relaxin-3 system drives feeding behaviors and highlight its therapeutic potential for metabolic wasting disorders.

papers.title: Neuroepigenetic programming by the maternal environment: part A-epigenome-wide DNA methylation profile in the offspring's olfactory bulb following preconceptional weight loss in mice.
papers.abstract: Experimental models and epidemiological data suggest that the maternal nutritional environment during gestation plays important roles in brain development with consequences on cognitive health. Epigenetic marks, such as methylation and histone modifications, are likely to be involved in this programming, but little addressed the impact of maternal metabolism at the preconceptional period. In mice, we recently demonstrated lasting effects of a maternal preconceptional weight loss on metabolic outcomes and behaviors related to food intake in the male offspring, exhibiting a reduction in olfactory sensitivity, along with a lack of fasting-induced olfactory-based motivation. To evaluate if this effect was driven by epigenetic modifications in the olfactory bulb, we profiled brain DNA methylation, a fundamental process in mediating the relation between early life environment and long-term behaviors in mice according to the maternal status. Using oxidative reduced representation bisulfite sequencing to specifically target 5mC in mice exposed to preconceptional weight loss versus controls, we identified 11,055 differentially methylated cytosines and 150 differential methylated regions (DMRs) located in 111 genes in the olfactory bulb, a main region involved in odor processing and integration. Among the cytosines differentially methylated, half were hypermethylated. Methylation remodeling according to the maternal group preferentially affected noncoding intragenic regions, distal regulatory elements, and open sea CpGs, while promoter CpG islands remain relatively resistant to modification in DNA methylome. The functional annotation of DMRs pointed out genes related to histones kinases, energy signaling, synaptic function, and cellular differentiation, suggesting that targeted methylation changes may simultaneously influence epigenetic regulation, metabolism, and neurobiology. Thanks to a single-base analysis of differential methylated CpGs, we present novel evidence that the maternal dietary environment prior to conception exerts maternally-driven epigenetic effects, markedly altering 5-methylcytosine patterns in the adult offspring brain. This long-lasting remodeling of the offspring's olfactory bulb methylome may underlie the described alterations in olfactory-driven behaviors of offspring born to WL mother.

papers.title: The central neurometabolic fingerprint of persistent spinal pain syndrome type 2: A prospective [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT neuroimaging study.
papers.abstract: Persistent spinal pain syndrome type 2 (PSPS-T2) is a disabling pain condition that persists after spinal surgery. While spinal cord stimulation (SCS) offers symptomatic relief, objective biomarkers to guide diagnosis and treatment are lacking. In this prospective cohort study, fifteen PSPS-T2 patients underwent dedicated [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT brain imaging prior to SCS implantation. Group-level metabolic patterns were compared to matched healthy controls using statistical parametric mapping. Regional metabolism was correlated with pain scores and neurotransmitter PET atlases using JuSpace. PSPS-T2 patients exhibited a distributed pattern of altered glucose metabolism involving frontal, temporal and cerebellar regions. Significant hypermetabolism was observed in the left temporal pole, right inferior temporal gyrus, and bilateral cerebellar lobule VIII, whereas hypometabolism was identified in the right fusiform gyrus, right superior frontal gyrus, left gyrus rectus, and cerebellar vermis. Moreover, there were significant spatial correlations between these metabolic changes and serotonergic and glutamatergic neurotransmitter systems. Furthermore, higher baseline pain was associated with increased frontal and temporal metabolism, whereas post-intervention pain was negatively correlated with metabolism in the temporal pole. These findings suggests that PSPS-T2 is characterized by network-level alterations in brain regions integrating sensory, emotional, and cognitive aspects of pain, with a neurochemical signature implicating serotonergic and glutamatergic systems. Although preliminary, this works provides evidence for a disease-relevant neurometabolic profile and highlights the potential of [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT for investigating central pain mechanisms. Future research should focus on validating this marker in larger populations.

papers.title: DA-S 2 RL: Disease-aware shared-specific representation learning for heterogeneous image-EHR Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.
papers.abstract: Combining electronic health records (EHR) with medical images is important for improving the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, neuroimages and EHR differ greatly in semantic content and data distribution. Neuroimages mainly reflect brain structure and metabolic abnormalities, while EHR records clinical symptoms and behavioral changes. Directly fusing these heterogeneous modalities may mix shared disease information with modality-specific diagnostic cues, resulting in redundant and ambiguous representations. To address this problem, we propose DA-S 2 RL, a disease-aware shared-specific multimodal representation learning framework for AD diagnosis. DA-S 2 RL organizes heterogeneous image and EHR features into disease-related shared semantics and modality-specific diagnostic residuals. The core of DA-S 2 RL is the shared-specific cross-modal coding (SCC) module. It strengthens cross-modal semantic consistency, suppresses redundant correlations, and enables mutual refinement between shared semantics and diagnostic residuals. Before SCC, image features are integrated into a compact image representation, and EHR features are encoded into the same feature space. Experiments on ADNI and NACC demonstrate that explicitly organizing heterogeneous image-EHR representations into shared disease semantics and modality-specific residuals improves multimodal diagnostic learning under different image-EHR settings.
