Kidney.description: Chronic kidney disease and diabetes share features such as insulin resistance [7], and over 10 years 15.8% of CKD participants developed diabetes compared with 11.0% of non-CKD participants [7]. Metabolic intermediates also shape renal function: elevated levels of S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) in patients with diabetes are closely associated with renal dysfunction [3], and inhibition of SAH hydrolase (SAHH) increases SAH levels, promotes apoptosis, and exacerbates streptozotocin-induced diabetic nephropathy [3]. Through epigenetic control, SAHH inhibition downregulated DNA methyltransferase 3b (DNMT3b) expression, leading to hypomethylation of the Moap1 promoter and subsequent upregulation of Moap1 transcription [3]. Persistent renal effects of hyperglycemia are described as an exposure-history-dependent cellular phenotype [6]. The kidney's hormonal environment includes local renin-angiotensin components, as adipose tissues surrounding blood vessels and kidneys can locally generate components of the renin-angiotensin system [2]. Incretin-based agents act on the kidney directly, with natriuresis through inhibition of the sodium-hydrogen exchanger (NHE)-3 [1], and indirectly through weight loss, blood pressure lowering, and improvement of heart failure [1]. Finally, the neuropeptide orexin-A is relevant because its receptors are found in a variety of tissues, such as the brain and kidney [9], and its serum level showed a significant decrease in patients with CKD [9].

papers.title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists and Multi-hormone Receptor Modulators for Kidney Protection in Nondiabetic Kidney Disease.
papers.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), together with newer multi-hormone receptor modulators that target glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), glucagon and amylin, have emerged as promising therapies for chronic kidney disease. This review examines the mechanisms through which these agents may protect the kidney and summarizes the emerging clinical evidence in populations without diabetes. Kidney protection appears to arise through complementary direct and indirect routes. Direct effects include natriuresis through inhibition of the sodium-hydrogen exchanger (NHE)-3, modulation of glomerular hemodynamics through effects on afferent arteriolar tone and vasoconstrictor pathways, and attenuation of renal inflammation; mechanisms that are largely independent of glucose lowering. Indirect mechanisms include reductions in the metabolic, hemodynamic and cardiac burden on the kidney through weight loss, blood pressure lowering, and improvement of heart failure. Beyond selective GLP-1R-agonism, the added hormonal components of multi-hormone receptor modulators engage distinct physiological pathways whose interactions may be additive, synergistic or counteracting, but remain incompletely understood. The efficacy of GLP-1 RAs and multi-hormone receptor modulators in people without diabetes is currently supported by results from secondary kidney endpoints in phase-3 obesity and cardiovascular outcome trials, including reductions in albuminuria and preservation of estimated glomerular filtration rate. Several dedicated outcome studies of GLP-1 RAs and multi-hormone receptor modulators are now underway and will determine whether these therapies become a new pillar of care in nondiabetic kidney disease.

papers.title: Renin-Angiotensin System Activation Drives Early Cardiorenal Dysfunction in Normotensive Prediabetes.
papers.abstract: Prediabetes is increasingly recognised as a stage at which cardiovascular and renal dysfunction begin to develop despite the absence of overt metabolic disease. The mechanisms underlying these early alterations remain poorly understood. Because adipose tissues surrounding blood vessels and kidneys can locally generate components of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS), we hypothesised that subclinical RAS activation contributes to early cardiorenal dysfunction in prediabetes. Using a pre-established normotensive, non-obese rat model of prediabetes induced by 12 weeks of mild hypercaloric feeding, we examined the impact of systemic angiotensin II (AngII) elevation and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition on cardio-, cerebro- and renovascular function by invasive hemodynamics, ex vivo pressure myography, and ex vivo renal perfusion experiments, respectively. Prediabetic rats exhibited impaired parasympathetic baroreceptor sensitivity and altered renovascular endothelium-dependent vasodilation despite preserved blood pressure and cardiac function. Systemic AngII infusion further exacerbated autonomic and renovascular dysfunction. In contrast, treatment with a non-hypotensive dose of the ACE inhibitor captopril restored baroreceptor sensitivity, improved renovascular endothelial function, reduced brainstem inflammation, and attenuated renal tubular fibrosis. Examination of perivascular and perirenal adipose tissues revealed significantly higher protein concentration of ACE1 in prediabetic rats compared to controls. These findings are consistent with an early activation of RAS contributing to subclinical cardiovascular and renal dysfunction during prediabetes independently of hypertension. Targeting RAS signalling at this early stage may therefore represent a strategy to limit progression of cardiorenal complications along the continuum from prediabetes to diabetes.

papers.title: The Mechanism of S-adenosylhomocysteine Hydrolase in Regulating Podocyte Apoptosis and Diabetic Nephropathy via Moap1.
papers.abstract: Elevated levels of S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) in patients with diabetes are closely associated with renal dysfunction. Inhibition of SAH hydrolase (SAHH) increases SAH levels, promotes apoptosis, and exacerbates streptozotocin (STZ)-induced diabetic nephropathy. However, the precise mechanism by which SAHH inhibition induces podocyte apoptosis remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate how SAHH inhibition specifically induces podocyte apoptosis and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. We established an STZ-induced podocyte-specific SAHH knockout mouse model and an in vitro model of high-glucose-treated podocytes. Our results showed that podocyte-specific SAHH deletion significantly exacerbated streptozotocin (STZ)-induced diabetic kidney injury. SAHH inhibition significantly upregulated the expression of modulator of apoptosis 1 (Moap1), which in turn promoted podocyte apoptosis through activation of the pro-apoptotic protein BAX. Knockdown of Moap1 partially reversed this apoptotic phenotype. Mechanistically, SAHH inhibition downregulated DNA methyltransferase 3b (DNMT3b) expression, leading to hypomethylation of the Moap1 promoter and subsequent upregulation of Moap1 transcription. ChIP-qPCR and dual-luciferase reporter assays confirmed that DNMT3b directly bound to the region of the Moap1 promoter and regulated its transcriptional activity. Restoration of DNMT3b expression reversed Moap1 upregulation and partially rescued the apoptotic phenotype induced by SAHH inhibition. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that SAHH inhibition promotes podocyte apoptosis by upregulating Moap1 expression through a DNMT3b-dependent hypomethylation mechanism, which in turn activates BAX. This study provides novel potential therapeutic targets for diabetic nephropathy with elevated SAH levels.

papers.title: Chronic kidney disease as a systemic disorder: filtration phenotypes, inflammation and cardiovascular risk in the cardio-kidney metabolic era.
papers.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is increasingly recognized as a systemic disorder driven by metabolic dysfunction, vascular injury, inflammation, and emerging filtration phenotypes. In the cardio-kidney-metabolic (CKM) era, renal biomarkers such as estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and albuminuria provide essential insight into early metabolic-renal stress and cardiovascular (CV) vulnerability. This narrative review synthesizes contemporary evidence linking CKD to cardiovascular disease (CVD), emphasizing the multidimensional interactions among filtration impairment, glomerular barrier injury, metabolic dysfunction, and inflammatory pathways. Novel filtration phenotypes defined through creatinine-cystatin C (Cr-CysC) eGFR (including glomerular hyperfiltration and selective hypofiltration) highlight the limitations of classical staging and underscore the need for refined risk assessment. The integration of kidney markers into the AHA PREVENT equations represents a major advance, enabling absolute CVD risk estimation across the CKM continuum. Simulation-based analyses of 5000 virtual patients visually demonstrate the nonlinear and synergistic effects of eGFR, albuminuria, age, hypertension, diabetes, and lipid abnormalities on CV risk. Furthermore, disease-modifying therapies such as SGLT2 inhibitors, finerenone, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and anti-obesity interventions provide multisystem benefits that align with CKM pathophysiology. Together, these developments support a unified, continuum-based approach to CKD detection, risk stratification, and prevention, positioning CKD as a central driver of long-term CV outcomes.

papers.title: Endothelial dysfunction and long-term survival in cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome stages 0-3: An EASIX-based national cohort study.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo assess the association of the endothelial activation and stress index (EASIX) with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in adults at cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome stages 0-3.MethodsThis retrospective analysis of a population-based cohort included 10,885 adults aged ≥30 years from NHANES 1999-2018, with mortality follow-up through 2019. EASIX was calculated as lactate dehydrogenase × creatinine/platelet count. Survey-weighted Cox models, restricted cubic splines, subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses evaluated mortality associations.ResultsDuring a median follow-up of 97 months, 1,122 participants died, including 295 from cardiovascular causes. Each one-unit increase in EASIX was associated with all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 1.41, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.24-1.61) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.13-1.49). There was no evidence of non-linearity for all-cause mortality (P = 0.466), while the cardiovascular association was non-linear (P = 0.008). Associations persisted after additional lifestyle adjustment. CKM-stage interactions were not significant in the full cohort.ConclusionsHigher EASIX was associated with greater all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in CKM stages 0-3. Its potential role in clinical risk assessment warrants further validation.

papers.title: Metabolic memory in diabetic complications: evidence for persistent cellular states and limits of therapeutic reversal.
papers.abstract: Metabolic memory is defined here as an exposure-history-dependent cellular phenotype that persists beyond immediate carry-over after verified withdrawal of the initiating exposure, principally high glucose and is accompanied by a specified functional impairment or an altered response to the same defined secondary stimulus. This operational definition separates cellular memory from clinical legacy effects, continuing local stimulation and residual structural injury. We critically examine evidence from longitudinal clinical studies, human biospecimens, animal models and controlled cell experiments, distinguishing molecular persistence, measured signaling activity, causal maintenance and treatment-free durability. DCCT/EDIC and UKPDS establish lasting benefits of earlier glycemic management but do not independently identify cellular memory as the mechanism. Experimental evidence supports selected endothelial redox circuits, epigenetic regulation and hematopoietic progenitor training; human causal evidence is substantially more limited. Persistent chromatin marks do not necessarily imply continuously active signaling, and latent priming may become apparent only after rechallenge. In kidney, cardiovascular, retinal and wound disease, candidate cellular memory coexists with hypoxic or inflammatory niches and structural loss. Pancreatic β-cell plasticity is considered a comparative endocrine model rather than an established complication-memory circuit. The proposed interactions among epigenetic, mitochondrial, metabolic and inflammatory mechanisms remain a framework supported by selected local feedback loops, not a universally demonstrated network. Therapeutic evidence is organized into prevention, modification or suppression of established abnormalities, and sustained molecular and functional recovery after treatment cessation after intervention withdrawal. The latter remains unestablished in patients for the mechanisms reviewed. Early glycemic and multifactorial management remains essential, while mechanistic translation requires explicit recovery, perturbation and post-treatment follow-up designs.

papers.title: Incident Type 2 Diabetes in Individuals With CKD: The REGARDS Study.
papers.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and diabetes are comorbid metabolic diseases that share common factors such as insulin resistance. Few studies have examined the association between CKD and incident diabetes, with limited consensus and associated risk factors. We conducted an analysis of participants in the Reasons for Geographic and Racial Differences in stroke study to investigate incident diabetes among participants with CKD compared with non-CKD participants. A prospective cohort study. Total of 7,511 participants who completed 10 years of follow-up were included in the analysis, of whom 994 had CKD (an estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min/1.73m 2 or albumin-to-creatinine ratio >30mg/g) at baseline. CKD. Incident diabetes. Logistic regression analysis was performed to estimate the odds of incident diabetes among CKD participants, with odds ratio (OR) and 95% CI. Risk factors for incident diabetes among CKD participants were also examined. After 10 years of follow-up, 11.0% (717) of non-CKD participants and 15.8% (157) of CKD participants developed diabetes. Incident diabetes was higher among CKD participants than in non-CKD participants using creatinine-based equations, which was not seen when using a creatinine-based and cystatin C-based equation for CKD. Several risk factors such as race, prediabetes, age, body mass index, hypertension, current smoking, and exercise ≥ 4 times/week increased the odds of incident diabetes, whereas current alcohol use had a lower risk of incident diabetes. Prediabetes had the highest risk of incident diabetes (OR = 4.94, 95% Cl: 4.22-5.78; P < 0.01). Attrition bias, limited generalizability, and limited diagnostic classification. The association between CKD and incident diabetes depends on how CKD is defined. These findings highlight the need for future studies to explore how renal function is assessed when determining adverse outcomes related to CKD. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and diabetes are common chronic diseases that might share similar causes for their development. Our study looked at 7,511 participants in the Reasons for Geographic and Racial Differences in Stroke study to look at the odds of developing diabetes in participants with CKD versus those without CKD within 10 years. The odds of developing diabetes changed based on how CKD was calculated. Prediabetes was the strongest risk factor, but others included body mass index, hypertension, current smoking, and exercise. Interestingly, individuals who drink alcohol had a lower odds of developing diabetes. Our study suggests that how CKD is defined plays a big role in determining future outcomes related to CKD.

papers.title: Longitudinal sleep duration trajectories and their association with cardio-renal-metabolic multimorbidity risk in postmenopausal women: evidence from the CHARLS study.
papers.abstract: To investigate the association between longitudinal sleep duration trajectories and the risk of cardio-renal-metabolic multimorbidity (CRMM) in a population of postmenopausal women. A total of 2,859 postmenopausal women from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) were included, with 4 repeated measurements of night sleep duration collected from 2011 to 2018. Group-based trajectory modeling was adopted to identify distinct sleep duration trajectory patterns. Multivariable logistic regression was used to examine the associations between sleep trajectories and incident CRMM ascertained between 2018 and 2020. Subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses were further conducted to validate the robustness of the findings. Three sleep duration trajectory patterns were identified: normal-stable (33.9% of the cohort), normal-fluctuating decline (52.0%), and short-rapid decline (14.1%). During a median follow-up of 2 years, the primary outcome (incident CRMM) occurred in 108 participants (3.8%). Compared with normal-stable group, those in normal-fluctuating decline and short-rapid decline groups had an increased risk of CRMM (ORs of 2.30 [95%CI, 1.35-3.91] and 3.75 [95%CI, 1.99-7.07], respectively) after adjustment for multiple covariates. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these associations, which were independent of key baseline characteristics and missing data. In postmenopausal women, short and declining sleep duration trajectories are strong, independent risk factors for CRMM. Public health and clinical interventions should prioritize maintaining stable, adequate sleep to mitigate multimorbidity risk in this population.

papers.title: Dysregulation of Orexin-A and Implications for Renal Function Assessment in Chronic Kidney Disease.
papers.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a long-standing kidney condition in which the kidneys are gradually damaged. It usually has multiple symptoms and is often accompanied by complications, such as hormonal imbalances, high blood pressure, anemia, and sleep disorders. Orexin, occasionally mentioned as hypocretin, is a neuropeptide that is mostly generated by orexin-containing neurons in the hypothalamus. Their receptors are found in a variety of tissues, such as the brain and kidney. This study aims to evaluate the impact of renal function on orexin-A levels in CKD. The study included 44 adult patients diagnosed with CKD, and their results were compared with 44 healthy participants of the same age and sex. An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay kit was used to measure orexin-A, while urea, creatinine, and lipid profile were measured using spectrophotometric methods. Association with orexin-A was performed using Pearson's correlation analysis. The results showed a significant decrease in serum orexin-A (P < 0.001) in patients with CKD. Correlation analysis showed that orexin-A in CKD patients was positively correlated with serum creatinine (r = 0.353, P = 0.018) and high-density lipoprotein (r = 0.354, P = 0.017), while negatively correlated with glomerular filtration rate (GFR) (r = -0.424, P = 0.004). Orexin-A levels decreased in patients with CKD, and this decrease reflects the disruption of the orexin system, which was inversely related to the GFR and directly related to creatinine and high-density lipoprotein levels. Résumé Contexte: La maladie rénale chronique (MRC) est une affection rénale chronique caractérisée par une détérioration progressive de la fonction rénale. Elle est généralement associée à diverses manifestations cliniques et complications, notamment des troubles hormonaux, l’hypertension artérielle, l’anémie et les troubles du sommeil. L’orexine-A, également appelée hypocrétine-A, est un neuropeptide principalement produit par les neurones orexinergiques de l’hypothalamus. Ses récepteurs sont exprimés dans différents tissus, notamment au niveau du cerveau et des reins. Cette étude visait à évaluer l’impact de la fonction rénale sur les concentrations sériques d’orexine-A chez les patients atteints de MRC. Matériels et Méthodes: L’étude a inclus 44 patients adultes atteints de MRC, dont les résultats ont été comparés à ceux de 44 sujets sains appariés selon l’âge et le sexe. Les concentrations sériques d’orexine-A ont été déterminées à l’aide d’un kit immuno-enzymatique (ELISA), tandis que l’urée, la créatinine et le profil lipidique ont été dosés par des méthodes spectrophotométriques. Le coefficient de corrélation de Pearson a été utilisé pour évaluer les associations entre les concentrations d’orexine-A et les paramètres étudiés. Résultats: Les résultats ont montré une diminution significative des concentrations sériques d’orexine-A chez les patients atteints de MRC par rapport aux sujets sains (P < 0.001). Chez les patients atteints de MRC, l’analyse de corrélation a révélé une corrélation positive entre les concentrations d’orexine-A et la créatinine sérique (r = 0.353; P = 0.018), ainsi qu’avec les lipoprotéines de haute densité (HDL) (r = 0.354; P = 0.017). En revanche, une corrélation négative a été observée entre les concentrations d’orexine-A et le débit de filtration glomérulaire (DFG) (r = −0.424; P = 0.004). Conclusions: Les concentrations sériques d’orexine-A sont significativement diminuées chez les patients atteints de MRC. Elles présentent une association inverse avec le DFG et des associations directes avec les concentrations sériques de créatinine et de HDL. Ces résultats suggèrent une implication potentielle du système orexinergique dans les altérations associées à la MRC.

papers.title: Frailty transitions and the risk of multisystem burden of chronic disease: a prospective cohort study in China.
papers.abstract: Frailty, defined by a decline in physiological reserve, is a key determinant of adverse health outcomes in older populations. While baseline frailty has been shown to predict the development of chronic diseases, the impact of changes in frailty status over time, particularly in rapidly ageing populations like China, remains poorly understood. This study aimed to assess how baseline frailty and its longitudinal transitions influence the incidence of chronic diseases across multiple organ systems. We analysed data from 17,708 adults (aged ≥ 40) in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) collected between 2011 and 2018. Frailty was assessed using the Rockwood Frailty Index at baseline and at two-year follow-up, categorised as stable, improved, or worsened. We applied Cox proportional hazards models to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the onset of 13 major chronic diseases spanning cardiovascular, metabolic, respiratory, neurological, psychiatric, digestive, renal, and musculoskeletal systems. The study included 9,807 to 16,882 participants across 13 disease-specific subgroups, with a median follow-up period of 6.2-6.8 years for baseline frailty status and 4.4-5.0 years for frailty transitions. Frail individuals were typically older, more likely to be female, unmarried, with lower education, higher BMI, and reported fewer hours of sleep. Baseline frailty was associated with significantly higher risks for all 13 chronic diseases, with the strongest association observed for psychiatric problems (HR 5.17, 95% CI 3.24-8.24). Worsening frailty over time was linked to elevated risks, particularly for asthma (HR 3.91, 95% CI 1.28-11.91), while improvements in frailty showed reduced risks, notably for kidney diseases (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.22-0.63). The association was particularly strong in adults aged 40-65 years, indicating greater potential for risk modification in midlife. Frailty is a dynamic and modifiable predictor of multisystem chronic disease risk. Changes in frailty status offer valuable insights into future disease development, especially among middle-aged adults. Routine frailty monitoring in clinical settings may offer a strategic opportunity to delay or prevent the onset of chronic diseases through timely interventions. These findings emphasize the need for incorporating frailty-targeted strategies into public health and clinical care policies to enhance ageing-related disease prevention.

papers.title: Endocrine determinants of MASLD: mechanisms and therapeutic targets.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects approximately 30% of adults worldwide, yet is still framed largely as a hepatological disorder despite being driven substantially by endocrine and metabolic dysfunction. This review proposes a unified endocrine framework organised around seven hormonal axes, presenting each in terms of molecular pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and therapeutic implications. Insulin resistance is the central driver, coupling chronic caloric excess to hepatic de novo lipogenesis through selective hepatic insulin resistance, although genetic variants in PNPLA3 and TM6SF2 can uncouple steatosis from metabolic risk. Adipose tissue dysfunction contributes through adipocyte senescence, adipokine imbalance, and inflammatory adipose-liver signalling. Reduced hepatic thyroid hormone sensitivity, even in euthyroid individuals, predicts steatosis and fibrosis and underpins the first approved liver-directed therapy. Gonadal steroids exert sexually dimorphic effects, with testosterone deficiency, menopausal oestrogen loss, and polycystic ovary syndrome representing distinct risk states. Glucocorticoid dysregulation is stage-dependent, shifting from enhanced hepatic cortisol clearance in steatosis to local amplification in steatohepatitis. The gut-liver-endocrine axis, encompassing incretin, bile acid, and fibroblast growth factor signalling, has proved the most therapeutically tractable. Reduced GH/IGF-1 signalling, whether from pituitary disease or obesity-induced functional suppression, promotes both steatosis and fibrogenesis. Biological sex and life-course influences spanning developmental programming and ageing further modify these determinants. Two agents, resmetirom and semaglutide, now have US FDA accelerated approval for noncirrhotic MASH with moderate-to-advanced fibrosis, supporting the principle that correcting axis-specific endocrine dysfunction can produce measurable hepatic benefit; however, both approvals are accelerated and await confirmatory outcome data, while others remain investigational. An endocrine framework offers both a coherent account of pathogenesis and a rational basis for biomarker-guided, phenotype-targeted therapy.

papers.title: Macrophage interferon regulatory factor 7 aggravates the progression of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) represents a growing clinical burden with increasing prevalence and lacking approved pharmacological therapies. Interferon regulatory factor 7 (IRF7) is a central mediator of type I interferon-dependent immune responses, yet the precise mechanisms by which macrophage-expressed IRF7 shapes inflammatory and metabolic events during MASH pathogenesis remain incompletely defined. This study aimed to dissect the functional role of IRF7 in MASH development. We assessed IRF7 expression in human and mouse liver specimens, and utilized myeloid-specific Irf7-deficient mice fed with high-fat high-cholesterol diet (HFHCD) or methionine-choline-deficient diet (MCD) to recapitulate MASH pathology. IRF7 was significantly elevated in MASH-affected livers, and myeloid-specific Irf7 deletion markedly mitigated MASH progression. Mechanistically, loss of IRF7 blunted IFN-α and IFN-β production, suppressing macrophage-derived type I interferon-dependent immune cascades. IRF7 directly bound to the promoters of pro-inflammatory Tnfa and Il1b to boost their transcription, and interacted with SMAD3 to activate Tgfb1 transcription. The E3 ubiquitin ligase HUWE1 mediated IRF7 monoubiquitination to enhance its nuclear translocation, driving transcription of pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic genes. This molecular cascade aggravated hepatic steatosis and triggered hepatic stellate cell (HSC) activation, accelerating MASH deterioration. Pharmacological IRF7 inhibition effectively counteracted these pathological alterations. Collectively, myeloid IRF7 fuels MASH progression by amplifying macrophage-mediated liver inflammation, suggesting IRF7 as a promising therapeutic target against MASH.

papers.title: Leptin Insensitivity in NAFLD Is Produced by Oxidative Stress and Cytokine Overexpression.
papers.abstract: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) pathogenesis is caused by an imbalance in the biochemistry and immunology of the liver. The aim of the present study was to evaluate the role of oxidative stress and inflammatory factors in the serum concerning leptin concentration. This study was carried out on 67 females, including 20 healthy and 47 patients diagnosed by liver scan. Anthropometric analysis and routine biochemical tests, including alanine and aspartate transaminase, triglycerides, cholesterol, fasting blood sugar, low-density lipoprotein, high-density lipoprotein, and their ratio, were carried out. Also, the concentration of malondialdehyde and total antioxidant capacity concentration as well as the activity of catalase, superoxide dismutase, and glutathione peroxidase, were estimated. In addition, the concentration of leptin, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-α was analyzed. Data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test, with P <0.05 considered statistically significant. Patients with NAFLD had significantly higher BMI (33.63±6.37 kg/m² vs. 25.33±2.53 kg/m²), waist circumference (90.6±9.85 cm vs. 81.38±5.44 cm), and hip circumference (93.43±10.06 cm vs. 86.14±5.57 cm) compared with controls ( P <0.05). Their lipid profile showed elevated triglycerides (209.12±73.41 mg/dl vs. 121.19±38.51 mg/dl) and cholesterol (229.73±43.42 mg/dl vs. 171.19±22.91 mg/dl), as well as a higher prevalence of diabetes mellitus (30%). Although total antioxidant capacity did not differ ( P >0.05), MDA levels were significantly increased from controls (1.01±0.22 nmol/L) to Grade 1 (1.24±0.41 nmol/L), Grade 2 (1.33±0.32 nmol/L), and Grade 3 NAFLD (1.43±0.44 nmol/L), while SOD, CAT, and GPx activities were reduced (all P <0.05). IL 6, TNF α, and leptin concentrations were markedly elevated from grade 1 to 3, with the highest at Grade 3 (17.63±10.19 pg/mL, 104.63 ± 14.43 ng/mL, and 2.23±0.92 μg/mL, respectively, for each one; P <0.05). Although leptin controls fat metabolism via satiety, results revealed that the overproduction of leptin might be a consequence of oxidative stress and inflammatory response to fat accumulation in the liver. Therefore, measuring leptin along with IL-6 and TNF-α might help to diagnose liver injury.

papers.title: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum Strains LP5 and BX62 Alleviate Liver Injury of NAFLD in Rats via Regulating Hepatic Cholesterol Metabolism and Antioxidant Signaling Pathways.
papers.abstract: Disorders of lipid metabolism and oxidative stress are pivotal factors in the advancement of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). This study aims to investigate the liver-protective effects of two Lactiplantibacillus plantarum (L. plantarum) strains, LP5 and BX62, either individually or in combined, on NAFLD in rats induced by high fat and cholesterol diet. Strain L. plantarum LP5 showed potential for modulating cholesterol metabolism, whereas L. plantarum BX62 exhibited enhanced antioxidant properties. All three intervention strategies alleviated liver injury, as evidenced by reduced hepatic lipid accumulation, intestinal permeability, inflammation, and liver injury markers. Notably, L. plantarum LP5 showed greater effects on reducing weight gain and hepatic steatosis, while L. plantarum BX62 provided additional protection against hepatic oxidative damage. Metabolic and molecular analyses suggested that the beneficial effects of L. plantarum LP5 were associated with altered bile acid homeostasis and increased expression of hepatic primary bile acid synthesis-related proteins (CYP7A1 and CYP8B1), whereas L. plantarum BX62 was associated with activation of the Nrf2-HO-1 antioxidant pathway (Nrf2, HO-1, and FTH). Furthermore, all intervention strategies activated AMPK signaling (p-AMPK/AMPK), accompanied by decreased expression of lipogenesis-related proteins (SREBP-1c, FASN, and SCD1) and increased expression of fatty acid oxidation-related proteins (PPARα and CPT1a), contributing to improved hepatic lipid metabolism. Collectively, our findings indicate that L. plantarum LP5 and L. plantarum BX62 alleviate HFHC diet-induced hepatic metabolic disturbances by complementary mechanisms involving cholesterol metabolism and antioxidant responses, highlighting their potential as dietary probiotics for supporting liver health and preventing NAFLD progression.

papers.title: Multi-omics Profiling Reveals the Effects of Xihuangcao on Hepatic Fibrosis Attenuation through Gut Microbiota and Metabolic Reprogramming.
papers.abstract: In various chronic liver diseases, hepatic fibrosis represents a frequent pathological event. This process involves the activation of hepatic stellate cells, along with the consequent excessive deposition of extracellular matrix. Emerging evidence highlights the contribution of gut microbiota dysbiosis and intestinal barrier dysfunction to its progression, underscoring the potential of targeting the liver-gut axis. Xihuangcao, a traditional Chinese medicinal herb used for acute cholecystitis and jaundice hepatitis, exhibits antifibrotic activity, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, hepatic fibrosis models were established to evaluate the antifibrotic effects of 3 botanical sources of Xihuangcao ( Isodon lophanthoides (Buch.-Ham. ex D.Don) H.Hara, Isodon lophanthoides var. graciliflorus (Benth.) H.Hara, and Isodon serra Kudô) through integrating histopathological, transcriptomics, metabolomics, 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) sequencing, and network pharmacology analyses. The results indicated that all 3 botanical sources of Xihuangcao markedly alleviated hepatic fibrosis and reduced collagen deposition. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that Xihuangcao down-regulated profibrotic mediators (Toll-like receptor 5, transforming growth factor-β, and platelet-derived growth factor) and modulated mitogen-activated protein kinase, steroid biosynthesis, bile secretion, and retinol metabolism pathways, highlighting its coordinated suppression of inflammation-driven fibrogenic activation in hepatic fibrosis. Liver metabolomics revealed Xihuangcao's effect on restoration of energy metabolism, amino acid turnover, and redox homeostasis. Xihuangcao also corrected fibrosis-induced gut dysbiosis, characterized by reduced Verrucomicrobia and increased S24-7 abundance, while suppressing pathogenic genera such as Clostridium and Prevotella . Moreover, Xihuangcao decreased profibrotic metabolites (androstan-3α,17β-diol) and suppressed choline-related metabolic pathways associated with fibrogenic signaling. Network pharmacology and experimental validation further identified PI3K/Akt inhibition as a key mechanism suppressing hepatic stellate cell activation. In summary, this study, based on integrative multi-omics analyses (metabolomics, transcriptomics, and 16S rRNA sequencing), found that Xihuangcao alleviates liver fibrosis by modulating inflammatory responses, metabolic disorders, and gut microbiota dysbiosis via the gut-liver axis. Furthermore, network pharmacology combined with in vitro experiments revealed that inhibition of hepatic stellate cell activation through the PI3K/Akt pathway may be the critical mechanism underlying its therapeutic efficacy.

papers.title: Targeting hepatic CREBZF protects against atherosclerosis via exosomal miR-210-3p mediated inhibition of endothelial inflammation.
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) continue to be the primary cause of mortality globally. Abnormal liver function has been widely recognized as an independent risk factor for atherosclerotic CVDs. However, how alterations in liver function affect distal vascular function remains largely unknown. CREBZF, a bZIP transcription factor of the CREB/ATF family, has been identified as a driver of hepatic steatosis and fibrosis. Here, we provide the first demonstration that hepatic CREBZF acts as a critical regulator driving atherosclerotic progression. In vivo , hepatic-specific deletion of CREBZF attenuates endothelial inflammation and reduces macrophage infiltration, thereby ameliorating plaque formation in both high-fat diet-fed and spontaneous atherosclerotic mouse models. In vitro , overexpression or knockdown of CREBZF in hepatocytes correspondingly promotes or attenuates endothelial inflammation. Mechanistically, hepatocyte CREBZF regulates endothelial inflammation via exosomes, an effect independent of cholesterol metabolism or of soluble cytokines. Furthermore, CREBZF dynamically modulates the expression of exosomal miR-210-3p and its subsequent levels in recipient endothelial cells. miR-210-3p, in turn, suppresses endothelial inflammation by targeting C-Rel, a component of the NF-κB transcription factor family. Importantly, the pro-inflammatory effect of exosomes derived from CREBZF-overexpressing hepatocytes on endothelial cells is abrogated by a miR-210-3p mimic. Collectively, these findings unveil a novel mechanism by which hepatic CREBZF regulates atherosclerosis through liver-vascular crosstalk mediated by the exosomal miR-210-3p/C-Rel signaling axis, suggesting a potential therapeutic strategy for atherosclerotic CVDs.

papers.title: Three Decades of Liver X Receptor Agonist Chemistry: Structural Motifs, Structure-activity Relationship, and Therapeutic Prospects.
papers.abstract: Liver X receptors (LXRs) are nuclear receptors that play an important role in the regulation of gene expression involved in lipid metabolism, cholesterol homeostasis and inflammation. Certain modifications in endogenous LXR activity have been associated with pathological conditions and diseases. The dysregulation of LXR activity can lead to vascular and metabolic diseases, neurological degeneration and formation of malignant tumors. One of the solutions to treat the diseases or at least to slow down the progression is the development of different strategies to modulate LXR signaling for the treatment or prevention of these pathological conditions. Many researchers and pharmaceutical companies are developing selective LXR modulators to precisely control receptor activity and achieve specific pharmacological effects. The activation of LXRs has been linked to the inhibition of cell proliferation and metastasis, the promotion of apoptosis and re-differentiation of tumor cells that drives exosome release to stimulate anti-tumor immunity in certain cancer types. The main challenge is to minimize the adverse effects of LXR induction on lipid metabolism via selective activation of LXRβ isoform. Several lead compounds were identified and tested in clinical trials for few pathologies discussed above. The discovery of a potent and selective LXR ligand involves a combination of multiple steps from lead discovery, optimization, preclinical and clinical testing before getting to marketing authorization. This review offers an overview of synthetic agonists for LXRs developed over the past three decades. Though multiple investigations have been in progress, no FDA-approved LXR-targeting drug is available so far.

papers.title: Assessing in vitro long-term liver metabolism models to characterize intrinsic clearance determination in NGRAs.
papers.abstract: In Next Generation Risk Assessments, measurements of hepatic intrinsic clearance (CL int , in vitro ) and metabolite(s) formation can markedly impact in vitro to in vivo extrapolations and subsequent testing of parent and/or metabolites in in vitro bioassays. It is especially important for slowly metabolized chemicals to use the most suitable model and experimental design to ensure that the IVIVE is accurate. We evaluated four long-term hepatic models (sandwich cultures of primary human hepatocytes (PHH), HepatoPac, HµREL and TruVivo), as well as PHH suspensions, using salicylic acid, 1-methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP) and valproic acid. Assay designs differed in terms of positive and negative controls, cell densities and incubation durations. All models generated a measurable CL int , in vitro value for salicylic acid i.e. depletion >20%. Differences may be due to donor differences and the cell number. HepatoPac generally resulted in higher values compared with the other models. NMP was not metabolized by HµREL and TruVivo models and a reliable value was only possible using HepatoPac. NMP was metabolized by sandwich cultures; however, the half-life was much longer than the incubation duration. To derive a more robust value, follow up testing could include longer incubation times. Valproic acid was only metabolized in one of the three models in which it was detected, namely sandwich cultures. In conclusion, PHH sandwich cultures, HepatoPac, HµREL and TruVivo models are superior to PHH suspensions with respect to maintaining XME activities over days and for measuring CL int, in vitro values for slowly metabolized chemicals. To gain regulatory acceptance and better interpret data from different labs, we recommend increasing the number of chemicals tested and harmonization of protocols.

papers.title: Abnormal lipid profiles are associated with markers of impaired fibrinolysis in patients with cirrhosis.
papers.abstract: Patients with liver cirrhosis exhibit abnormalities in lipid metabolism and in circulating proteins of clot breakdown. Recent studies have shown relationships between dyslipidemia and fibrinolytic abnormalities in noncirrhotic populations. We investigated associations between lipid profiles and fibrinolytic markers in patients with cirrhosis. This observational study analyzed samples from 147 patients with stable cirrhosis, decompensated cirrhosis, acute-on-chronic liver failure, and sepsis without pre-existing chronic liver disease, and from 38 healthy controls. We studied fibrinolysis by clot lysis time (CLT), plasminogen, plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1), and tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA), and lipid profiles by apolipoproteins A1 and B, common lipoproteins, triglycerides, and total cholesterol. CLT was slightly enhanced in stable and decompensated cirrhosis, but prolonged in acute-on-chronic liver failure and sepsis. Plasminogen levels decreased, whereas PAI-1 and tPA increased with cirrhosis severity. All lipid parameters decreased with cirrhosis severity, besides triglyceride levels, which were preserved. In an analysis of all patients with cirrhosis combined, apolipoprotein A1 correlated inversely with CLT, levels of PAI-1 and tPA, and positively with plasminogen. Apolipoprotein B, low-density lipoprotein, and lipoprotein(a) correlated positively with plasminogen. Triglycerides correlated positively with CLT. Cirrhosis is characterized by decreased (apo)lipoprotein levels, preserved triglyceride levels, and a shift from enhanced to impaired fibrinolysis with increasing disease severity. Lower apolipoprotein A1 levels and higher triglyceride levels are associated with impaired fibrinolysis, which may reflect biological interactions between lipid metabolism and fibrinolysis or parallel alterations secondary to hepatic dysfunction.

papers.title: BRD9 Enhances Activation of Pregnane X Receptor Pathway and the Resistance of Hepatocellular Carcinoma Cells to Molecular Targeted Agents.
papers.abstract: Bromodomain-containing protein 9 (BRD9) is a newly identified oncogenic regulatory factor in multiple human malignancies, yet its precise roles in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remain largely unknown. This study aimed to investigate the function and mechanism of BRD9 in HCC, particularly its involvement in molecular targeted drug resistance. BRD9 expression was either overexpressed or knocked down in HCC cells. PXR transcription factor activity was assessed using luciferase reporter assays, quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), and chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP). HCC cells were treated with serial concentrations of molecularly targeted drugs. Antitumor activity was evaluated by MTT assays, colony formation assays, flow cytometry for apoptosis analysis, and subcutaneous tumor models. Drug metabolic rates were quantified using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Overexpression of BRD9 significantly enhanced the transcriptional activity of PXR and promoted the expression of PXR-dependent multidrug resistance-related genes, including CYP3A4 and ABCB1. Mechanistically, BRD9 overexpression facilitated the recruitment of PXR to the promoter and enhancer regions of CYP3A4, thereby accelerating the metabolic clearance of sorafenib in HCC cells. Functionally, enforced expression of BRD9 rendered HCC cells more resistant to molecularly targeted agents, whereas knockdown of BRD9 sensitized them to these drugs. Muscle.description: Exercise training increases OXPHOS proteins, mitochondrial volume density, and ATP production capacity across species, as mitochondrial biogenesis and function were consistently responsive across species, particularly for OXPHOS proteins, mitochondrial volume density, ATPmax, and SIRT1/SIRT3 signaling [1]. Muscle also produces reactive oxygen species that act as signals, which exercise promotes through transient ROS-mediated signaling through NADPH oxidases, activation of Nrf-2 and PGC-1α-dependent pathways, mitochondrial quality control, and metabolic remodeling [2]. Lipids are an important substrate, since lipotoxicity develops when adipose storage and oxidative capacity are exceeded, increasing fatty-acid flux and accumulation of ceramides, diacylglycerols, and oxidizable phospholipids [9] in muscle. Metabolomic profiling also revealed alterations in arachidonic acid metabolism, glycerophospholipids, amino acids, and energy-related metabolites [7] in tumor-bearing mice. Dietary phosphate affects this machinery, as high-phosphate feeding led to significantly decreased mitochondrial respiration in skeletal muscle from trained HPD-fed mice [3]. Insulin regulates muscle through AKT, which normally interacts with Miro1 at the outer mitochondrial membrane, but in type 2 diabetes this inadequate insulin-mediated interaction between AKT and Miro1 [4] leads to Miro1 accumulation, and exercise reverses this while improving insulin sensitivity in patients with T2D [4]. GLP-1-based drugs may also act on muscle metabolism, with improved insulin sensitivity, reduced inflammation, and modulation of mitochondrial function and protein turnover [10] reported in preclinical studies.

papers.title: Exercise training and mitochondrial remodeling in aging skeletal muscle: A translational systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Aging skeletal muscle shows impaired mitochondrial function, altered redox regulation, disrupted fusion-fission balance, and reduced mitochondrial turnover. This translational systematic synthesis and meta-analysis evaluated whether exercise training remodels mitochondrial and functional outcomes in aging muscle. PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science were searched to June 26, 2026 following PRISMA 2020. Twenty-eight studies involving aged exercise groups compared to sedentary groups were included. Outcomes covered oxidative stress, mitochondrial dynamics, mitophagy, mitochondrial biogenesis/function, skeletal muscle morphology, and physiological performance. Random-effects meta-analysis showed a significant improvement in VO₂max/VO₂peak after exercise training (SMD = 0.46, p < 0.001; I² = 0%), whereas pooled changes in citrate synthase (SMD = 0.18, p = 0.450) and BMI (SMD = -0.09, p = 0.557) were not significant. The directional synthesis showed that mitochondrial biogenesis and function were consistently responsive across species, particularly for OXPHOS proteins, mitochondrial volume density, ATPmax, and SIRT1/SIRT3 signaling. Human and rodent studies assessed different, only partly overlapping mitophagy and mitochondrial dynamics markers. Therefore, differences in pathway responsiveness across species cannot be separated from differences in which markers were measured. Exercise training and lifelong physical activity were associated with changes in mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics, mitophagy-related signaling, and muscle function in aging skeletal muscle. The observed patterns varied by training protocol and study design, but indirect comparisons and heterogeneous outcome measures preclude conclusions about the superiority of any modality. Human and rodent findings should therefore be interpreted as complementary evidence rather than equivalent estimates of biological response.

papers.title: Redox resilience in skeletal muscle aging: cellular adaptations and exercise-mediated homeostasis.
papers.abstract: Aging progressively impairs skeletal muscle function, leading to sarcopenia, frailty, and loss of independence. Although oxidative stress has long been considered a central driver of muscle aging, increasing evidence indicates that reactive oxygen species (ROS) also serve essential signaling functions that coordinate mitochondrial remodeling, proteostasis, metabolism, and tissue repair. Consequently, age-related muscle dysfunction is increasingly understood as reflecting impaired adaptive redox signaling rather than excessive oxidant production alone. In this review, we propose the concept of redox resilience as an integrative framework describing the capacity of skeletal muscle to preserve structural integrity and functional performance through the dynamic regulation of oxidant production, antioxidant defenses, and redox-sensitive signaling in response to physiological challenges. We discuss how aging disrupts this resilience through impaired redox-sensitive signaling, including the attenuation of exercise-induced Nrf-2 activation, together with alterations in the multicellular organization of skeletal muscle. Recent advances in single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomics have revealed that muscle aging involves profound remodeling of specialized myonuclear populations, stromal cells, immune cells, and intercellular communication networks, highlighting the multicellular complexity of skeletal muscle aging and providing a framework to investigate how redox-dependent processes may interact with tissue-wide signaling networks. We further examine how regular physical exercise reinforces redox resilience by promoting transient ROS-mediated signaling through NADPH oxidases, activation of Nrf-2 and PGC-1α-dependent pathways, mitochondrial quality control, and metabolic remodeling. These adaptations enhance the capacity of skeletal muscle to respond to physiological stress while preserving tissue homeostasis. Finally, we discuss future perspectives for targeting adaptive redox networks to promote healthy muscle aging and propose that restoring redox resilience may preserve physiological ROS signaling while strengthening endogenous antioxidant responses and limiting excessive oxidative damage, thereby contributing to the maintenance of muscle function and health span.

papers.title: Exercise training does not mitigate high-phosphate diet-induced mitochondrial dysfunction in skeletal muscle in male mice.
papers.abstract: Inorganic phosphate consumption in adults is two-to-three-fold higher than the recommended daily allowance due to its widespread use as a preservative and flavor enhancer in processed foods. We previously reported that 12 weeks of high-phosphate diet (HPD) reduced VO 2max and altered metabolic gene expression and mitochondrial dysfunction in mouse skeletal muscle. Here, we investigated whether exercise training reverses the negative consequences of HPD. Male mice were fed normal (NPD) or HPD for 5 weeks, then continued on NPD or HPD with 9 weeks of voluntary exercise training. Serum, urine, and fecal phosphate increased within 1 day of HPD-feeding and remained elevated throughout the study. Trained NPD- and HPD-fed mice performed similarly on forced exercise tests, but mitochondrial respiration was significantly decreased in skeletal muscle from trained HPD-fed mice. RNA sequencing revealed distinct sets of differentially expressed genes when comparing sedentary versus exercise-trained muscle of HPD-fed mice relative to the same comparison in NPD-fed mice. These findings indicate that voluntary exercise training preserves endurance but does not fully restore gene expression or mitochondrial function in muscle from HPD-fed mice. Thus, HPD-induced skeletal muscle dysregulation is not completely reversible with exercise, underscoring the importance of both diet and exercise for metabolic health.

papers.title: Miro1 mediates skeletal muscle insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes.
papers.abstract: Imbalanced skeletal muscle mitochondrial dynamics contribute to the onset and progression of type 2 diabetes (T2D) by mechanisms that remain incompletely understood. Here, we examined the role of Mitochondrial Rho GTPase 1 (Miro1), an outer mitochondrial membrane enzyme, in regulating skeletal muscle insulin action and glucose homeostasis in type 2 diabetes (T2D). In a cross-sectional clinical study, we show that Miro1 accumulates in the skeletal muscle of patients with obesity and T2D, which was further replicated in mouse models of T2D. This accumulation is explained by inadequate insulin-mediated interaction between AKT and Miro1 at the outer mitochondrial membrane. In a randomized controlled trial (NCT02977442), we show that exercise training relieves skeletal muscle Miro1 accumulation while improving insulin sensitivity in patients with T2D. Muscle-specific Miro1 deletion improves oxidative capacity and insulin sensitivity in mice and cells. Taken together, these data support a key regulatory role for skeletal muscle Miro1 in the pathophysiology of T2D. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02977442.

papers.title: Circular RNAs in Skeletal Muscle Aging and Sarcopenia: Mechanistic Evidence, Biomarker Potential, and Therapeutic Readiness.
papers.abstract: Skeletal muscle aging arises from interacting defects in proteostasis, mitochondrial quality control, inflammatory signaling, neuromuscular integrity, regenerative capacity, and mechanical-metabolic plasticity, and may culminate in sarcopenia. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are plausible regulators and biomarker candidates, but most evidence derives from developmental myogenesis, expression profiling, or non-aging atrophy models. This critical review organizes the literature around skeletal muscle aging and applies a four-level framework encompassing discovery, mechanistic support, in vivo causality, and functional intervention. We assess human linkage, species, treatment timing, locus of action, and endogenous or engineered modality separately. circSnd1 and circDdb1 currently provide the strongest combination of functional preclinical evidence and association with aged human skeletal muscle. circFUT10, circBBS9, circNEB, and circGLIS3 define less mature regenerative, discovery, histological, or muscle-quality domains. Non-aging atrophy studies, including circTmeff1 and engineered circmiR-29b, test whether proposed mechanisms remain active under defined catabolic stress. Human blood and serum-vesicle studies provide discovery-level associations with strength or mobility, but clinical validation of a circulating circRNA biomarker for sarcopenia remains insufficient. Therapeutic development is constrained by quantitative target credibility, systemic skeletal-muscle exposure, post-onset functional efficacy in aged organisms, safety, reversibility, and independent replication. The field should now prioritize rigorous validation over additional descriptive cataloging.

papers.title: Targeting ubiquitin-dependent mitochondrial autophagy and apoptosis in sarcopenia: the therapeutic potential of phytochemicals.
papers.abstract: Sarcopenia is a progressive degenerative disease of skeletal muscle closely associated with aging, disuse, and chronic diseases, affecting approximately 10-16% of the global older adult population. Its core pathological basis lies in the disruption of skeletal muscle cell proteostasis and mitochondrial dysfunction. At the molecular level, excessive degradation of structural proteins mediated by the ubiquitin-proteasome system forms an intertwined vicious cycle with the inability of ubiquitin-dependent mitophagy to clear damaged organelles, ultimately triggering irreversible cell death programmes within an oxidative stress and inflammatory microenvironment. Due to the high complexity and molecular crosstalk within this cell fate-determining network, traditional single-target interventions often yield limited therapeutic efficacy. In recent years, phytochemicals (such as polyphenols, flavonoids, alkaloids, and coumarins) have demonstrated significant therapeutic potential in the field of sarcopenia due to their unique multi-target, multi-pathway synergistic regulatory advantages. This article reviews the dual-faceted regulatory mechanisms of ubiquitination in skeletal muscle mitochondrial quality control, protein hydrolysis, and apoptosis escape and provides an analysis of how phytochemicals achieve autophagy-promoting, anti-apoptotic, and anti-degradative skeletal muscle protection. However, oral bioavailability is often below 1%, microbiota-dependent metabolism, and the absence of phase III clinical trials have hindered the translational application of phytochemicals. This paper explores the use of nano-delivery systems to overcome the bioavailability bottleneck of phytochemicals, as well as translational application strategies based on the gut-muscle axis to reshape the in vivo metabolism of natural products. This review aims to provide a solid theoretical foundation for the development of novel phytochemical-derived drugs targeting ubiquitination and apoptosis networks and to chart a course for reversing skeletal muscle ageing and enhancing human healthspan.

papers.title: Identification of Kaempferol for Skeletal Muscle Wasting in Cancer Cachexia Through Bibliometric Analysis and Network Pharmacology: Metabolomic and Experimental Evaluation.
papers.abstract: Cancer cachexia (CC) is a multifactorial syndrome characterized by progressive skeletal muscle wasting, systemic inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) contains numerous bioactive compounds with potential multitarget effects, but systematic strategies for identifying and experimentally evaluating candidate compounds for CC remain limited. This study aimed to identify and evaluate a TCM-derived candidate compound for CC-associated skeletal muscle wasting. Bibliometric analysis was used to identify frequently studied TCM formulas and core herbs in cachexia-related research, followed by network pharmacology analysis of candidate compounds and associated pathways. Kaempferol (KA) was then evaluated in A549 tumor-bearing mice by assessing tumor burden, cachexia-related phenotypes, skeletal muscle histology, untargeted metabolomics, inflammatory mediators, muscle degradation-related markers, autophagy-associated endpoints, and ultrastructure. A549-conditioned medium (A549-CM)-treated C2C12 myotubes were used for complementary in vitro evaluation under conditions with or without supplemental prostaglandin E2 (PGE2). KA was selected as a representative candidate based on its distribution among the core herbs, network associations, and reported pharmacological activities. In A549 tumor-bearing mice, high-dose KA (100 mg/kg/day) significantly reduced tumor weight and was accompanied by improvements in food intake, estimated tumor-free body weight, gastrocnemius weight, myofiber cross-sectional area, and forelimb grip strength compared with the model group (all P < 0.05). KA treatment was also associated with lower serum TNF-α, IL-6, and PGE2 concentrations; reduced skeletal muscle COX-2, Atrogin-1, and MuRF1 expression; lower LC3B-II/LC3B-I ratio and p62 protein level; and fewer autophagic vacuole-like structures (all P < 0.05). Untargeted metabolomics revealed KA-associated alterations in arachidonic acid metabolism, glycerophospholipids, amino acids, and energy-related metabolites. In A549-CM-treated C2C12 myotubes, KA modulated atrophy-related gene expression, autophagy-associated endpoints, and cytoplasmic vacuolation in both the absence and presence of supplemental PGE2 (P < 0.05). KA reduced tumor burden and was accompanied by improvements in cachexia-related phenotypes and skeletal muscle outcomes. The molecular, metabolic, and cell-based findings further associated KA treatment with lower systemic inflammatory mediator levels, reduced muscle protein degradation-related markers, and alterations in inflammatory lipid metabolism and autophagy-associated endpoints. These findings support further investigation of KA as a TCM-derived candidate for CC-associated skeletal muscle wasting. Future studies should distinguish its direct muscle-related effects from the systemic benefits associated with reduced tumor burden and clarify whether KA alters PGE2-related signaling and autophagic flux.

papers.title: Targeting host ferroptosis in cancer cachexia: Tumor-immune triggers, tissue wasting, and the therapeutic paradox.
papers.abstract: Cancer cachexia is a systemic wasting syndrome driven by tumor burden, chronic inflammation, disrupted nutrient handling, and neuroendocrine stress. Supportive nutrition, exercise, and symptom management rarely restore lean mass, function, or treatment tolerance once wasting is established. Ferroptosis, iron-dependent cell death caused by phospholipid peroxidation, may connect inflammatory iron redistribution, lipid remodeling, mitochondrial stress, and impaired antioxidant defenses. This review critically evaluates ferroptosis in cachexia from a tumor-host pharmacology perspective, distinguishing causal evidence from associated oxidative signatures. We highlight two experimentally supported mechanisms: neutrophil-derived lipocalin-2 in lung cancer cachexia and tumor exosomal miR-203a-3p in pancreatic cancer-associated muscle wasting. We also examine the paradox that tumor ferroptosis induction may weaken host-tissue resistance and worsen muscle and adipose loss. We propose a "split-ferroptosis" strategy combining tumor sensitization with host-protective iron modulation, lipid peroxide scavenging, endogenous defense reinforcement, and biomarker-guided patient selection to expand the tumor-host therapeutic index.

papers.title: The lipotoxicity-ferroptosis axis in the transition from insulin resistance to type 2 diabetes: mechanistic integration and therapeutic opportunities.
papers.abstract: Insulin resistance is an early feature of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), but progression to persistent hyperglycemia requires failure of pancreatic β-cell compensation. Lipotoxicity develops when adipose storage and oxidative capacity are exceeded, increasing fatty-acid flux and accumulation of ceramides, diacylglycerols, and oxidizable phospholipids in liver, skeletal muscle, and pancreatic islets. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by uncontrolled phospholipid peroxidation. Lipotoxicity can increase ferroptosis susceptibility by enriching polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing membrane phospholipids, increasing organelle-derived reactive oxygen species, and weakening system Xc--glutathione-glutathione peroxidase 4 defense; however, expansion of a redox-active iron pool is a distinct, cell- and context-dependent requirement. We organize these processes into a four-state working model spanning metabolic compensation, systemic lipid overflow and insulin resistance, ferroptosis sensitization, and β-cell decompensation. This is a non-obligate conceptual trajectory rather than a universally recognized clinical sequence. Evidence is strongest in pancreatic β-cell and liver models; direct skeletal-muscle causality is limited, and a causal role in human T2DM has not been established. Ferroptosis also has cell-specific effects: protecting β cells may be beneficial, whereas ferroptotic removal of selected inflammatory or lipid-storing cell populations can improve metabolic outcomes in some models. Upstream lipid unloading through weight loss and established metabolic treatments has the greatest clinical maturity. ACSL4/LPCAT3-dependent membrane remodeling, GPX4-centered defense, ferritinophagy, labile iron, parallel suppressor systems, and targeted delivery remain predominantly preclinical or candidate approaches. Multidimensional biomarker panels may support future mechanistic studies, but no individual marker or composite panel is currently validated to diagnose ferroptosis or a ferroptosis-susceptible phenotype in T2DM. The lipotoxicity-ferroptosis axis should therefore be viewed as a testable, tissue-specific amplifier rather than a universal or solitary cause of T2DM.

papers.title: GLP-1-Based Pharmacotherapies and Skeletal Muscle Health in Obesity: A Narrative Review of Body Composition, Muscle Function, and Sarcopenia-Related Outcomes.
papers.abstract: Background: Obesity is associated with impaired skeletal muscle health and sarcopenic obesity. GLP-1-based pharmacotherapies induce weight loss, but accompanying reductions in fat-free or lean mass raise concerns about skeletal muscle loss. Conversely, reductions in adiposity, inflammation, insulin resistance, and intramuscular fat may be beneficial. Objective: This narrative review evaluated the effects of GLP-1-based pharmacotherapies on body composition, muscle quantity, composition and function, and their potential role in sarcopenia. Methods: PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for clinical and experimental studies published primarily between 2016 and 2026. Results: Preclinical studies identified potentially protective mechanisms, including improved insulin sensitivity, reduced inflammation, and modulation of mitochondrial function and protein turnover, but some also indicated muscle loss or proteolysis. Clinical studies reported greater reductions in fat mass than in fat-free or lean mass, neither of which represents skeletal muscle exclusively. Direct muscle and functional outcomes were assessed in few studies and yielded mixed results. Incident sarcopenia was rarely evaluated. Conclusions: GLP-1-based pharmacotherapies may influence sarcopenia risk through competing pathways. Metabolic improvements may support muscle health, whereas energy restriction, inadequate protein intake, gastrointestinal adverse effects, and lean tissue loss may increase vulnerability. Current evidence is insufficient to determine their net effect on sarcopenia risk.

Glucose-stimulated insulin secretion is suppressed in a concentration-dependent manner by several small-molecule immunosuppressants, while calcineurin and mTOR inhibitors preserved GSIS within their therapeutic ranges but progressively distorted its time-profile at higher concentrations [2]. Fatty acids also shape islet metabolism, since lipotoxicity develops when adipose storage and oxidative capacity are exceeded, increasing fatty-acid flux and accumulation of ceramides, diacylglycerols, and oxidizable phospholipids in liver, skeletal muscle, and pancreatic islets [5], and disrupted mitochondrial dynamics contributes to pancreatic β-cell dysfunction [7]. Glucagon from α-cells and somatostatin from δ-cells act as paracrine regulators, as somatostatin limits oscillation frequency primarily by suppressing α-cell glucagon release [1]. Somatostatin also inhibits insulin release directly, and hypersomatostatinemia in CF was inversely associated with C-peptide and insulin responses to the mixed meal [4]. papers.title: A coordinated paracrine islet cell network regulating β-cell Ca 2+ dynamics.
papers.abstract: Pulsatile insulin secretion originates from oscillations in cytosolic free Ca 2+ in pancreatic islet β-cells. Decades of work have identified multiple determinants of these oscillations, including glucose metabolism, ion channels, ER Ca 2+ handling, cellular heterogeneity, and paracrine and neurohormonal signaling. Yet their relative contributions under physiological conditions remain unresolved because each experimental preparation preserves only a subset of these regulatory layers. Here, we review evidence that intercellular paracrine signaling, in addition to cell-autonomous β-cell machinery, is an important determinant of oscillation frequency and coordination. Simultaneous Ca 2+ imaging of α-cells and β-cells reveals tightly coordinated activity, with α-cells following β-cells after a conserved ∼20-s delay. Perturbation of glucagon signaling further indicates that α-cell signaling can modulate β-cell oscillation frequency. Complementing these findings, in vivo imaging of islets engrafted in the anterior chamber of the eye shows that α-cell expansion enhances β-cell Ca 2+ coordination in a glucagon-receptor-dependent manner. Extending this circuit to δ-cells, somatostatin limits oscillation frequency primarily by suppressing α-cell glucagon release, thereby enabling the δ-cell-α-cell-β-cell paracrine circuit to shift β-cell oscillations between fast, mixed, and slow regimes. Importantly, a glycemia-dependent slow-to-fast transition is lost in diabetic mice and rescued by GLP-1 receptor agonism. Under anesthesia-free conditions, however, islets in awake animals occupy a slow, highly synchronized oscillatory regime in which glucose modulates amplitude, period, and plateau fraction without altering network coordination. Together, these findings suggest that the δ-cell-α-cell-β-cell circuit represents an important regulatory layer shaping β-cell Ca 2+ oscillations alongside intrinsic β-cell mechanisms and extrinsic physiological inputs. β-cell dysfunction may therefore involve not only altered oscillation frequency and coordination, but also disrupted paracrine regulation by glucagon and somatostatin.

papers.title: Effect of immunosuppressive drugs on glucose-stimulated insulin secretion: concentration-response studies in dynamic perifusion assays.
papers.abstract: Immunosuppressive drugs, which are required to maintain graft function in transplant recipients, are associated with many unavoidable side effects including posttransplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM) that involves both peripheral insulin resistance and impairment of insulin secretion. To characterize in detail the concentration-dependency of the effect of well-known immunosuppressive drugs on glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS), we performed dynamic perifusion studies with human pancreatic islets. The effect on the time-profile of GSIS has been assessed over a wide concentration range for several clinically relevant immunomodulatory therapies, including small-molecule drugs (cyclosporine, sirolimus, tacrolimus, prednisolone acetate, and loteprednol etabonate) and biologics (abatacept and anti-CD40L), plus a prospective β-cell proliferation-inducing agent (harmine). While biologics showed no significant detrimental effects after one-day treatment even at relatively high concentrations (5 µM), all small-molecule drugs inhibited insulin secretion in a concentration-dependent manner, although glucocorticoids showed a distinct response pattern. Calcineurin and mTOR inhibitors preserved GSIS within their therapeutic ranges but progressively distorted its time-profile at higher concentrations and completely suppressed secretion at the highest levels, where they were also cytotoxic. Cyclosporine exhibited the least, only about 35-fold, separation between its therapeutic target ( C targ ) and half-maximal GSIS inhibitory (IC 50 ) concentrations. Glucocorticoids did not alter the shape of the time-profile but inhibited overall insulin secretion even at therapeutic levels without affecting islet viability. Their inhibitory effect only increased slowly with concentration and did not follow a classic sigmoid pattern that has unity Hill slope. These findings establish quantitative benchmarks for immunosuppressant-induced β-cell toxicity and provide a framework for optimizing immunosuppressive regimens to reduce the risk of PTDM.

papers.title: L-Histidine alleviates tacrolimus-induced islet dysfunction via the gut-pancreas axis.
papers.abstract: Tacrolimus is widely used after organ transplantation but can impair pancreatic β-cell function and glucose homeostasis. Using rodent models, antibiotic-mediated microbiota depletion, fecal microbiota transplantation, 16S rRNA sequencing, metabolomic profiling, and MIN-6 cells, we examined whether microbiota-associated L-histidine contributes to β-cell protection. Tacrolimus altered gut microbial composition and increased histidine-associated microbial and metabolic signals. L-histidine supplementation improved glucose tolerance and insulin secretion, reduced β-cell apoptosis, and increased PI3K/Akt/mTOR/p70S6K signaling and PDX-1, NeuroD1, and MafA expression. Microbiota depletion attenuated several protective effects of L-histidine, supporting a contribution of the gut microbiota to this response. These findings connect a microbiota-associated amino acid with tacrolimus-related β-cell dysfunction and provide a framework for investigating microbiota-metabolite contributions to metabolic complications of immunosuppression.

papers.title: Impaired insulin secretion in response to mixed meal ingestion is associated with hypersomatostatinemia in individuals with cystic fibrosis.
papers.abstract: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a monogenic disease characterized by exocrine pancreas insufficiency, glucose intolerance, and a high prevalence of diabetes. Diminished insulin secretion is a key contributor to glucose intolerance and diabetes in people with CF, yet the pathophysiology of this deficiency is not fully understood. Somatostatin is a hormone secreted by several tissues in the body, including the delta cells of the pancreas, and is known to inhibit insulin secretion; however, its role in postprandial hypoinsulinemia in people with CF remains unclear. This cross-sectional study included 16 people with CF (CF group) and 8 healthy control subjects (HC), each of whom underwent a mixed meal tolerance test, during which their glucoregulatory responses were assessed. We hypothesized that impaired insulin secretion in CF would be associated with hypersomatostatinemia. Plasma glucose responses to the mixed meal were higher in CF compared to HC (AUC of 27,656±2,215 and 20,564±1,028 mg/dL*180 min, respectively, p<0.05), whereas the AUC for insulin (5866±730 and 11090±1628 µU/mL*180 min, respectively; p<0.05), and C-peptide (608±42 and 998±127 pg/mL*180 min, respectively; p<0.05), were both lower. Hypersomatostatinemia in CF (AUC of 4682±278 and 3353±277 pg/mL*180 min in CF and HC, respectively, p<0.01), was inversely associated with C-peptide (r=-0.54; p<0.01), and insulin (r=-0.60; p<0.01) responses to the mixed meal. These data suggest that hypersomatostatinemia is associated with diminished insulin secretion in people with CF, and that it could be a target for improving glucose tolerance in this population.
