papers.title: Design of short-sequenced collagen type III-derived peptides with GPR56 dependent biological activity.
papers.abstract: We have previously shown that activation of G protein-coupled receptor 56 (GPR56) by its endogenous ligand collagen type III (Coll III) improves pancreatic β-cell function and potentiates glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS). In the current study, alignment of Coll III and GPR56 genomic DNA revealed three complementary nucleotide regions, enabling the design of three short peptides (NQGCKL.NH2, H.LLSSR.NH2 and NH2.GYYCG.COOH). The peptides in double or triple combinations markedly increased cellular cAMP levels, enhanced GSIS, and improved cell viability both in human (EndoC βH1 cells) and rat pancreatic β-cell lines (INS-1 832/13 cells). These effects were markedly absent in GPR56-knockdown (GPR56-KD) cells, supporting receptor-dependent specificity. The peptide mixtures also counteracted cytokine- and glucotoxicity-induced cellular stress, restoring cAMP generation and insulin secretion. Comparable effects were not observed with dapagliflozin while glibenclamide decreased cell viability under similar conditions. In hepatic cell lines (HepG2, Hep1-6), peptide combinations enhanced cell survival in a GPR56-dependent manner, consistent with a broader role of GPR56 in metabolic regulation. Collectively, the data identify three short sequence collagen III-derived peptides whose biological effects are dependent on GPR56 expression and support their further investigation as tools for studying GPR56-associated cellular signaling for the future in vivo validation.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Dynamics in Diabetes Mellitus and Its Complications: Mechanisms, Pathological Roles, and Therapeutic Implications.
papers.abstract: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a progressive metabolic disorder in which mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a central contributor to metabolic deterioration and diabetic complications. However, whether dysregulated mitochondrial dynamics represents a primary pathogenic driver, an adaptive response, or a consequence of metabolic stress remains incompletely understood. This review summarizes current advances in the molecular mechanisms governing mitochondrial fission, fusion, and mitophagy, with particular emphasis on their coordinated roles in mitochondrial quality control rather than isolated morphological changes. We discuss how disrupted mitochondrial dynamics contributes to pancreatic β-cell dysfunction, insulin resistance, diabetic nephropathy (DN), diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM), diabetic retinopathy (DR), and diabetic osteoporosis (DOP) through context-dependent regulation of oxidative stress, bioenergetics, inflammation, and endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondria crosstalk. Furthermore, we critically evaluate emerging therapeutic strategies, including metformin, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, mitochondrial fission inhibitors, and mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, highlighting both their therapeutic potential and current translational challenges. We propose that restoring the physiological equilibrium among mitochondrial fission, fusion, and mitophagy, rather than unidirectionally inhibiting a single pathway, represents a more promising strategy for preventing and treating diabetes and its complications.

papers.title: Excess Liver Fat in Type 2 Diabetes Stratified by Intrapancreatic Fat Deposition: A Meta-Analysis of Dual-Organ MRI Studies.
papers.abstract: Both liver fat content (LFC) and intrapancreatic fat deposition (IPFD) are frequently increased in Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). We meta-analysed dual-organ MRI studies comparing LFC between individuals with T2DM and non-diabetic controls and explored whether study-level differences in LFC varied according to IPFD burden. Seventeen studies (2142 participants) were included. Individuals with T2DM had significantly higher LFC than non-diabetic controls (standardised mean difference [SMD] 0.89, 95% CI 0.60-1.18). In exploratory subgroup analyses, liver fat excess was larger in studies with mean IPFD ≥ 10% than in those with IPFD < 10% (SMD 1.20 vs. 0.62; p = 0.04), though this finding was not consistently retained in leave-one-out analyses. Alternative IPFD cutoffs yielded directionally similar but non-significant subgroup differences. Study-level differences in IPFD were associated with differences in LFC (β = 0.383, p = 0.006) in univariable meta-regression, but not after BMI adjustment. These findings suggest that higher IPFD is associated with greater liver fat excess in T2DM at the study level. Individual-level analyses are now warranted to clarify this relationship.

papers.title: Pancreatic cancer cell and stellate cell-derived exosome crosstalk mediates pancreatic cancer-related diabetes.
papers.abstract: Diabetes is a known risk factor, and a distinct form termed pancreatic cancer-related diabetes (PCRD) often precedes the diagnosis of cancer by 3-5 years, offering a potential window for intervention. We hypothesised that interactions between stromal pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs) and cancer cells trigger secretion of exosomal factors that impair islet function and insulin signalling, contributing to PCRD pathogenesis. KC (KrasLSL-G12D/+; Pdx1-Cre) mice were fed a high-fructose diet (HFrD) or control diet for 16 weeks. Exosomes were isolated from monocultures and co-cultures of cancer/PanIN cells with PSCs, characterised by nanoparticle tracking analysis and transmission electron microscopy, and incubated with mouse β-cells (MIN6) and peripheral cells (hepatocytes, adipocytes, skeletal myocytes). Effects on insulin secretion and insulin-signalling factors were examined. Exosomal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) expression was modulated by siRNA to assess functional impact. HFrD induced marked glucose intolerance in KC mice and was accompanied by enhanced PSC activation, macrophage infiltration, inflammation, and accelerated PanIN progression. Exosomes from PSCs, cancer cells, and co-cultures displayed typical morphology and marker expression and were efficiently internalised by β-cells and hepatocytes. Functionally, exosomes significantly impaired glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in mouse and human β-cells without altering insulin content. In hepatocytes, PSC-, cancer-, and co-culture-derived exosomes reduced key insulin-signalling components, including IR, IRS, AKT, FOXO1 and GLUT2, and inhibited glucose uptake. Silencing exosomal G6PD partially restored hepatocyte insulin signalling. This study identifies a potential contributor to PCRD and suggests a possible mechanistic role for exosomal G6PD in impaired insulin signalling associated with PCRD.

papers.title: Gjb2 V37M Modifies Metabolic Responses to Chronic High-Fat Feeding in Mice.
papers.abstract: GJB2 encodes connexin 26 (Cx26), and pathogenic GJB2 variants are among the most common genetic causes of hereditary hearing loss; because Cx26 is expressed in metabolically relevant tissues including liver, pancreas, and adipose tissue, whether the hearing-loss-associated c.109G>A (p.V37M) variant also modifies systemic metabolic responses to high-fat diet (HFD) exposure remains unclear. Three-month-old male wild-type (WT) and homozygous Gjb2 V37M mice were assigned to low-fat diet (LFD) or high-fat diet (HFD) groups, generating four study groups: WT-LFD, WT-HFD, V37M-LFD, and V37M-HFD. The mice were followed until 12 months of age, with dietary intervention continued for 9 months. Body weight, body mass index (BMI), fasting blood glucose, serum triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol were assessed at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months. An oral glucose tolerance test was performed at 9 months, and omental fat was measured at 12 months. WT-HFD mice showed marked progressive increases in body weight and BMI, whereas increases were less pronounced in V37M-HFD mice. At 12 months, body weight and BMI did not differ significantly between V37M-LFD and V37M-HFD mice. Fasting glucose, glucose tolerance, triglyceride, and HDL cholesterol profiles differed among groups. Omental fat weight also differed significantly, although the only significant post hoc comparison was between WT-HFD and V37M-LFD mice. These findings indicate that Gjb2 V37M is associated with distinct weight, glycemic, and lipid responses during chronic dietary exposure, suggesting that GJB2 variants may modify systemic metabolic adaptation to chronic high-fat feeding.

papers.title: High Fat Diet Alters Gastrointestinal Function and Results in Reduced Enteric Neuron Density.
papers.abstract: Obese patients suffer from cardiovascular, metabolic and gastrointestinal disorders, including constipation, proposed to result from high fat diet (HFD)-induced enteric neuron loss. However, these studies used high-fat purified diets, containing reduced amounts of fiber compared to non-purified diets, known to alter gut physiology and microbiome composition. Therefore, we evaluated the effect of purified HFD-induced obesity on enteric neuron density and gastrointestinal transit compared to its proper control diet, that is, a purified control diet. Wild type mice were fed a standard chow diet, purified low fat diet (LFD) or HFD. Colonic transit was measured via glass bead expulsion following 12, 18, and 24 weeks of diet. Colonic muscularis externa was collected for immunofluorescent stainings of enteric neurons. Starting from 18 weeks of HFD, a decline in enteric neuron number was observed compared to LFD. In addition, delayed colonic transit was observed in HFD-fed mice when compared to LFD-fed animals after 18 weeks of exposure. Our study demonstrates that prolonged exposure to a HFD results in a reduced enteric neuron density and delayed colonic transit, and underscores the need to use a proper control diet when evaluating the impact of a HFD on gut physiology.

papers.title: Disentangling microbiota-dependent and -independent impacts of antibiotics on host physiology.
papers.abstract: Antibiotics are believed to affect host physiology by altering the gut microbiota. However, it remains unclear which effects of antibiotics are microbiota dependent and which are microbiota independent. Here we present a resource encompassing host and microbiota responses to antibiotic treatment and a computational tool with which to analyse them. Metagenomic and transcriptomic analyses of conventional and germ-free mice revealed that antibiotic administration routes and their combinations affect host and microbiota responses. We developed CompoRes-a computational tool that distinguishes the microbiota-independent impact of antibiotic-induced perturbations, revealing that antibiotics directly impact host physiology. We found that diurnal expression of major histocompatibility complex class II in the mouse colon is controlled by glucose via feeding. This pattern was lost during antibiotic treatment as vancomycin altered feeding behaviour in a microbiota-independent and evolutionarily conserved manner. Together, our study establishes a direct, non-microbial pathway by which antibiotics reshape host immunity and circadian physiology.

papers.title: Protein malnutrition facilitates intestinal colonization with highly resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae through disrupted intestinal microbial metabolism.
papers.abstract: Pediatric infections with highly resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (HR-Kp) disproportionately affect low-income countries where childhood malnutrition is prevalent. Malnutrition is an identified risk factor for infection with HR-Kp and other antimicrobial-resistant Enterobacterales, but the mechanistic underpinnings of this link and independence from other common exposures, like antibiotics, in children are unclear. Using a murine model of pediatric malnutrition, we found that mice fed a protein-deficient diet (PD) were more susceptible to colonization with HR-Kp at a 4-log lower challenge inoculum and developed a 3-log higher intestinal burden in comparison to adequately nourished mice. HR-Kp colonization in PD-fed mice persisted beyond 5 weeks, and colonization was transmitted to diet-matched cage mates. Antibiotic treatment resulted in similar HR-Kp colonization burdens regardless of diet, suggesting that nutrition-dependent colonization risk is driven by altered intestinal microbiota. Despite reduced dietary protein intake, intestinal amino acid content was maintained in PD-fed mice, supporting optimal HR-Kp growth. Furthermore, secondary bile acids, prototypic intestinal microbiota-derived molecules, were reduced in PD-fed mice, demonstrated an inverse correlation with HR-Kp burden in vivo , and partially inhibited the growth of HR-Kp in vitro . Collectively, these findings reveal a role for dietary protein intake in determining nutrition-dependent colonization resistance to HR-Kp.IMPORTANCEAntimicrobial-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae are responsible for a growing mortality burden worldwide, with disproportionate rates of infection in low-income countries where childhood malnutrition is prevalent. Several publications have demonstrated high rates of intestinal colonization with antimicrobial-resistant K. pneumoniae in children admitted with severe malnutrition in sub-Saharan Africa. However, numerous confounding risk factors in malnourished children (antibiotic use, healthcare exposure, and immune dysfunction) make it difficult to assess the direct impact of nutrition on K. pneumoniae colonization. In this study, we utilized a novel mouse model of protein malnutrition to demonstrate that dietary protein deficiency renders mice susceptible to a higher burden of intestinal colonization at a lower inoculating dose of K. pneumoniae . Furthermore, reduced microbiota-derived bile acid metabolites correlate with increased burden of colonization in protein-deficient mice. These results are the first to establish a direct mechanistic link associating dietary protein deficiency, bile acid metabolism, and intestinal colonization with antimicrobial-resistant K. pneumoniae .

papers.title: GART expression is associated with a proliferative and purine-metabolic ISC-like epithelial state in ulcerative colitis.
papers.abstract: To characterize the epithelial state associated with GART expression in ulcerative colitis (UC) and determine whether this association reflects a GART-specific program or a broader proliferative and purine-metabolic phenotype. Four independent bulk transcriptomic cohorts were analyzed and synthesized by random-effects meta-analysis. Human colonic scRNA-seq datasets (GSE214695 and SCP259) were integrated, with principal comparisons repeated using donor-aware pseudobulk or mixed-effects approaches and adjustment for sequencing depth, gene detection, and cell-cycle covariates. GART detection was defined from raw counts and tested using alternative thresholds. Pseudotime, scTenifoldKnk, CellChat/LIANA, and transcriptional-network analyses were used as exploratory analyses. Spatial transcriptomics (GSE189184), human colonic multiplex immunofluorescence, and acute DSS-induced colitis tissues were used for tissue-level localization. Across the four bulk cohorts, GART expression showed an overall increase in UC (pooled Hedges' g = 0.743, 95% CI 0.239-1.248; P = 0.0183). In the single-cell atlas, GART detection localized preferentially to an ISC-like epithelial compartment, although the magnitude of the UC-associated detection difference varied between cohorts. Within UC ISC-like cells, donor-paired pseudobulk analyses identified proliferative and nucleotide-metabolic transcriptional differences associated with GART detection. Across the broader ISC-like epithelial atlas, donor-aware module analyses showed positive associations of GART detection with purine-biosynthesis, DNA-replication, DNA-repair, and mitotic programs, and these associations remained positive within cell-cycle strata. Comparison with other de novo purine-synthesis enzymes did not support a uniquely GART-specific alteration. Exploratory network analyses linked the GART-associated state to proliferative and nucleotide-metabolic programs but did not establish functional dependence. In seven independent spatial donors, the single-cell-derived epithelial program was consistently higher in GART-detected than GART-undetected epithelial regions (mean within-donor difference = 0.0262, 95% CI 0.0140-0.0407; exact P = 0.0156). Human tissue immunofluorescence further showed co-enrichment of GART with OLFM4-positive ISC-like, MYBL2/Ki67-positive proliferative, and MIF/CD74-associated inflammatory regions across the corresponding panel-specific participant sets. GART identifies a proliferative and purine-metabolic ISC-like epithelial state in UC but is not established as a specific driver of epithelial regeneration. The findings support an association between GART detection, nucleotide-demand programs, proliferative epithelial activity, and the inflammatory tissue context, providing a framework for future direct functional studies.

papers.title: L-Histidine alleviates tacrolimus-induced islet dysfunction via the gut-pancreas axis.
papers.abstract: Tacrolimus is widely used after organ transplantation but can impair pancreatic β-cell function and glucose homeostasis. Using rodent models, antibiotic-mediated microbiota depletion, fecal microbiota transplantation, 16S rRNA sequencing, metabolomic profiling, and MIN-6 cells, we examined whether microbiota-associated L-histidine contributes to β-cell protection. Tacrolimus altered gut microbial composition and increased histidine-associated microbial and metabolic signals. L-histidine supplementation improved glucose tolerance and insulin secretion, reduced β-cell apoptosis, and increased PI3K/Akt/mTOR/p70S6K signaling and PDX-1, NeuroD1, and MafA expression. Microbiota depletion attenuated several protective effects of L-histidine, supporting a contribution of the gut microbiota to this response. These findings connect a microbiota-associated amino acid with tacrolimus-related β-cell dysfunction and provide a framework for investigating microbiota-metabolite contributions to metabolic complications of immunosuppression.

papers.title: Histidine alleviates copper-induced intestinal inflammation through oxidative stress-mediated mitochondrial damage and the Hif1α-Tnfα/Il1β pathway.
papers.abstract: Copper (Cu) is an essential trace element for vertebrates, but excessive intake can induce intestinal toxicity. Whether nutritional intervention can alleviate Cu overload-induced intestinal damage and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we combined in vivo animal experiments with in vitro cell models to investigate the protective effect of histidine against Cu-induced intestinal inflammation and its molecular mechanisms. Rainbow trout (weight: 7.24 ± 0.03 g) were fed diets containing 3.11 mg Cu/kg and 6.89 g His/kg (Control), 12.69 mg Cu/kg and 6.71 g His/kg (Cu), 3.24 mg Cu/kg and 10.94 g His/kg (His), 12.37 mg Cu/kg and 10.87 g His/kg (Cu+His) for 8 weeks. Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) were isolated from rainbow trout and incubated for 24-h in Cu (10 μM) and His (2.5 mM) solution. Histopathology, ultrastructural structure, oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage, and inflammation were determined in the intestine and IECs; fluorescence staining (DCFH-DA and JC-1), immunoblotting, immunofluorescence, siRNA, and ChIP were performed on IECs. Our research results indicate that Cu can induce intestinal oxidative stress, which in turn leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and activation of the Hif1α-Tnfα/Il1β signaling axis, ultimately exacerbating intestinal inflammatory responses. In contrast, co-treatment with Cu and histidine markedly attenuated the intestinal inflammatory phenotype. Mechanistically, histidine exerts anti-inflammatory effects by inhibiting oxidative stress, improving mitochondrial function and suppressing Hif1α, thereby preventing the occurrence of intestinal inflammation. This study is the first to elucidate the mechanism by which histidine alleviates Cu-induced intestinal inflammation and delineated the critical regulatory role of mitochondrial damage and the Hif1α-Tnfα/Il1β pathway in this process within a fish model. It provides a new theoretical basis for mitigating heavy metal toxicity through nutritional intervention.

papers.title: 2'-Fucosyllactose enhances indole-3-lactic acid production by Bifidobacterium bifidum DNG-08 and alleviates colitis-associated bone loss: Associations with microbiota remodeling and intestinal AHR-related responses.
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease is frequently associated with an imbalance in bone remodeling and a decline in bone mass, however, there is a lack of systematic research on microbiome-based intervention strategies targeting colitis-associated bone loss. In this study, Bifidobacterium bifidum DNG-08 (DNG-08) was selected from four candidate strains based on its favorable 2'-fucosyllactose (2'-FL) utilization and indole-3-lactic acid (ILA) production. Genomic annotation revealed that DNG-08 harbors functional genes related to fucosylated oligosaccharide utilization and the conversion of tryptophan to ILA. In a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model, combined intervention with DNG-08 and 2'-FL significantly alleviated colitis-associated phenotypes, and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels by 13.33%-58.69%, while increasing IL-10-1.23 times that of the DSS group. Simultaneously, the combined intervention improved trabecular bone microstructure, increasing the bone formation marker procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (PINP) by 14.61%-56.37%, decreasing the bone resorption marker C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX-I) by 17.03%-21.77%, and upregulating the expression of Wnt3a, β-catenin, and Runx2. Gut microbiota analysis showed that combined intervention could partially reverse DSS-induced dysbiosis, enriching potentially beneficial bacterial taxa while reducing inflammation-associated genera. Notably, combined treatment group exhibited elevated serum ILA levels, increased colonic aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) fluorescence, and upregulatied CYP1A1 expression. Correlation analysis identified significant associations among serum ILA, AHR-related indicators, selected bacterial genera, and bone remodeling parameters. This study highlights that strain-substrate matching may serve as a precise synbiotic strategy to improve inflammation-related gut-bone axis dysfunction.

papers.title: Linking the fine structural characteristics of cereal β-glucans to their differential protective effects against colitis.
papers.abstract: Although cereal β-glucans exert protective effects against experimental colitis, the relationship between their fine structural and physicochemical properties and differential in vivo responses remains unclear. This study directly compared highland barley β-glucan (BBG) and oat β-glucan (OBG), two high-purity mixed-linkage β-(1 → 3)/(1 → 4)-D-glucans, under identical experimental conditions. BBG had a higher cellotriosyl-to-cellotetraosyl (DP3/DP4) ratio than OBG (2.33 vs. 1.51) and a lower weight-average molecular weight. In dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis mice, both β-glucans alleviated clinical signs of disease, while BBG showed greater protection at the tissue and biochemical levels. BBG preserved colon length at 4.88 cm, compared with 4.46 cm for OBG. It reduced myeloperoxidase activity, nitric oxide, and malondialdehyde levels to 1226 U g -1 , 0.42 μmol g -1 , and 78.8 nmol mg -1 , respectively, and fully restored Claudin-1 expression. BBG was also associated with enrichment of Ligilactobacillus , Limosilactobacillus , Romboutsia , and Turicibacter and suppression of Escherichia-Shigella . Fecal metabolomics showed higher levels of selected indole derivatives and taurine-conjugated bile acids, accompanied by lower uric acid and prostaglandin-related inflammatory metabolites. These in vivo differences were accompanied by distinct physicochemical behaviors. BBG showed faster self-aggregation, with a shorter lag time than OBG (112.9 vs . 256.0 min), accompanied by a markedly higher storage modulus (360 vs. 66 Pa). BBG also showed stronger intestinal-phase reassembly under simulated gastrointestinal conditions, approximately threefold greater bile acid retention during dynamic dialysis, and higher DPPH radical-scavenging activity (11.8% vs. 4.8%). Overall, the differential intestinal responses to BBG and OBG were accompanied by distinct physicochemical, microbial, and metabolic profiles, supporting a potential aggregation between cereal β-glucan fine structure, supramolecular behavior, and protective effects against colitis.

papers.title: Comparative dietary profiling of smoked and non-smoked paprika ( Capsicum annuum L.) in Wistar rats: metabolomic, biochemical and gut microbiota responses in a healthy animal model.
papers.abstract: Paprika ( Capsicum annuum L.) is a widely consumed spice whose bioactive composition is substantially influenced by processing conditions. Traditional smoking, as applied in the production of PDO Pimentón de la Vera, enriches paprika with wood smoke-derived phenolics while also introducing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), warranting an integrated evaluation of processing-related biological responses and safety considerations. This study compared physiological, biochemical, metabolomic, and cecal microbiota responses to dietary supplementation with smoked and non-smoked paprika in healthy Wistar rats. Thirty animals of both sexes (16 females and 14 males) received a control diet or diets supplemented with 5% smoked or non-smoked paprika for 30 days. Histological examination revealed no treatment-related alterations in the organs evaluated. Hematological and biochemical analyses showed diet- and sex-associated differences in hematocrit, plasma glucose, total antioxidant capacity, and lipid-related parameters, although all values remained within normal physiological ranges. Untargeted urinary metabolomics, restricted to males because of insufficient urine volume in females, identified features tentatively annotated as phenolic conjugates and other metabolites associated with paprika intake, with several signals showing higher abundance in the smoked paprika group. Cecal metagenomic analyses showed sex-dependent changes across taxon-level abundance, alpha diversity, and beta diversity. In females receiving smoked paprika, lower TC and LDL-C coincided with higher alpha diversity and lower cecal lipid content, suggesting a potential link between intestinal microbial ecology and lipid handling. Overall, paprika processing was associated with distinct biochemical, metabolomic, and cecal microbiota response patterns in this healthy animal model.

papers.title: Impact of mixed nut consumption on faecal lipid content and gut microbiota composition in healthy adults.
papers.abstract: Nuts are a source of dietary fibre and are considered a nutritious snack despite their high fat content. The effects of nut consumption on the microbiota and the role of nut-derived lipids in altering the large intestinal microbial community remain poorly understood. This study examined changes in faecal characteristics and microbiota composition in 15 healthy volunteers consuming unrestricted diets during a cross-over dietary intervention consisting of three weeks of daily mixed-nut consumption (30 g almonds, macadamias and pistachios) and three weeks of nut abstinence. Microscopic examination of faecal samples revealed lipid-containing nut particles following nut consumption, which were not observed during the nut abstinence. Mixed nut consumption was associated with a significant increase in total faecal lipid content compared with nut abstinence ( P < 0.05), suggesting incomplete digestion and absorption of nut-derived lipids. In contrast, faecal pH, dry matter, ash content, short-chain fatty acids and ammonium concentrations were not significantly altered by the intervention. 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis demonstrated substantial inter-individual variation in gut microbial community composition, with only modest differences associated with nut consumption. Predicted functional profiling suggested variation in pathways related to lipid metabolism between intervention periods. Overall, the findings indicate that a portion of consumed nut cells likely reaches the large intestine intact. Upon degradation of the nut cell wall, encapsulated lipids may become available to the colonic microbiota, potentially contributing to microbial metabolism and community responses observed.

Spleen.description: In grass carp, pyridaben exposure disrupted splenic mitochondrial morphology, suppressed glycometabolism-related genes and reduced ATP levels [4], and 6-Gingerol effectively mitigated these PDB-induced mitochondrial dysfunctions [4], an effect linked to AMPK, which counteracts PDB-induced decline of PGC1α in spleen [4]. Redox metabolism is also implicated: in infected goslings, the spleen showed increased iron content, elevated malondialdehyde (MDA) production, decreased glutathione (GSH) content, and reduced glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px) activity [3], alongside upregulated genes and proteins linked to ferroptosis and mitophagy [3]. Transcriptomic data from infected fish show that a substantial portion of these genes clustered within biological activities linked to immunity and metabolic regulation [5]. The spleen also acts as a site of xenobiotic accumulation, as black phosphorus and its degradation products primarily accumulated in the liver and spleen [10], and its transformation was driven by nitric oxide synthase (NOS)-mediated nitric oxide (NO) generation [10]. Documents do not describe spleen-specific hormonal control; the closest evidence is that BPA significantly increased insulin resistance [7].

papers.title: Stepwise derivatization GC-MS/MS of 39 FFAs in spleen-deficiency rat liver.
papers.abstract: Free fatty acids (FFAs) are important targets in metabolic diseases. However, accurate quantification of a wide range of C2-C24 FFAs in the liver is challenging due to their structural diversity and large variations in abundance. To address this, a stepwise derivatization pretreatment was employed in this study: after liver homogenization, short-chain fatty acids were first extracted with diethyl ether-water (1:1, V/V). The ether layer was dehydrated with anhydrous Na 2 SO 4 and then derivatized with BSTFA. The remaining pellet was extracted with chloroform-methanol (1:2, V/V), and after nitrogen evaporation, the extract was subjected to methyl esterification. A quantitative method for 39 FFAs was established on a Trace1600-TSQ9610 platform (TG-SQC column, MRM mode). Methodological validation showed that for all FFAs, the linear correlation coefficients R 2 were ≥ 0.991, intra- and inter-day accuracies ranged from 85.94% to 115.28%, precision RSD ≤ 13.16%, stability RSD ≤ 14.91%, and the LLOQ ranged from 0.03 to 10 μg/mL. When applied to the livers of spleen-deficiency SD rats, the method revealed significant decreases in C14:0, C15:0, and C18:0, and significant increases in C9:0, C18:1n9c, and C20:4n6 (VIP > 1, |Log 2 FC| > 1, P < 0.05). This method provides a reliable tool for hepatic FFA profiling and the discovery of preliminary candidate biomarkers. Limitations of this study include a small sample size (n = 3 per group), which may affect the robustness of the supervised OPLS-DA model and the interpretation of the differential findings, and the extraction recovery was not independently evaluated.

papers.title: Total Ginsenosides from Panax ginseng Improve Exercise Tolerance in Rats with Spleen Qi Deficiency-like Features: Integrated Metabolomics of Serum and Hepatic Mitochondria-enriched Fractions.
papers.abstract: Panax ginseng C.A.Mey. has traditionally been used to replenish Qi and strengthen the spleen, including for poor appetite and weakness associated with spleen deficiency. Ginsenosides are major constituents, but their metabolic effects under spleen Qi deficiency-like conditions remain to be clarified. To evaluate whether total ginsenosides (TGS) improve spleen Qi deficiency-like features in rats and characterize systemic and hepatic metabolic changes. A rat model was established using 50% food restriction combined with repeated weight-loaded swimming, and TGS (75, 150, or 300 mg·kg -1 ) was administered for 21 days. Body weight, grip strength, swimming endurance, biochemical indices, and mitochondrial ultrastructure were evaluated. Untargeted metabolomic analyses of serum and hepatic mitochondria-enriched fractions were performed in the control (CON), model (MOD), and high-dose TGS (TGS-H) groups, and hepatic SIRT1 and PGC-1α protein expression was measured. Lipid accumulation, mitochondrial membrane potential, and SIRT1 and PGC-1α expression were also examined in oleic acid-treated HepG2 cells. TGS, particularly at 300 mg·kg -1 , attenuated the suppression of body-weight gain and improved grip strength and swimming endurance. These functional improvements were accompanied by increased ATP content and ATPase activities and attenuation of mitochondrial ultrastructural abnormalities. After TGS-H treatment, serum levels of several amino acids increased, and lipid profiles shifted toward the control pattern. In hepatic mitochondria-enriched fractions, accumulation of selected fatty acids decreased, and levels of selected organic acids increased. TGS increased hepatic PGC-1α protein expression at all three doses, whereas SIRT1 expression increased significantly only at the high dose. In oleic acid-treated HepG2 cells, increased expression of both proteins was accompanied by reduced lipid accumulation and partial recovery of mitochondrial membrane potential. In rats with spleen Qi deficiency-like features induced by limited nutritional supply and repeated physical exertion, TGS attenuated the suppression of body-weight gain and improved exercise tolerance, accompanied by changes in energy-related indices. These findings provide experimental support for the traditional use of ginseng to replenish Qi and strengthen the spleen in relation to symptoms of weakness.

papers.title: GoAstV Induced Mitophagy and Ferroptosis in the Spleen of Goslings.
papers.abstract: A novel goose astrovirus (GoAstV) has emerged in various provinces of China, leading to a mortality rate of up to 50% among GoAstV goslings. The spleen is an important immune organ in geese. Studies have shown that goslings infected with GoAstV exhibit higher viral loads in their spleens, and the spleens sustain damage. However, the mechanism underlying its induction of spleen injury remains to be elucidated. Therefore, a gosling infection model with GoAstV was established in this experiment. The Con group was subcutaneously injected with 0.2 mL of saline, while the GoAstV group was subcutaneously injected with GoAstV JX01 (2 × 10 6 TCID50/0.2 mL). Spleen tissues were collected on days 1, 3, 6, 9 post-infection (dpi). The results showed that the body weight of the GoAstV group decreased significantly, while the spleen weight and spleen index increased significantly. Post-mortem examination revealed that the spleen of the GoAstV group was significantly enlarged. The viral load in the spleen reached its peak at 6 dpi. Histopathological and electron microscopy revealed lymphocyte necrosis, autophagic lysosomes, and mitochondria autophagosomes. The spleen of the GoAstV group exhibited increased iron content, elevated malondialdehyde (MDA) production, decreased glutathione (GSH) content, and reduced glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px) activity. RT-qPCR and Western blot analyses revealed that GoAstV upregulated mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and inhibited anti-inflammatory cytokines. GoAstV also upregulated genes and proteins linked to ferroptosis and mitophagy, while downregulating those associated with anti-ferroptosis and SQSTM1. In conclusion, our findings suggest that GoAstV infection may induce mitophagy and ferroptosis in the gosling spleen, thereby contributing to splenic injury.

papers.title: Effects of pyridaben on the spleen and T lymphocytes and intervention strategy in grass carp (Ctenopharyngodon idella).
papers.abstract: The widespread use of pyridaben (PDB) poses serious threat to aquatic organism health. 6-Gingerol, a bioactive component of ginger, has been demonstrated to possess both antioxidant and immunomodulatory properties. However, the effects of spleen injury of PDB in aquatic species and the potential mitigating effects of 6-Gingerol remain insufficiently characterized. The present study aimed to characterize the toxic effects of PDB on the spleen of grass carp and to evaluate whether 6-Gingerol could effectively counteract PDB-induced toxicity. The results showed that PDB exposure could induce splenic erythrocyte extravasation, vacuolization, interstitial arrangement loose and apoptosis. Flow cytometry further revealed that PDB exposure decreased the proportion of splenic CD4 T-lymphocytes by 9.47% while increasing CD8 T-lymphocytes by 5.91%. In contrast, 6-Gingerol treatment reversed above pathological spleen injury and recover splenic CD4/CD8 T lymphocytes disturbance. Meanwhile, PDB exposure could disrupt mitochondrial morphology in grass carp spleen, accompanied by the suppression of glycometabolism-related genes and reduction in ATP levels. In contrast, treatment with 6-Gingerol effectively mitigated these PDB-induced mitochondrial dysfunctions. Further analyses confirm that 6-Gingerol inhibits PDB-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) overload and 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) overproduction, accompanied restoration of Nrf2 nuclear accumulation. Importantly, 6-Gingerol positively regulates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) to counteract PDB-induced decline of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma coactivator 1 α (PGC1α) in spleen. In conclusion, our results suggest that 6-Gingerol alleviates PDB-induced immunotoxicity and protects mitochondrial function in grass carp, an effect associated with the regulation of the AMPK signaling pathway. These findings provide theoretical basis for understanding the aquatic toxicity induced by PDB and offer new insights into the protective strategy of 6-Gingerol against toxic substances.

papers.title: Transcriptomic analysis reveals the immune response mechanisms of Acrossocheilus fasciatus against Citrobacter freundii infection.
papers.abstract: Acrossocheilus fasciatus is an economically important freshwater fish species in China. In recent years, Citrobacter freundii infection has caused significant harm to the aquaculture industry. In this study, we performed histological observation and RNA-seq analysis of the intestines and spleens of control (CK) and C. freundii infected A. fasciatus (EG). The results showed that infected fish exhibited abdominal haemorrhage, intestinal villous shedding, hydropic degeneration of hepatocytes and splenic sinus dilation with congestion. RNA-seq analysis identified 3054 DEGs in the intestine and 7706 DEGs in the spleen, with 1247 overlapping DEGs identified by combined analysis. A substantial portion of these genes clustered within biological activities linked to immunity and metabolic regulation, particularly engaging immune-related routes such as endoplasmic reticulum-based protein maturation, alongside the complement system and coagulation signalling cascades. This study systematically reveals the synergy and division of labor between the intestine and spleen during C. freundii infection, providing fundamental data for understanding the immune response mechanisms of A. fasciatus and a theoretical basis for optimising disease prevention and control strategies.

papers.title: Theabrownin from Pu-erh Tea Restores Intestinal Immunity via Gut Microbiota-Metabolite Network in Immunosuppressed Mice.
papers.abstract: Theabrownin (TB), a polymeric pigment derived from ripened Pu-erh tea, demonstrates beneficial effects on lipid reduction, weight management, and mitigation of metabolic syndrome. However, the role of TB in restoring immune function in vivo has not been studied. This study evaluated the therapeutic effects and underlying mechanisms of TB in cyclophosphamide (CTX)-induced immunosuppressed mice. TB was administered at doses of 1.215, 0.608, and 0.304 mg/kg body weight, with levamisole hydrochloride (40 mg/kg) serving as a positive drug control. Each experimental group comprised eight mice. Evaluations primarily consisted of histopathological examination, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, Western blotting, flow cytometry, 16S rRNA sequencing, and ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS)-based untargeted metabolomics. The results demonstrate that high- and medium-dose TB treatment significantly alleviated immunosuppression, as evidenced by restored body and organ weights, colon length, splenic and colonic histoarchitecture, blood cell counts, and immunoglobulin levels. These improvements correlated with upregulated colonic cytokines, claudin-1, occludin, toll-like receptor 2/4, and reduced regulatory T cell populations. High- and medium-dose TB treatment also enriched beneficial gut microbiota, including Lactobacillus and Candidatus saccharimonas , accompanied by strong microbiota-metabolite correlations (M 2 = 0.725, p = 0.003). Metabolic KEGG pathway enrichment analysis revealed that moderate-dose TB significantly activated caffeine metabolism and histidine metabolism, accompanied by the enrichment of multiple immune signaling pathways driven by diacylglycerol series lipid metabolites, whereas high-dose TB induced a greater number of immune signaling pathways. Overall, TB may reverse CTX-induced immunosuppression by integrating gut microbiota-metabolite reprogramming, highlighting TB's potential as an immunomodulatory functional component of medicine-food homologous products.

papers.title: High Normal dietary casein attenuates bisphenol A-induced multiorgan toxicity in rats: Preservation of renal integrity, glucose homeostasis, and immune surveillance via modulation of oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis.
papers.abstract: Bisphenol A (BPA) causes multiorgan toxicity via oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis, and the effect of nutritionally relevant elevation of casein intake is unknown. To evaluate whether a nutritionally relevant elevation of dietary casein (18% vs. 14%) attenuates BPA-induced multiorgan toxicity in rats, male Wistar rats were divided into four groups (n = 8/group) and treated for 35 days: control (14% casein), casein 18% alone, BPA (50 mg/kg/day +14% casein), and BPA + 18% casein. We measured oxidative and inflammatory markers, renal function, metabolic parameters, hematological parameters, histopathology and immunohistochemistry in kidney, spleen, and pancreas. BPA significantly increased malondialdehyde, interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, creatinine, kidney injury molecule-1, insulin resistance, white blood cells, neutrophils, and monocytes, and decreased reduced glutathione, glutathione S-transferase, superoxide dismutase, catalase, interleukin-4, serum soluble CD4 and CD8 protein levels, hemoglobin, red blood cells, platelets, and lymphocytes. BPA also caused renal tubular necrosis, splenic degeneration, pancreatic fibrosis, and upregulated caspase-3 and inducible nitric oxide synthase. Co-administration of 18% casein partially attenuated these effects, reducing malondialdehyde by 35-40%, creatinine by 40%, and insulin resistance by 53%, and restoring antioxidant enzymes and glucose tolerance. However, several parameters remained significantly different from controls. Nutritionally relevant elevation of casein (18%) provides significant partial protection against BPA-induced toxicity, supporting dietary protein modulation as a supportive strategy.

papers.title: A Metabolomics and Network Pharmacology Approach Using LC-MS to Investigate the Mechanisms of Fufang Ejiao Jiang in Treating Chemotherapy-Induced Myelosuppression.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the mechanism and pharmacologically active compounds of Fufang Ejiao Jiang (FFEJJ) in the prevention and treatment of myelosuppression after chemotherapy (MAC) through a combination of serum metabolomics and network pharmacology. Sprague Dawley rats were randomly assigned to three groups: the blank group, the model group, and the FFEJJ group (10.8 g/kg). A MAC rat model was induced using cyclophosphamide. Simultaneously with model establishment, rats were intragastrically administered once daily for 15 consecutive days. The routine blood parameters of the rats were measured, and pathological changes in the spleen and bone marrow were observed. Nontargeted serum metabolomics was employed to identify differential metabolites associated with MAC and their related pathways. Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) was used to analyze the chemical composition of FFEJJ, and its mechanism and pharmacologically active compounds in the treatment of MAC were further predicted using network pharmacology. FFEJJ significantly improved the hematopoietic function of bone marrow in the MAC model rats. Compared to the blank group, the model group exhibited obvious spleen injury and bone marrow disorder, with noticeable fatty infiltration in the bone marrow cavity. Following FFEJJ treatment, the condition of spleen tissue and bone marrow in MAC rats was significantly improved. Serum metabolomics analysis of endogenous metabolites identified 14 differential metabolites associated with the MAC mechanism in both positive and negative ion modes, primarily involving pathways such as aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis, primary bile acid biosynthesis, and unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis. Using LC-MS, 31 components were identified in FFEJJ. Network pharmacology predictions suggest that the potential pharmacologically active compounds of FFEJJ in the treatment of MAC include apigenin, oleanolic acid, maslinic acid, and azelaic acid. The underlying mechanism may be partly associated with the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/serine-threonine kinase (PI3K-Akt) signaling pathway. FFEJJ promotes hematopoietic recovery in MAC rats, likely by regulating endogenous metabolic disorders. Apigenin, oleanolic acid, maslinic acid, and azelaic acid are predicted to be multitarget active compounds, with PI3K-Akt signaling as a candidate pathway.

papers.title: Tirzepatide alleviates hepatic steatosis and inflammation in MASLD partly through suppression of macrophage Dectin-1/Syk/NF-κB signaling.
papers.abstract: Metabolic stress, hepatic lipid accumulation, and macrophage-associated sterile inflammation are closely involved in the development of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Tirzepatide improves metabolic outcomes, but its effects on macrophage inflammatory signaling in MASLD remain unclear. This study investigated the protective effects of tirzepatide against high-fat, high-fructose diet (HFHFD)-induced MASLD and examined the potential involvement of macrophage Dectin-1/spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk)/nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling. After 7 weeks of HFHFD feeding to establish the MASLD model, male C57BL/6J mice received tirzepatide (10 nmol/kg, subcutaneously, every 3 days) for an additional 7 weeks. Biochemical assays, histology, hepatic RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence were performed. Palmitic acid (PA)-stimulated RAW264.7 cells, siRNA-mediated Dectin-1 knockdown, and a RAW264.7 cell-derived conditioned medium-based macrophage-hepatocyte indirect interaction model were used for mechanistic validation. Tirzepatide treatment improved HFHFD-induced metabolic dysfunction, liver injury, hepatic steatosis, and inflammatory responses in mice. RNA-seq revealed enrichment of C-type lectin receptor and NF-κB signaling pathways, while HFHFD-induced Clec7a upregulation was reversed by tirzepatide. Tirzepatide reduced hepatic macrophage accumulation, Dectin-1 expression, and Syk/p65 phosphorylation. In PA-stimulated RAW264.7 cells, tirzepatide suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokine expression and secretion and inhibited Dectin-1/Syk/NF-κB activation. Conditioned medium from tirzepatide-treated RAW264.7 cells attenuated lipid accumulation and abnormalities in lipid metabolism- and inflammation-related gene expression in HepG2 cells. Dectin-1 knockdown itself attenuated PA-induced inflammatory responses and was associated with a reduced additional response to tirzepatide. These findings suggest that tirzepatide alleviates HFHFD-induced MASLD, with suppression of macrophage Dectin-1/Syk/NF-κB signaling potentially contributing to these effects.

papers.title: Mass Spectrometry Imaging Reveals Biodistribution and Biotransformation of Black Phosphorus.
papers.abstract: Black phosphorus (BP) holds significant potential in biomedicine, biosensing, and phototherapy; however, its instability and the poor understanding of its in vivo fate have limited its applications. Here, we developed an integrated label-free mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) platform to investigate BP's in vivo distribution, transformation, clearance, and metabolism in tumor-bearing mice. We detected BPs and related nitrogen/oxygen-containing phosphorus (P) clusters in six organs and tumor tissues, revealing distinctive tissue distributions. BP and its degradation products primarily accumulated in the liver and spleen, with the liver showing a radial distribution pattern around hepatic lobules. Notably, BP and related clusters can cross the blood-brain barrier into brain parenchyma. We further establish the in vivo transformation and metabolic pathways of BPs. Cellular experiments confirmed that nitric oxide synthase (NOS)-mediated nitric oxide (NO) generation drives BP nitridation during its transformation and metabolism under physiological conditions. This work not only provides vital information for biomedical applications of BP, but also establishes a platform for understanding in vivo translocation and transformation of nanomaterials, aiding their biosafety and health impact assessments.

Thyroid.description: Athyreotic patients lack intrinsic thyroidal triiodothyronine secretion and depend entirely on the peripheral conversion of levothyroxine to generate circulating and intracellular triiodothyronine [1]. In experimental diabetes, myocardial triiodothyronine (T3) can decline despite preserved circulating thyroid hormone concentrations, accompanied by type 3 iodothyronine deiodinase (DIO3) induction and altered TH transport [6]. Downstream effectors of this signaling include mitochondrial biogenesis, reactive oxygen species control, mitophagy and calcium handling [6]. In the liver, reduced hepatic thyroid hormone sensitivity, even in euthyroid individuals, predicts steatosis and fibrosis [9], and in men with obesity, liver function markers (ALT, AST, GGT) and thyroid hormones (fT3, tT3) [5] were positively correlated. Peripheral thyroid hormone handling also tracks with physiological status, as lower FT3 levels and FT3/FT4 ratios were associated with greater frailty in hospitalized older adults [2]. Absorption and supply are affected by gut factors, since after bariatric surgery FT4 AUC0-6h increased significantly after surgery [3], and the observed microbiome-LT4 association was modest and should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than causal [3]. Thyroid status also intersects with glucose handling, as thyroid dysfunction was prevalent in T2DM patients and was associated with poorer glycemic control [4]. Finally, in differentiated thyroid cancer, locally advanced differentiated thyroid cancers appear to exhibit a metabolic phenotype characterized by adrenergic suppression, immune evasion, invasive membrane remodeling, nucleotide and methylation flux, bioenergetic collapse, and resource shunting, all at the expense of differentiated and homeostatic functions [10].

papers.title: Athyreosis and Thyroid Hormone Signaling: A System-Based Framework for Long-Term Endocrine Health.
papers.abstract: Thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine therapy are definitive treatments for Graves' disease, toxic nodular disease, and differentiated thyroid cancer. With improving survival rates and expanding indications for definitive therapy, a growing population is living for decades in a state of athyreosis requiring lifelong thyroid hormone replacement. Current management strategies largely emphasize serum thyroid-stimulating hormone targets and oncological surveillance, yet the long-term metabolic and physiological implications of chronic athyreosis remain incompletely explored. The potential longevity implications of long-term athyreosis are examined through a system-based framework integrating hormonal balance, mitochondrial regulation, metabolic adaptation, skeletal and cardiovascular health, and inflammatory signaling. This narrative review synthesizes evidence from endocrinology, metabolism, oncology, and aging research to evaluate physiological differences between endogenous thyroid hormone secretion and pharmacological replacement in athyreotic patients. Particular attention is given to tissue-level triiodothyronine availability, deiodinase activity, and downstream bioenergetic effects. Athyreotic patients lack intrinsic thyroidal triiodothyronine secretion and depend entirely on the peripheral conversion of levothyroxine to generate circulating and intracellular triiodothyronine. Emerging evidence suggests that levothyroxine monotherapy may not fully replicate physiological thyroid hormone dynamics in all individuals, potentially influencing mitochondrial biogenesis, resting energy expenditure, body composition, bone turnover, and cardiovascular remodeling. In thyroid cancer survivors, chronic thyroid-stimulating hormone suppression introduces additional considerations for skeletal and cardiac outcomes. Patients treated for autoimmune thyroid disease may also exhibit persistent immune dysregulation despite gland ablation. Athyreosis represents a distinct and permanent endocrine state with implications extending beyond biochemical euthyroidism. A system-based perspective that considers mitochondrial resilience, cardiometabolic integrity, skeletal preservation, and inflammatory tone may enhance long-term management strategies for this expanding survivorship population. Prospective studies are needed to clarify the impact of various thyroid hormone replacement paradigms on functional aging and longevity outcomes.

papers.title: Thyroid function and frailty in hospitalized older adults: the role of FT3 and FT3/FT4 ratio.
papers.abstract: Frailty is a crucial factor in managing older adults, given its strong predictive power for adverse health outcomes. Recent attention has focused on the relationship between frailty and thyroid function, particularly the so-called low T3 syndrome. However, the relationship between frailty and peripheral thyroid hormone metabolism remains under-investigated. This cross-sectional study included 112 patients hospitalized in a single-centre geriatric unit. Data on thyroid function, cognitive performance (MMSE), handgrip strength, and comorbidities were collected. Frailty was assessed using the Rockwood Frailty Index (FI), with FI > 0.25 indicating frailty. The study population (58 men, 54 women; median age 81 years) showed mild cognitive impairment (MMSE median 22.0; IQR 18.0-26.3) and reduced handgrip strength (13 kg; 10-20 kg). Median FI was 0.304 (0.196-0.383), and 62.5% of patients were frail. Frail patients were older and had significantly lower MMSE scores, weaker handgrip strength, and poorer renal function. FT3 levels and the FT3/FT4 ratio were significantly lower in frail than non-frail patients (P = 0.001 and P = 0.005, respectively). Increasing FT3/FT4 quartiles were associated with progressively lower FI values and frailty prevalence (P = 0.032 and P for trend = 0.042, respectively). In multivariable analysis, age (P = 0.017), MMSE (P < 0.001), and the FT3/FT4 ratio (P = 0.016) were independently associated with FI. Lower FT3 levels and FT3/FT4 ratios were associated with greater frailty in hospitalized older adults. Prospective studies are warranted to validate their clinical utility as biomarkers of frailty.

papers.title: Levothyroxine dose requirements, oral bioavailability and gut microbiome enterotype dynamics during the early post-bariatric period: a single-centre, prospective, cohort study.
papers.abstract: Bariatric surgery induces profound metabolic changes; however, its impact on levothyroxine (LT4) requirements, hormone pharmacokinetics, and gut microbiome composition remains incompletely understood. The current study is aimed to evaluate longitudinal changes in metabolic parameters, LT4 dose requirements, free thyroxin (FT4) absorption (AUC₀-₆h), and gut microbiome features following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) and sleeve gastrectomy (SG). In this prospective cohort study, 79 patients with hypothyroidism undergoing bariatric surgery (RYGB n = 40; SG n = 39) were followed at baseline, 3 month, and 6 months postoperatively. Metabolic parameters, thyroid function, LT4 dose, FT4 AUC₀-₆h, and gut microbiome diversity were assessed using linear mixed-effects models. Both groups showed significant metabolic improvement at 6 months, including reductions in body mass index (RYGB: 44.5 → 32.1 kg/m²; SG: 42.9 → 33.0 kg/m², p < 0.001) and fasting blood sugar (RYGB: 114.8 → 92.4 mg/dL; SG: 109.9 → 96.1 mg/dL, p < 0.001). LT4 requirements increased significantly, particularly in RYGB (137.5 → 158.2 µg/day; p = 0.018) and SG (133.3 → 144.8 µg/day; p = 0.067), with a stronger effect in weight-adjusted dose (both p < 0.05). FT4 AUC₀-₆h increased significantly after surgery (RYGB: +330 ± 210, p = 0.003; SG: +185 ± 190, p = 0.041), indicating altered LT4 pharmacokinetics. Gut microbiome analysis revealed increased Shannon diversity (RYGB p-trend = 0.048) and significant enrichment of Akkermansia muciniphila (1.20% → 2.40%, p < 0.001), particularly in RYGB. After false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment, the major longitudinal changes remained significant, particularly for metabolic parameters, LT4 dose (µg/kg/day), and Akkermansia muciniphila in the RYGB group. Patient-level analyses showed a modest positive association between changes in A. muciniphila abundance and FT4 AUC₀-₆h after multivariable adjustment, whereas other microbiome-LT4 associations were not significant. Bariatric surgery was associated with substantial metabolic improvement, increased LT4 requirements, increased systemic FT4 exposure, and changes in gut microbiome composition. The observed microbiome-LT4 association was modest and should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than causal. These findings highlight the need for individualized thyroid function monitoring and LT4 dose adjustment during the postoperative period. Not applicable.

papers.title: Thyroid Dysfunction and Its Association with Glycemic Control in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM): A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is characterized by metabolic anomalies, such as hyperglycemia, resulting from pancreatic β-cell dysfunction. In this context, thyroid dysfunction is the second most prevalent endocrine disorder after DM, and the interaction with glycemic control in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) remains a topic of debate. Therefore, this meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the impact of thyroid dysfunction on glycemic control in T2DM patients. A systematic literature search was conducted using ScienceDirect, the Cochrane Library, and PubMed up to December 8, 2024, under PRISMA guidelines. Research evaluating the effect of thyroid dysfunction on glycemic control in T2DM was included, with Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels as the primary outcome measure. Furthermore, research lacking relevant outcome data, full-text availability, or appropriate design was excluded. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed collaboratively, using the STROBE checklist. Meta-analysis was conducted using Review Manager 5.4, with mean difference (MD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) as the effect size. Random-effects models were used to account for anticipated clinical heterogeneity, assessed by Higgins' I-squared (I²) statistic. The initial search identified 1,397 research studies, with only 3 papers meeting the inclusion criteria. A pooled analysis reported a significant increase in HbA1c levels in T2DM patients with thyroid dysfunction (MD: 1.94, 95% CI: 0.73 - 3.14; p < 0.000001) with high heterogeneity (I² = 98%). Thyroid dysfunction was prevalent in T2DM patients and was associated with poorer glycemic control. Routine thyroid function assessment could also be integrated into T2DM management to optimize metabolic outcomes.

papers.title: The hepato-thyroid axis in male obesity: unraveling inter-organ crosstalk through non-invasive biomarkers.
papers.abstract: To investigate the relationship between liver function and thyroid function tests in men with overweight and obesity. Body-mass-index (BMI), relative-fat-mass (RFM), Fibrosis-4-index (FIB-4), hepatic-steatosis-index (HSI), fatty-liver-index (FLI), albumin-bilirubin-grade (ALBI), and triglyceride-glucose-index (TyG-index) were used to perform a correlation study on liver and thyroid functions in the male participants with overweight/obesity. We utilized data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2011-2012. We performed correlation analysis to examine these relationships. This study enrolled 811 male participants, including 263 lean and 548 individuals with overweight/obesity based on BMI. Analysis showed that 133 subjects had RFM of < 22.8%, while 678 were overweight/obese. Significant positive correlations were found between liver function markers (ALT, AST, GGT) and thyroid hormones (fT3, tT3), as well as between non-invasive liver indices (HSI and FLI for steatosis, ALBI for function and prognosis, and FIB-4 for fibrosis risk) and thyroid function parameters. ALBI was positively correlated with globulin, BMI, and tT4, and it had significant negative correlation with tT3, fT3, fT4, total protein, ALT, and AST. FIB-4 was positively correlated with TSH, and tT4 ( p  = 0.0026, and 0.0147, respectively). It had significant negative correlation with tT3, fT3, and BMI ( p  = 0.0122, < 0.0001, and 0.0008, respectively). FIB-4 had significant weak correlation with TSH in euthyroid subjects ( r  = 0.077 and p  = 0.034). In this study, several non-invasive liver indices were significantly associated with thyroid function parameters in men with obesity. Indices may assist in identifying individuals at higher risk of liver-thyroid dysfunction, though prospective studies are needed to confirm their utility. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40200-026-02107-y.

papers.title: Disrupted thyroid hormone-mitochondrial coupling in diabetic cardiomyopathy: a candidate upstream amplifier of metabolic and redox maladaptation.
papers.abstract: Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is characterized by mitochondrial metabolic inflexibility, redox imbalance and defective organelle quality control, yet the endocrine program coordinating these abnormalities remains incompletely defined. Thyroid hormone (TH) is a major regulator of cardiac energy metabolism and mitochondrial adaptation. In experimental diabetes, myocardial triiodothyronine (T3) can decline despite preserved circulating thyroid hormone concentrations, accompanied by type 3 iodothyronine deiodinase (DIO3) induction and altered TH transport. We propose that this local defect disrupts thyroid hormone-mitochondrial coupling and may thereby constrain adaptation of substrate oxidation, oxidative phosphorylation, redox defense and organelle turnover. Preclinical diabetic-heart studies demonstrate local TH dysregulation and show that appropriately dosed T3 treatment can reverse selected structural and functional abnormalities. Complementary cardiac studies identify mitochondrial biogenesis, reactive oxygen species control, mitophagy and calcium handling as plausible downstream effectors. Together, these findings support impaired local TH signaling as an underrecognized candidate upstream mechanism linking the diabetic endocrine environment to mitochondrial maladaptation. A tissue-specific therapeutic-window model may reconcile the adverse consequences of both deficient and excessive TH signaling while providing a framework for biomarker development, mechanistic testing and precision intervention in DCM.

papers.title: Overt and subclinical hypothyroidism during pregnancy: effects on neonatal amino acids, acylcarnitines, and TSH levels.
papers.abstract: Maternal hypothyroidism during pregnancy, including overt and subclinical hypothyroidism, is a common endocrine disorder complicating pregnancy and is associated with increased risks of adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. However, its effects on neonatal metabolism remain inadequately understood. This study aimed to assess the association between hypothyroidism in pregnancy and neonatal amino acid and acylcarnitine levels. This retrospective case-control study included 1,987 pregnant women with overt hypothyroidism in pregnancy, 2,023 with subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy, and 2,043 euthyroid pregnant women from Fujian Provincial Maternity and Children's Hospital between 2016 and 2024. Their newborns all underwent newborn screening for 11 amino acids and 31 acylcarnitines using tandem mass spectrometry. After adjusting for potential confounding factors including gestational age at delivery, birth weight, and neonatal sex, newborns born to mothers with hypothyroidism in pregnancy (overt and subclinical) showed significant differences in the levels of 9 amino acids compared with those born to mothers with normal thyroid function. These amino acids are involved in the arginine-proline metabolism, glycine metabolism, and the urea cycle pathway. Amino acid levels also differed between the two subtypes. In addition, the levels of short-chain, medium-chain, and long-chain acylcarnitines in newborns from the hypothyroidism groups were significantly higher than those in the control group, with several acylcarnitine indicators (C16, C16:1, C16OH, C18:1OH, and C6DC) exhibiting characteristic differences between the two subtypes. The levels of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in newborns from both hypothyroidism groups were significantly higher than those in the control group, whereas no statistically significant difference in TSH levels was observed between the overt and subclinical hypothyroidism groups. Our findings revealed a significant association between hypothyroidism in pregnancy (overt and subclinical) and neonatal amino acid and acylcarnitine levels, which were mainly involved in branched-chain amino acid, arginine, proline, and glycine metabolism, as well as the urea cycle and fatty acid oxidation pathways. These results underscore the importance of identifying maternal conditions that correlate with neonatal metabolites, providing a reference for exploring strategies to optimize neonatal nutrition and improving long-term health outcomes.

papers.title: Neudesin alterations in hypothyroidism with and without metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes: association with metabolic disturbances and potential biomarker value.
papers.abstract: Hypothyroidism is one of the common endocrine disorders that often coexists with metabolic syndrome (MS) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), affecting glucose metabolism, lipids balance and insulin resistance. Neudesin, neuron-derived neurotrophic factor (NENF), is a protein responsible for neurotrophic and metabolic effects; however, the role of neudesin in the development of metabolic disorders associated with thyroid disorders is still unknown. The aim of the study was to investigate the association between the blood neudesin level and metabolic changes in hypothyroid patients with or without MS. The case-control study was performed by comparing three groups of patients: hypothyroidism + metabolic syndrome; hypothyroidism only, and control group. Clinical and biochemical parameters were evaluated: glycemic indices, insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), lipid profile, and thyroid hormone test (TSH, total triiodothyronine [TT3] and total thyroxine [TT4]). Serum neudesin was detected and the level was compared between three groups. The greatest metabolic changes in patients with hypothyroidism and MS include increased fasting glucose, triglyceride, HOMA-IR, TSH, and decreased HDLC, TT4. Although all patients receive levothyroxine 100 μg daily, TSH remained elevated in both patient groups (12.94 ± 4.26 and 11.83 ± 3.79 μIU/mL vs. 1.47 ± 0.74 μIU/mL in controls). Patients with MS had the least favorable profile, with greater adiposity, blood pressure, glycemia, triglycerides, and HOMA-IR and lower HDLC. Serum neudesin was approximately 4.5-fold higher in both hypothyroid groups (6.47 ± 2.21 and 6.11 ± 1.27 ng/mL) than in controls (1.39 ± 0.50 ng/mL; p < 0.001) but did not differ between patients with and without MS (p = 0.720) and did not discriminate between them (AUC 0.509, 95% CI 0.356-0.663). Serum neudesin is therefore raised in treated, incompletely controlled hypothyroidism irrespective of MS status. Because both patient groups were also dysglycemic, the rise cannot be attributed to thyroid status alone, and the separation from controls requires independent validation. Increased level of serum neudesin is associated with hypothyroidism in presence of MS and reflects the association between thyroid disorders and metabolic disorders. Therefore, neudesin could be considered as a biomarker of metabolic risks in hypothyroid patients.

papers.title: Endocrine determinants of MASLD: mechanisms and therapeutic targets.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects approximately 30% of adults worldwide, yet is still framed largely as a hepatological disorder despite being driven substantially by endocrine and metabolic dysfunction. This review proposes a unified endocrine framework organised around seven hormonal axes, presenting each in terms of molecular pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and therapeutic implications. Insulin resistance is the central driver, coupling chronic caloric excess to hepatic de novo lipogenesis through selective hepatic insulin resistance, although genetic variants in PNPLA3 and TM6SF2 can uncouple steatosis from metabolic risk. Adipose tissue dysfunction contributes through adipocyte senescence, adipokine imbalance, and inflammatory adipose-liver signalling. Reduced hepatic thyroid hormone sensitivity, even in euthyroid individuals, predicts steatosis and fibrosis and underpins the first approved liver-directed therapy. Gonadal steroids exert sexually dimorphic effects, with testosterone deficiency, menopausal oestrogen loss, and polycystic ovary syndrome representing distinct risk states. Glucocorticoid dysregulation is stage-dependent, shifting from enhanced hepatic cortisol clearance in steatosis to local amplification in steatohepatitis. The gut-liver-endocrine axis, encompassing incretin, bile acid, and fibroblast growth factor signalling, has proved the most therapeutically tractable. Reduced GH/IGF-1 signalling, whether from pituitary disease or obesity-induced functional suppression, promotes both steatosis and fibrogenesis. Biological sex and life-course influences spanning developmental programming and ageing further modify these determinants. Two agents, resmetirom and semaglutide, now have US FDA accelerated approval for noncirrhotic MASH with moderate-to-advanced fibrosis, supporting the principle that correcting axis-specific endocrine dysfunction can produce measurable hepatic benefit; however, both approvals are accelerated and await confirmatory outcome data, while others remain investigational. An endocrine framework offers both a coherent account of pathogenesis and a rational basis for biomarker-guided, phenotype-targeted therapy.

papers.title: Metabolic reprogramming in differentiated thyroid cancer progression: A tumor metabolomics analysis.
papers.abstract: Differentiated thyroid cancers exhibit biologic and clinical heterogeneity not fully explained by conventional staging. Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer, and its contribution to differentiated thyroid cancer progression is an ongoing area of study. Metabolomics-the comprehensive analysis of metabolites within biologic systems-may identify stage-specific metabolic signatures. Fifty-five differentiated thyroid cancer specimens underwent untargeted metabolomic profiling using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Stage was assigned per American Joint Committee on Cancer, Eighth Edition criteria. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed, and specific metabolites were evaluated to define metabolic phenotypes of early-stage (I/II; n = 49) versus advanced-stage (III/IV; n = 6) tumors. Over 10% of 17,270 metabolic features were significantly (P < .05; |fold change| >1.5) altered in advanced-stage differentiated thyroid cancers. Pathway analysis demonstrated remodeling of fatty acid, linoleate, pyrimidine, and alanine/aspartate metabolism with tumor progression. Advanced-stage tumors accumulated metabolites associated with nucleotide and epigenetic flux (guanosine monophosphate, adenosine monophosphate, S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine, and 1-methylnicotinamide), invasive membrane remodeling (γ-linolenate, oleate), and immune evasion (kynurenine, serotonin) while attenuating markers of oxidative metabolism (α-ketoisocaproate, acetyl phosphate) and adrenergic signaling (adrenaline). Correlation analysis demonstrated internal synchrony among these markers and a counter-regulatory relationship between differentiated function and biosynthetic expansion. Locally advanced differentiated thyroid cancers appear to exhibit a metabolic phenotype characterized by adrenergic suppression, immune evasion, invasive membrane remodeling, nucleotide and methylation flux, bioenergetic collapse, and resource shunting, all at the expense of differentiated and homeostatic functions. These hypothesis-generating findings suggest that metabolomic profiling could complement existing risk-stratification frameworks. Prospective validation of metabolic phenotypes as predictors of recurrence and progression is warranted.

citations.quote: Particular attention is given to tissue-level triiodothyronine availability, deiodinase activity, and downstream bioenergetic effects. Athyreotic patients lack intrinsic thyroidal triiodothyronine secretion and depend entirely on the peripheral conversion of levothyroxine to generate circulating and intracellular triiodothyronine.

Thyroid hormone (TH) is a major regulator of cardiac energy metabolism and mitochondrial adaptation. In experimental diabetes, myocardial triiodothyronine (T3) can decline despite preserved circulating thyroid hormone concentrations, accompanied by type 3 iodothyronine deiodinase (DIO3) induction and altered TH transport.
Complementary cardiac studies identify mitochondrial biogenesis, reactive oxygen species control, mitophagy and calcium handling as plausible downstream effectors.
