WAT.description: In 3T3-L1 cells, Vps13c knockdown impaired adipocyte differentiation, evidenced by reduced lipid droplet formation and lower intracellular levels of triglycerides, glycerol, and fatty acids [2]. Lipid synthesis varies by depot: VAT showed elevated expression of genes linked to inflammation, complement activation, stress signaling, cell death, lipid biosynthesis, and mRNA processing [3]. In obesity, SAT showed reduced de novo lipogenesis and cholesterol synthesis [3], and after bariatric surgery SAT showed restored expression of lipogenic and adipogenic genes [3]. Lipolysis is also a regulated process, as myeloid ACSL4 deletion ... correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory ATMs and enhanced adipocyte lipolysis and thermogenesis [5] in mice. Energy handling relies on mitochondrial pathways: PM 2.5 significantly suppressed thermogenesis, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, disrupted mitochondrial quality control networks, and downregulated the AMPK/SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling pathway [6]. Similarly, RNF126 deficiency suppressed the mRNA and protein expression of UCP-1, SIRT1, and PGC-1α in the liver and white adipose tissue, indicating impaired mitochondrial biogenesis [8]. Hormonal and external signals also shape this tissue, as plasma steroid metabolomics identified 11-deoxycorticosterone (11-DOC), a mineralocorticoid metabolite, as positively associated with VSR in premenopausal ACS women independent of cortisol [1]. Nutrition and circadian timing further influence visceral adipose function, which is regulated by a complex interplay between nutrition, circadian rhythms, intestinal melatonin secretion, and the gut microbiota [7].

papers.title: Multi-omics profiling reveals molecular features of visceral adiposity in autonomous cortisol secretion.
papers.abstract: Autonomous cortisol secretion (ACS) from adrenal adenomas increases cardiometabolic risk. Visceral adiposity is a hallmark of ACS. We characterized ACS-associated visceral adiposity using multi-omics profiling of periadrenal adipose tissue and plasma. ACS exhibited higher visceral-to-subcutaneous fat ratio (VSR), adipocyte hypertrophy, and inflammation-related pathway enrichment than non-functioning adrenal tumors. RNA-seq deconvolution and immunohistochemistry indicated increased macrophage infiltration. Plasma steroid metabolomics identified 11-deoxycorticosterone (11-DOC), a mineralocorticoid metabolite, as positively associated with VSR in premenopausal ACS women independent of cortisol. The 11-DOC-associated gene module correlated with inflammation-related pathways, notably macrophage activation. Lipidomics identified ceramides as ACS discriminators, with Cer(d18:1/16:0) most strongly associated with inflammation- and lipid metabolism-related pathways. Mendelian randomization showed genetically predicted plasma Cer(d18:1/16:0) was positively associated with trunk fat mass. These findings identify circulating 11-DOC and adipose ceramide accumulation as molecular features associated with adipose inflammation and visceral adiposity in ACS, providing hypothesis-generating insights that require functional validation.

papers.title: VPS13C regulates triglyceride homeostasis and adipocyte differentiation.
papers.abstract: Hypertriglyceridemia is a major risk factor for cardiometabolic diseases. VPS13C is a genome-wide significant locus for triglyceride with an incomplete understanding of its functional role in triglyceride biology. In this study, we investigated the transcriptomic associations and functional roles of VPS13C in triglyceride metabolism. We analyzed VPS13C expression in subcutaneous adipose tissue and assessed fasting serum lipid levels (including total cholesterol and triglycerides) in participants from the Africa America Diabetes Mellitus (AADM) study. In parallel, we conducted functional studies in 3T3-L1 mouse adipocytes, where Vps13c was knocked down using siRNA. We then evaluated markers of adipogenesis, lipogenesis, and triglyceride metabolism. In human subjects, VPS13C expression in subcutaneous adipose tissue was inversely associated with fasting triglyceride levels but showed non-significant correlation with total cholesterol. In 3T3-L1 cells, Vps13c knockdown impaired adipocyte differentiation, evidenced by reduced lipid droplet formation and lower intracellular levels of triglycerides, glycerol, and fatty acids. This knockdown also led to significant downregulation of Pparg expression and suppression of PPARγ-mediated pathways, as well as genes involved in adipogenesis and lipogenesis. VPS13C is associated with circulating triglyceride levels and plays a critical role in adipocyte differentiation, adipogenesis and lipogenesis. These findings suggest that VPS13C may play an important role in triglyceride-related metabolic disorders.

papers.title: Adipose tissue transcriptome before and after surgery: effects on genes driving lipid metabolism, inflammation, and RNA processing.
papers.abstract: Obesity, marked by excess adipose tissue, is strongly associated with increased cardiometabolic risk. Metabolic bariatric surgery (MBS) leads to significant and sustained weight loss and improves metabolic profiles in persons with severe obesity. However, how MBS induces persistent transcriptional changes in adipose tissue and their contributions to cardiometabolic improvements remain unclear. This study examined subcutaneous (SAT) and visceral (VAT) adipose tissue transcriptome profiles in people with severe obesity, tracking changes in SAT after MBS, with a focus on lipid metabolism, inflammation, RNA processing, and cholesterol handling. This study included 42 women with severe obesity undergoing MBS and 15 sex-matched healthy people without obesity as controls. Targeted RNA expression profiling was performed on SAT and VAT samples. In people with obesity, SAT showed higher expression of genes related to adipocyte function, anti-inflammatory markers, extracellular matrix remodeling, lipid metabolism, cell-death regulation, oxidative stress protection, mRNA processing, and cholesterol handling compared to VAT. In contrast, VAT showed elevated expression of genes linked to inflammation, complement activation, stress signaling, cell death, lipid biosynthesis, and mRNA processing. Compared with controls, SAT in obesity showed increased inflammatory and stress-response gene expression and upregulation of RNA processing regulators, but reduced de novo lipogenesis and cholesterol synthesis. Following MBS, SAT showed restored expression of lipogenic and adipogenic genes alongside downregulation of inflammatory, cholesterol biosynthesis, and splicing-factor genes. These findings demonstrate SAT and VAT remodeling in obesity and show that MBS partially reverses transcriptional changes in SAT, providing mechanistic insight into its metabolic benefits. They also highlight the need for targeted therapeutic strategies to more fully restore adipose tissue function and improve long-term metabolic outcomes. NCT00793143 and NCT01373892.

papers.title: Protocol for the isolation, enrichment, and culture of murine adipose progenitor cells.
papers.abstract: We present a protocol for isolating and culturing murine adipose progenitor cells (APCs) from adipose tissue. We describe steps for tissue dissection, unit-normalized enzymatic digestion, stromal vascular fraction (SVF) isolation, APC enrichment, and cell culture. We then detail quality control procedures that maximize cell yield, viability, and purity. This protocol combines enzymatic SVF isolation with magnetic-activated cell sorting enrichment to obtain a highly enriched APC population. It emphasizes reproducibility through unit-normalized digestion, controlled processing conditions, and standardized quality control metrics.

papers.title: CRISPR screens identify ACSL4 as a key regulator in macrophage activation and metabolic inflammation.
papers.abstract: Pro-inflammatory macrophages drive obesity-associated metabolic inflammation. Identifying key regulators of their activation is crucial for new therapies. This study aimed to identify novel regulators of pro-inflammatory adipose tissue macrophage (ATM) activation and assess their therapeutic potential. We combined genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening with scRNA-seq data from human adipose tissue and identified long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase 4 (ACSL4) as critical for pro-inflammatory ATM activation. Validation used myeloid-specific Acsl4 knockout mice (Acsl4 fl/fl Lyz2 Cre ) and shRNA-mediated knockdown in macrophage cell lines (RAW264.7, THP-1, and iBMDM). Mechanisms were explored via mutagenesis, immunostaining, co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP), bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), and transcriptional activity assays. A high-throughput screen of 8,685 DrugBank compounds was performed to identify candidates targeting ACSL4. ACSL4 deficiency markedly reduced pro-inflammatory factor expression (Tnfα, Il1β, and Il6). Myeloid ACSL4 deletion protected against high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity, correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory ATMs and enhanced adipocyte lipolysis and thermogenesis, without affecting food intake, water intake, or locomotor activity in mice. However, glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity were not significantly affected. Mechanistically, ACSL4 contributed to inflammation independent of its enzymatic/ferroptotic functions (Thr328 mutation, troglitazone insensitivity). Instead, ACSL4 translocated to the nucleus in a karyopherin β1 (KPNB1)-dependent manner. DrugBank screening identified abemaciclib as a potential inhibitor of the ACSL4-KPNB1 interaction. Notably, abemaciclib treatment reduced macrophage inflammation and attenuated HFD-induced obesity in mice. ACSL4 promotes pro-inflammatory macrophage activation through its KPNB1-dependent nuclear translocation and cooperation with IRF5. Targeting the ACSL4-KPNB1 interaction may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for metabolic inflammation.

papers.title: Metabolic Reprogramming by Time-Restricted Feeding Confers Resistance to PM 2.5 -Induced Metabolic Disturbances in Adipose Tissue.
papers.abstract: Recent research indicates that exposure to fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) not only impairs the respiratory system but also disturbs adipose tissue homeostasis, contributing to rising obesity rates and systemic metabolic disturbances. Time-restricted feeding (TRF), a dietary approach that confines daily food consumption to specific time windows, has demonstrated significant potential in preventing and managing metabolic disorders. However, it remains unclear if TRF can alleviate PM 2.5 -induced adipose tissue dysfunction, and the mechanisms involved require investigation. We established a PM 2.5 -exposed male mouse model and randomly assigned the animals to four groups: filtered air (FA), PM 2.5 exposure, TRF+FA, and TRF+PM 2.5 . The PM 2.5 and TRF+PM 2.5 groups underwent whole-body PM 2.5 exposure in inhalation chambers, while the remaining groups were maintained under FA conditions. Mice in the TRF+FA and TRF+PM 2.5 groups were subjected to an 8-hour feeding window during the active phase (ZT16-ZT24). Our results indicated that PM 2.5 exposure induced systemic energy metabolism dysregulation and obesity, characterized by reduced heat production and metabolic rate, along with adipocyte hypertrophy, lipid droplet expansion, adipokine dysregulation, and inflammatory activation in both inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) and brown adipose tissue (BAT). Furthermore, PM 2.5 significantly suppressed thermogenesis, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, disrupted mitochondrial quality control networks, and downregulated the AMPK/SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling pathway. Notably, TRF intervention reactivated these signaling pathways, systematically reversed the multi-level pathological alterations, and restored mitochondrial homeostasis and energy metabolic balance. This study suggests for the first time that TRF counteracts adipose tissue dysfunction caused by PM 2.5 , offering a promising lifestyle intervention strategy against environment-related metabolic diseases.

papers.title: Nutrition, Circadian Regulation, and the Gut-Melatonin-Visceral Adipose Tissue Axis: An Integrative Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) dysfunction is a major determinant of obesity-related metabolic disorders, including insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and chronic low-grade inflammation. Growing evidence indicates that VAT function is regulated by a complex interplay between nutrition, circadian rhythms, intestinal melatonin secretion, and the gut microbiota rather than by isolated metabolic pathways. The gastrointestinal tract represents an important interface between dietary exposures, microbial activity, immune signaling, and host metabolic regulation. Melatonin is a potential component of this network because it participates in circadian regulation and has been detected in gastrointestinal tissues, while experimental studies suggest that intestinal melatonin signaling may interact with gut microbial and metabolic processes. However, the cellular sources, quantitative contribution, local dynamics, and physiological significance of intestinal melatonin remain incompletely established, particularly in humans. This narrative review integrates current evidence regarding the interactions between nutrition, circadian regulation, intestinal melatonin, gut microbiota, and visceral adipose tissue. Rather than proposing a validated causal pathway, we introduce the Gut-Melatonin-Visceral Adipose Tissue (Gut-Melatonin-VAT) Axis as an integrative, hypothesis-generating conceptual framework that organizes established interactions together with candidate mechanisms requiring further experimental validation. Particular attention is given to the bidirectional relationships among dietary composition, meal timing, microbial rhythmicity, intestinal signaling, immune regulation, and VAT dysfunction. The framework may provide a basis for generating testable hypotheses concerning nutritional, chrononutritional, microbiota-targeted, and melatonin-related interventions, while recognizing that direct human evidence validating the complete pathway is currently lacking.

papers.title: E3 Ubiquitin Ligase RNF126 Contributes to Pathogenesis of Obesity by Induction Mitophagy Mediated by PINK1/Parkin Pathway.
papers.abstract: Obesity and its associated metabolic disorders have become major global public health challenges. Increasing evidence indicates that mitophagy plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of obesity and related metabolic diseases. This study aimed to investigate the role and underlying mechanisms of E3 ubiquitin ligase RNF126 in obesity and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Using Rnf126 + / - mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD), we found RNF126 deficiency markedly exacerbated body weight gain, elevated serum ALT and AST levels, inflammatory responses, apoptosis, and insulin resistance. Histological analysis with H&E and Oil Red O staining revealed that RNF126 deficiency aggravated hepatic inflammatory cell infiltration, lipid droplet accumulation, and adipocyte hypertrophy in HFD-fed mice. HFD feeding significantly inhibited RNF126 expression in liver and muscle. Moreover, Rnf126 + / - mice exhibited reduced oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide production and heat generation without changes in food intake. Mechanistically, qPCR and Western blot analyses demonstrated that RNF126 deficiency suppressed the mRNA and protein expression of UCP-1, SIRT1, and PGC-1α in the liver and white adipose tissue, indicating impaired mitochondrial biogenesis. Moreover, the protein levels of cleaved PINK1, Parkin, and LC3 were reduced, while p62 expression was increased in the liver of Rnf126 + / - mice, indicating inhibited autophagic activity. Consistently, oxidative stress was significantly elevated, as evidenced by increased MDA levels and decreased SOD and GSH contents. Rnf126 + / - mice livers displayed obvious mitochondrial swelling and partial cristae disorganization with an increase of mtDNA expression. Mitochondrial complex-III enzymatic activity, hepatic ATP, TOM20 protein expression and complex-III subunit UQCRFS1 expression were substantially decreased in HFD-fed Rnf126 + / - mice. At the cellular level, RNF126 overexpression in palmitic acid-treated HepG2 cells restored cleaved PINK1, Parkin, and LC3 protein levels, while reducing p62 expression, indicating that RNF126 promotes mitophagy. Furthermore, ROS fluorescence assays showed that RNF126 overexpression attenuated intracellular ROS accumulation. Rescue experiments demonstrated that the protective effects of RNF126 on mitochondrial membrane potential, lipid accumulation, and mitophagy marker expression are dependent on its ubiquitin ligase activity. Overall, RNF126 alleviates HFD-induced lipid accumulation and hepatic injury by promoting mitophagy and maintaining redox homeostasis, suggesting its potential as a novel therapeutic target for NAFLD.

papers.title: Diagnostic value of CT-quantified abdominal fat parameters for metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease.
papers.abstract: To analyze the diagnostic value of CT-derived abdominal fat indices in predicting MAFLD and establish an integrated diagnostic system. A retrospective study on 174 patients with a previous history of abdominal CT examination in our institute between January 2022 and June 2024 was conducted, comprising 120 diagnosed with MAFLD, and 54 controls without it. CT-derived measures including SAT, visceral adipose tissue volume(VAT), total liver volume, and average hepatic. The average value and CT attenuation value of the left and right lobe of liver and the VAT/SAT were compared using Mann-Whitney U test. were compared between both groups. Then, we used Spearman's rank correlation analysis to study whether there existed correlations between CT metrics and metabolic indicators. Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic(ROC)curve analysis were utilized to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of individual parameters.Calibration of a composite prediction model was evaluated by using calibration plots. In MAFLD groups, SAT, VAT, liver volume, and the VAT / SAT ratio were higher than those of the control group, while the mean hepatic CT attenuation value, as well as the mean attenuation value of the left lobe and right lobe, were all lower than those of the control group (all P < 0.05). The mean hepatic CT attenuation correlated negatively with BMI (r = -0.607) and TG (r = -0.418), while the sign was positive for VAT. In univariate logistic regression, we found that the mean hepatic CT attenuation is the best diagnostic indicator of MAFLD, with an AUC of 0.923, then were left and right hepatic attenuation (AUC = 0.886), liver volume (AUC = 0.814), and VAT's mean CT attenuation (AUC = 0.796). BMI (r = 0.554) and UA (r = 0.362) were also considered. Combining SAT, VAT, and mean hepatic CT attenuation together in one model resulted in an AUC of 0.928 (sensitivity: 91.7%, specificity: 85.2%). The calibration curves demonstrated an acceptable fit of the model. When multiple variables were combined, the sensitivity improved from 85.8% to 91.7% and specificity changed from 87.0% to 85.2%, yielding an AUC of 0.928 (ΔAUC = 0.005 compared with mean hepatic CT attenuation alone, P = 0.62). CT-measured abdominal fat may represent a reliable and noninvasive approach for the diagnosis of MAFLD.The greatest individual diagnostic utility was exhibited by mean liver CT attenuation alone; however, with multiple variables merged into a combined model, the sensitivity and specificity were also further increased, which could be an effective method to image MAFLD in clinical diagnosis.

papers.title: Integrative Transcriptomic Analysis of Obesity-Associated Candidate Genes in Pediatric Adipose Tissue.
papers.abstract: Tryptophan metabolism has been linked to pediatric obesity, although the transcriptomic evidence connecting obesity-associated genes with this pathway remains limited. Two public subcutaneous adipose tissue datasets, GSE205668 and GSE104815, were analyzed. GSE205668 included 26 obesity and 35 control samples, and GSE104815 included 4 obesity and 4 control samples. Differential expression screening, weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA), exploratory coexpression enrichment, immune score analysis, and regulatory network prediction were performed. Four candidate genes, APOL4, FASN, KRT79, and MACROD1, emerged from the exploratory intersection analysis. Their expression was higher in control samples than in obesity samples in both public datasets. Results derived from nominal p-value screens are interpreted as exploratory. The literature-derived tryptophan-related WGCNA score is considered separately from the canonical Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) tryptophan-metabolism pathway. These findings define obesity-associated transcriptomic candidates in pediatric adipose tissue and do not establish direct participation of the four genes in tryptophan metabolism or a causal role in obesity.

Heart.description: The heart's energy production runs through the TCA cycle, where the newly described micropeptide APPM binds the OGDH complex and modulates NADH and ATP output (APPM localizes to the mitochondrial matrix and inner membrane, where it directly binds to the E1 subunit (OGDH) of the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, thereby regulating NADH and ATP production [1]). Supplying APPM from outside raised ATP levels in vivo and improved cardiac function in a heart failure model (Exogenous APPM administration increased ATP levels in vivo and, in a mouse model of heart failure, restored cardiac function, outperforming the reference drug trimetazidine [1].). Lipids also change markedly as cardiomyocytes mature, with lipid categories such as monosialodihexosylganglioside, phosphatidylcholine (PC), lysophosphatidylcholine, and lysophosphatidic acid were markedly elevated in mature CMs [2]. Phosphatidylcholine appears functionally relevant, as it promotes the expression of mature CM marker genes and improves CM viability [2]. Disrupted energy metabolism is also tied to injury, since the NLRP3 inflammasome integrates danger-associated molecular patterns, mitochondrial dysfunction, ionic disturbance, metabolic stress, and innate immune signaling [6]. Circadian and neurohumoral signaling also shape cardiac energy handling, as normal circadian rhythms regulate neurohumoral regulation and energy metabolism, thereby playing a protective or modulatory role in ischemic heart disease [3]. Finally, the heart's metabolic and angiogenic responses to exercise involve HIF-1α and PGC-1α, since chronic resistance training showed significantly higher HIF-1 α and FSTL1 expression than CON, together with significantly higher PGC-1 α and VEGF expression [8].

papers.title: A Micropeptide Component of the OGDH Complex Modulates ATP Production in the TCA Cycle.
papers.abstract: Since its elucidation, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle has been regarded as a fully defined enzymatic pathway. Here, we report the discovery of a previously unrecognized micropeptide component of this central metabolic system. Through analyzing ribosome profiling data from the mouse sORFs.org database, we discovered APPM (ATP production-promoting micropeptide), a 29-amino acid peptide encoded by a non-canonical small open reading frame within the mouse Ctsb gene. APPM localizes to the mitochondrial matrix and inner membrane, where it directly binds to the E1 subunit (OGDH) of the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex (OGDHc). This interaction modulates OGDHc enzymatic activity, thereby regulating NADH and ATP production. We identified tyrosine-13 as the critical residue mediating the APPM-OGDH interaction and functional activation. Exogenous APPM administration increased ATP levels in vivo and, in a mouse model of heart failure, restored cardiac function, outperforming the reference drug trimetazidine. Collectively, our findings identify APPM as the first micropeptide regulator of the OGDH complex, expanding the known repertoire of the TCA cycle and presenting a potential therapeutic strategy for diseases characterized by bioenergetic insufficiency.

papers.title: Lipid metabolism remodeling in human cardiomyocyte differentiation and maturation.
papers.abstract: Cardiac development involves extensive metabolic remodeling, yet dynamic changes of endogenous lipid species during human cardiomyocyte (CM) differentiation remain poorly characterized. In this study, we systematically performed high-coverage lipidomic profiling across five consecutive CM differentiation stages, using high-performance liquid chromatography. MYL2 expression confirmed ventricular lineage specification in late-stage CMs. Ceramide levels peaked at the cardiac progenitor cell (CPC) stage, suggesting a stage-specific association with the mesendoderm (MES)-to-CPC transition. Meanwhile, lipid categories such as monosialodihexosylganglioside, phosphatidylcholine (PC), lysophosphatidylcholine, and lysophosphatidic acid were markedly elevated in mature CMs. Integrated transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility analyses further delineated the temporal regulatory landscape underlying stage-dependent lipid remodeling during cardiogenic differentiation. Functional assays revealed that PC promotes the expression of mature CM marker genes and improves CM viability. Collectively, these findings establish a comprehensive, high-resolution dynamic lipidomic atlas of in vitro hESC-derived CM differentiation, providing a valuable resource for understanding lipid-associated mechanisms in heart development.

papers.title: Circadian clock and its potential as a therapy for ischemic heart disease.
papers.abstract: According to an epidemiological survey, myocardial infarction, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and aortic rupture usually occur in the morning and summer and are characterized by more severe symptoms and poorer prognosis. The occurrence, development, treatment difficulties, and poor prognosis of ischemic heart disease are closely related to circadian rhythm disorders and the abnormal transcription of circadian clock genes. Normal circadian rhythms regulate neurohumoral regulation and energy metabolism, thereby playing a protective or modulatory role in ischemic heart disease (IHD). HIF1α links the IHD and circadian signaling pathways through the hypoxia response element (HRE) and Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS) domains in gene promoters and enhancers.

papers.title: Restoration of cyclin A2 by glabridin reverses pathological cell cycle arrest and drives cardiac repair in HFpEF.
papers.abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a pervasive clinical syndrome characterized by complex and elusive pathogenic mechanisms. In this study, we identify aberrant cardiomyocyte cell cycle arrest as a previously unrecognized pathological driver of HFpEF that hinders tissue repair. Using in vivo and in vitro models, we further demonstrate that Glabridin (Gla), a bioactive isoflavone, can induce cardiac repair and alleviate myocardial hypertrophy and fibrosis in HFpEF by targeting the cell cycle arrest pathway. Mechanistically, Gla exerts its protective effects by specifically inhibiting the degradation of Cyclin A2 (CCNA2) and mitigating cardiomyocyte oxidative damage. This stabilization of CCNA2 effectively abrogates cell cycle arrest and drives cardiomyocyte cell cycle re-entry, an effect that was successfully recapitulated by CCNA2 gain-of-function experiments. This reparative response is intrinsically coupled with the restoration of metabolic homeostasis and the attenuation of oxidative stress, as evidenced in both cardiac and hepatic cells. Collectively, our findings define cell cycle arrest as a novel target and position Gla as a potent inducer of CCNA2-mediated cardiac repair for HFpEF treatment.

papers.title: Blockade of EP3 attenuates cardiac fibrosis by suppressing TGF-β1-Smad2/3 signaling through the Smurf2-mediated Smad7 ubiquitination.
papers.abstract: Sustained β-adrenergic activation induces cardiac fibrosis, which is characterized by excessive deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) secreted by activated cardiac fibroblasts (CFs). Prostaglandin E 2 (PGE 2 ) is a dominant cyclooxygenase metabolite of arachidonic acid and exerts important biological actions by activating four G-protein-coupled receptors, including E-type prostanoid receptors 1-4 (EP1-EP4). The present study aimed to investigate the role of the EP3 receptor in isoproterenol (ISO)-induced cardiac fibrosis. To elucidate the role of EP3 in cardiac fibrosis, the global EP3 gene knockout mice (EP3 -/- ) and the LoxP-Cre system-based CF-specific EP3 gene knockout mice (EP3 cKO ) or cardiomyocyte (CM)-specific EP3 gene knockout mice (EP3 mKO ) were subcutaneously injected with ISO [5 mg/(kg·d)] for 7 d to establish a cardiac fibrosis model. In parallel, the EP3 agonist sulprostone and the EP3 antagonists DG041 and L798106 were used to elucidate the underlying mechanisms. Finally, the therapeutic potential of the EP3 antagonist DG041 was evaluated in the context of cardiac fibrosis. Echocardiography assay showed that both EP3 -/- and EP3 cKO mice exhibited a significant improvement in cardiac diastolic function. Histological staining revealed that EP3 -/- and EP3 cKO , but not EP3 mKO , exhibited a significant attenuation of ISO-induced CF activation and ECM accumulation. Further investigation uncovered that EP3 was highly expressed in the CFs rather than CMs. Inhibition of EP3 in the CFs suppressed transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1)-triggered phosphorylation of small mother against decapentaplegic (Smad)2/3 and the production of ECM proteins. Mechanistically, the blockade of EP3 in the CFs activated the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (Akt) pathway, which promoted the degradation of Smad ubiquitination regulatory factor 2 (Smurf2) and subsequently suppressed the ubiquitination of Smad7, an inhibitory Smad, leading to an increase in the protein level of Smad7. Furthermore, the administration of an EP3 antagonist, DG041, markedly improved ISO-induced cardiac diastolic dysfunction and fibrosis. papers.title: Targeting NLRP3 Inflammasome Signaling After Myocardial Infarction: Mechanistic Rationale, Regulatory Networks, and Translational Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) remains a major cause of death and heart failure despite advances in reperfusion and secondary prevention. Sterile inflammation triggered by ischemic myocardial injury is increasingly recognized as a determinant of infarct expansion, adverse ventricular remodeling, and subsequent clinical outcomes. The NOD-like receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome integrates danger-associated molecular patterns, mitochondrial dysfunction, ionic disturbance, metabolic stress, and innate immune signaling. Following activation, caspase-1 processes interleukin-1β and interleukin-18 and cleaves gasdermin D to generate the pore-forming GSDMD-N fragment, thereby promoting pyroptosis and inflammatory amplification. After MI, NLRP3 activity is shaped by extracellular adenosine triphosphate and P2X7 signaling, potassium efflux, reactive oxygen species, mitochondrial DNA release, lysosomal and endoplasmic reticulum stress, and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes signaling. Importantly, these responses are temporally and cell-type dependent: cardiomyocytes, macrophages, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts contribute differently to injury, debris clearance, vascular dysfunction, scar formation, and repair. This review differs from earlier pathway-centered summaries by integrating temporal regulation and cell-specific biology with emerging crosstalk among mitochondrial quality control, STING signaling, ferroptosis, pyroptosis, and immunometabolism. Translational evidence is considered alongside mechanism, including interleukin-1-directed studies such as CANTOS and the Virginia Commonwealth University Anakinra Remodeling Trial program, while emphasizing that clinical benefit from selective NLRP3 inhibition itself remains to be established. Direct inflammasome inhibitors, colchicine, metabolic modulators, RNA-based approaches, targeted delivery systems, and traditional Chinese medicine-derived compounds are critically discussed with attention to evidence level and limitations. We further examine biomarker-guided patient selection and unresolved questions concerning therapeutic timing, cell specificity, long-term safety, and preservation of reparative inflammation.

papers.title: Engineered ZFP36-overexpressing AC16 cell-derived extracellular vesicles attenuate ferroptosis-related endothelial injury and functionalize NiTi vascular interfaces.
papers.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) is associated with persistent myocardial injury and vascular dysfunction despite advances in reperfusion therapy. Delayed endothelial recovery, inflammation, and vascular remodeling remain important challenges during post-MI repair and vascular intervention. Here, we investigated whether extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from ZFP36-overexpressing AC16 cells could attenuate ferroptosis-related endothelial injury, improve cardiac function after MI, and be integrated into a bioactive NiTi surface for vascular repair. Bioinformatic screening identified ZFP36 as an MI-associated candidate linked to ferroptosis-related processes; increased expression was subsequently observed in the mouse MI model. ZFP36-overexpressing AC16 cells were generated, and the released EVs were designated ZFP36 OE -EV. In RSL3-treated HUVECs, ZFP36 OE -EV improved cell viability, reduced oxidative stress, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential, and partially restored ferroptosis-related molecular changes. In a mouse MI model, intramyocardial delivery of ZFP36 OE -EV improved cardiac function and reduced myocardial fibrosis. To explore the use of the same engineered EV preparation for vascular interface functionalization, ZFP36 OE -EV was immobilized onto a polydopamine/hyaluronic acid (PDA/HA)-modified NiTi surface to generate the NPH@Z-EV coating. The coating supported EV loading and gradual particle release in vitro. Under direct cell-material contact conditions, the NPH@Z-EV coating exhibited endothelial protective activity under ferroptosis-related stress. In a rat femoral artery injury model, the NPH@Z-EV coating supported vascular repair, with improved endothelial recovery, reduced local inflammatory activation, attenuated lipid peroxidation-associated vascular injury, and a VSMC marker pattern consistent with reduced phenotypic switching. These findings support further evaluation of engineered EVs as a strategy for functionalizing NiTi vascular interfaces to improve vascular healing after implantation.

papers.title: Acute and Chronic Resistance Training Differentially Modulate Myocardial Angiogenesis-Related Gene Expression in Wistar Rats.
papers.abstract: Myocardial angiogenesis contributes to the maintenance of myocardial perfusion and cardiac function. Resistance training (RT) induces cardiovascular adaptations, but the myocardial transcriptional responses to acute RT (ART) and chronic RT (CRT) remain incompletely understood. This study compared the expression of angiogenesis- and metabolic adaptation-related genes in the left ventricle following a single RT bout and 8 weeks of repeated RT in healthy male Wistar rats. Twenty-four rats were randomized to three groups: sedentary control (CON) ( n  = 8), ART (one ladder-climbing session), or CRT (ladder-climbing 5 days/week for 8 weeks). RT was performed on a 1-m ladder inclined at 80° using progressive loads attached to the tail. Left-ventricular tissue was collected 1 h after the exercise bout in ART and 1 h after the final training session in CRT. Compared to CON, ART showed significantly higher HIF-1 α and FSTL1 expression, whereas PGC-1 α and VEGF did not differ significantly. CRT also showed significantly higher HIF-1 α and FSTL1 expression than CON, together with significantly higher PGC-1 α and VEGF expression. No significant differences were observed between ART and CRT for any of the genes examined. These findings demonstrate distinct myocardial transcriptional profiles following ART versus CRT, characterized by an HIF-1α- and FSTL1-associated response after a single bout and a PGC-1α- and VEGF-associated response following CRT.

papers.title: Understanding the change in calcium ion-binding, protein dynamics, and hydration behavior from the wild type for two pathogenic mutants (D3V and G34R) of troponin-C : molecular dynamics simulation and network analysis.
papers.abstract: The protein Troponin-C is an important player in muscle contraction, and mutations in Cardiac Troponin-C (cTnC) have been associated with inherited cardiomyopathies. Till now, eight mutants of the N-domain of cTnC have been listed in the ClinVar database as pathogenic or likely pathogenic. Understanding the molecular mechanisms of these mutations is crucial for mitigating their effects. Previous work studied mutations A8V, A31S, and I4M and found that changes in the conformational landscape are a key feature of these mutations. In the current work, our focus is on two mutations, D3V and G34R, the only ones out of the eight mentioned that undergo a change of charge on mutation. We have performed molecular dynamics simulation and network analysis to calculate binding affinity between Ca 2+ and mutants vis-à-vis the wild type, the change of Ca 2+ coordination shell, the effect of water, protein dynamics, and the communication path from the mutation site to the binding site. Our findings show that both electrostatics and the location of the mutation are the key factors for the difference between WT and the two mutants. D3V, in a disordered region, disrupts long-range allostery through electrostatic and hydration changes, whereas G34R, near the binding site, induces local electrostatic and structural perturbations. The changed conformational landscape, as found for the previously studied mutants, is a general feature for these two mutations also; however, specific effects found here illustrate the diversity present in different mutants.

papers.title: Comprehensive cardiac, vascular, and pulmonary characterization of a cardiometabolic HFpEF model.
papers.abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a heterogeneous syndrome in which translational progress is limited by experimental models that insufficiently reflect the cardiometabolic phenotype while affecting endogenous endothelial function. We aimed to characterize a cardiometabolic "two-hit" HFpEF model combining metabolic stress (db/db) with chronic mineralocorticoid excess (d-aldosterone), focusing on integrated cardiac, vascular, and pulmonary phenotyping. Female db/db mice received 4-week d-aldosterone (0.3 µg/h) or vehicle via osmotic minipumps. Metabolic profiling, high-resolution echocardiography including strain and left atrial mechanics, invasive right-heart catheterization, and thoracic aortic wire myography were performed. Aldosterone-treated db/db mice developed cardiac hypertrophy and pulmonary congestion with preserved LVEF but marked diastolic dysfunction, left atrial remodeling with increased stiffness, and impaired global longitudinal LV strain. Pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular dysfunction was evidenced by elevated RVSP/estimated mPAP, reduced PAT/PET, and reduced TAPSE. Thoracic aortae from untreated db/db mice already showed impaired endothelium-dependent relaxation, which was further aggravated by aldosterone, whereas maximal endothelium-independent relaxation remained largely preserved. The db/db+d-aldosterone model recapitulates key features of cardiometabolic HFpEF across the cardiac-vascular-pulmonary axis and provides a translational platform for mechanistic and therapeutic studies targeting endothelial and ventricular-vascular dysfunction in HFpEF. New & Noteworthy: Current HFpEF animal models often limit the investigation of vascular dysfunction, a central component of cardiometabolic HFpEF. We provide a comprehensive functional characterization of a db/db+d-aldosterone two-hit model demonstrating obesity, diabetes, diastolic dysfunction, atrial remodeling, endothelial dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, and right ventricular impairment. By preserving endogenous endothelial nitric oxide signaling, this model offers a translational platform for studying vascular and cardiopulmonary mechanisms in cardiometabolic HFpEF.

papers.title: A latent metabolic dysfunction phenotype integrating insulin resistance and leptin is associated with disease severity in COPD.
papers.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is increasingly recognised as a systemic condition in which metabolic dysfunction may influence disease severity and exacerbation risk. The combined effects of insulin resistance and leptin dysregulation on COPD outcomes remain incompletely defined. This study evaluated their associations with exacerbation burden, airflow limitation and patient-reported outcomes, and assessed the discriminative performance of HOMA-IR and serum leptin for identifying advanced disease. A cross-sectional observational study was conducted at a tertiary care centre in southern Romania, including 96 patients with COPD and 24 healthy controls. Fasting insulin and serum leptin were measured, and insulin resistance was assessed using HOMA-IR. Spirometry and patient-reported outcomes (CAT, mMRC and SGRQ-C) were assessed in COPD patients. Metabolic markers were analysed individually and as a latent metabolic dysfunction phenotype using generalized structural equation modelling (GSEM). Compared with controls, COPD patients had higher HOMA-IR (+206.9%), insulin (+112.2%) and leptin (+52.8%) levels. Both HOMA-IR and leptin were inversely correlated with spirometric indices, with stronger associations observed for HOMA-IR. Within the COPD cohort, neither individual metabolic markers nor a latent metabolic dysfunction phenotype integrating HOMA-IR, body mass index and leptin was associated with annual exacerbation rate (latent factor IRR = 1.089, 95% CI: 0.841-1.410, p  = 0.517). HOMA-IR demonstrated better discrimination of advanced disease than leptin (AUC = 0.769 vs. 0.590, p  < 0.001). Metabolic dysfunction is substantially more pronounced in COPD than in individuals without airflow obstruction and correlates with the degree of airflow limitation, but does not independently predict exacerbation frequency within the COPD population. HOMA-IR outperformed leptin as a marker of disease severity, a finding that requires further validation.

papers.title: Cyclic stretch increases glucose uptake and pro-inflammatory response in rat alveolar epithelial type II cells.
papers.abstract: Mechanical ventilation (MV) is used to improve gas exchange but can exacerbate lung inflammation by increasing alveolar cell stretch, leading to ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI). Alveolar epithelial stretching promotes cytokine release, but its effects on glucose uptake remain unclear. In vitro studies suggest that high tidal volume ventilation corresponds to cyclic stretch levels of approximately 18%, whereas larger deformations represent supraphysiological and injurious conditions. Therefore, 30% cyclic stretch was used to reproduce severe alveolar deformation associated with volutrauma. We investigated the modulation of inflammation and glucose uptake in alveolar epithelial type II cells exposed to excessive cyclic stretch. We hypothesized that cells exposed to an overstretch of 30% at 1 and 4 hours would increase glucose uptake and pro-inflammatory responses. Rat alveolar epithelial type II cells (L2 AECs) treated and untreated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) were exposed to 1 or 4 hours of 30% cyclic stretch. Non-stretched cells, stimulated or not with LPS, served as a control. Glucose oxidase activity was measured using a colorimetric/fluorometric assay, while glucose uptake was assessed by immunofluorescence using the fluorescent glucose analog 2-[N-(7-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazol-4-yl)amino]-2-deoxyglucose (2-NBDG). Gene expression and secretion were measured by real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), respectively. Statistical analyses were performed using one-way ANOVA followed by Šidák's multiple comparisons test, with significance set at p  < 0.05. 30% cyclic stretch significantly increased glucose uptake and glucose oxidase activity in both LPS-treated and untreated cells. Inflammatory gene expression and mediator secretion were predominantly increased in LPS-primed cells, although the effects varied according to the marker and time point. Overall, excessive cyclic stretch increased the glucose-related readouts assessed in AECs L2 cells, whereas inflammatory responses were more strongly influenced by LPS stimulation and varied among mediators and time points.

papers.title: Tongsai Granules Ameliorate Airway Mucus Hypersecretion in AECOPD by Remodeling LIPA-Driven Ceramide Metabolism.
papers.abstract: Tongsai Granules (TSG) is a traditional Chinese medicine formula traditionally used for the treatment of acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) with phlegm-heat obstructing lung syndrome, a condition characterized by cough, excessive sputum production, and dyspnea; however, its underlying therapeutic mechanisms remain unclear. To investigate the mechanisms by which TSG alleviates airway mucus hypersecretion in AECOPD through regulation of the LIPA/ceramide axis. A murine AECOPD model and airway epithelial cells were used. Proteomic and lipidomic analyses, molecular docking, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), drug affinity responsive target stability (DARTS), and LIPA overexpression and knockdown assays were performed. TSG improved pulmonary function, attenuated lung injury and inflammation, and suppressed MUC5AC expression in AECOPD mice. Multi-omics analyses showed that TSG regulated lipid metabolism and reduced triglyceride and ceramide accumulation while downregulating lysosomal acid lipase A (LIPA). Several serum-exposed constituents of TSG inhibited MUC5AC expression. Bergenin (BER) was selected as a representative bioactive constituent for subsequent target-identification and mechanistic studies. Molecular docking, SPR, and DARTS assays demonstrated direct interaction between BER and LIPA. LIPA knockdown suppressed MUC5AC expression, whereas LIPA overexpression attenuated the inhibitory effect of BER. Moreover, exogenous ceramide reversed BER-mediated suppression of MUC5AC. TSG alleviates airway mucus hypersecretion in AECOPD by targeting the LIPA/ceramide axis. Bergenin directly targets LIPA to regulate lipid metabolism and suppress MUC5AC overexpression.

papers.title: Pharmacological Enhancement of O-GlcNAcylation Attenuates Lung Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury.
papers.abstract: Lung ischemia-reperfusion injury (LIRI) contributes substantially to primary graft dysfunction after lung transplantation and also occurs in other clinical settings involving transient interruption and restoration of pulmonary blood flow. O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification is rapidly altered by cellular stress, yet its role in acute pulmonary ischemia-reperfusion remains incompletely understood. We investigated this question using a murine model of transient left pulmonary hilar occlusion followed by reperfusion and an oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) model in MLE-12 cells. O-GlcNAcylation was increased pharmacologically with the O-GlcNAcase inhibitor Thiamet G and reduced with the O-GlcNAc transferase inhibitor OSMI-4. Global O-GlcNAc levels, indices of tissue and cellular injury, and Caspase-1/GSDMD-related pyroptotic signaling were then examined. In both models, O-GlcNAcylation increased early after ischemic stress, whereas pyroptosis-related changes became more pronounced as injury progressed. Thiamet G preserved MLE-12 cell viability, reduced LDH release, and lessened histopathological damage, pulmonary edema, and alveolar-capillary protein leakage in vivo. These effects were accompanied by lower Caspase-1 activation, reduced GSDMD cleavage, and fewer Caspase-1/PI double-positive cells. OSMI-4 produced the opposite pattern, with greater tissue and cellular injury and stronger pyroptosis-related signaling. The protective effect of Thiamet G was also weakened when OSMI-4 was given concurrently. These findings indicate that the early rise in O-GlcNAcylation is consistent with an acute stress response to LIRI. Pharmacologically maintaining higher O-GlcNAcylation was associated with less severe injury and weaker Caspase-1/GSDMD-related signaling, supporting further investigation of this modification as a therapeutic target in acute LIRI.

papers.title: Integrative multi-omics analysis defines a macrophage-associated phospholipid metabolism signature linked to immune remodeling and prognosis in lung adenocarcinoma.
papers.abstract: Phospholipid metabolism (PLM) has been implicated in macrophage polarization and tumor progression in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). Metabolic intermediates such as lysophosphatidylcholine modulate macrophage surface receptor signaling, while inhibition of phospholipid synthesis may attenuate tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) infiltration and suppress LUAD progression. However, macrophage-centered PLM-related prognostic signatures in LUAD remain incompletely characterized. We performed an integrative multi-omics analysis combining single-cell RNA sequencing, bulk transcriptomic profiling, and clinical data from TCGA and GEO cohorts. Macrophage-related genes (MacRGs) were identified using single-cell analysis and high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA). Phospholipid metabolism-related module genes were determined through differential expression analysis and WGCNA. Candidate genes were prioritized using machine learning and Cox regression analyses, followed by construction and external validation of a multigene risk model. Functional enrichment, immune microenvironment profiling, mutation landscape analysis, estimated drug sensitivity, and pseudotime trajectory analyses were performed to explore the biological relevance of the signature. Experimental validation was conducted using LUAD tissues and cell models. A four-gene macrophage-PLM-related signature was constructed to calculate a risk score that stratified patients into high- and low-risk groups with significantly different overall survival. The risk score and T stage were independent prognostic factors, and an integrated nomogram showed acceptable prognostic performance. Functional analyses revealed distinct metabolic and signaling pathway enrichment patterns between risk groups, with 40 shared pathways across the four hub genes. The high-risk group exhibited an altered immune microenvironment characterized by differential infiltration of 20 immune cell subsets, immune checkpoint expression changes, lower ESTIMATE scores, and distinct TIDE profiles. Somatic mutation patterns and tumor mutational burden differed between groups. Drug-sensitivity estimation identified 105 compounds with differential estimated IC50 values between risk groups. DPYSL2 expression was associated with macrophage polarization dynamics, and DPYSL2 overexpression suppressed LUAD cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and clonogenicity in vitro. We identified a macrophage-phospholipid metabolism-associated four-gene prognostic signature that provides prognostic information and reflects immune-metabolic remodeling in LUAD. These findings support further investigation of macrophage-phospholipid metabolism-related genes as candidate biomarkers and may inform future therapeutic stratification studies in LUAD.

papers.title: Alpha-ketoglutarate ameliorates systemic sclerosis-associated fibrosis by restoring endothelial function.
papers.abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a devastating autoimmune disease characterized by multi-organ fibrosis with limited therapeutic options. Using targeted metabolomics, we first observed that levels of alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG), a key TCA-cycle intermediate, were paradoxically elevated in bleomycin-induced fibrotic lungs and in TGF-β-stimulated fibroblasts, prompting us to test whether exogenous supplementation could augment this compensatory response. Using bleomycin-induced skin and lung fibrosis mouse models, we demonstrated that oral α-KG administration significantly attenuated dermal and pulmonary collagen deposition, reduced inflammatory infiltration, and improved survival. Although fibroblasts are conventionally regarded as the central effectors of fibrosis, integrated single-cell RNA sequencing and bulk transcriptomic deconvolution unexpectedly identified endothelial cells as the predominant cellular target of α-KG in fibrotic lungs. Consistently, α-KG restored endothelial cell proportions in vivo, rescued angiogenic function and preserved barrier integrity in association with upregulation of eNOS, and tight junction proteins in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) treated with bleomycin. Mechanistically, α-KG suppressed TGF-β/Smad activation and reversed bleomycin-induced metabolic repression, including restoration of fatty acid oxidation signatures and mitochondrial ultrastructure, accompanied by upregulation of the mitochondrial biogenesis regulator NRF1. Collectively, these findings reveal that α-KG exerts broad anti-fibrotic effects in SSc models by protecting endothelial function and inhibiting canonical pro-fibrotic signaling, highlighting its potential as a translatable metabolic therapeutic strategy for SSc.

papers.title: The PIEZO1/CISD1/IP3R Mechanotransduction Axis Drives Macrophage Mitochondrial Dysfunction and Inflammatory Activation in Pulmonary Fibrosis.
papers.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive and fatal interstitial lung disease characterized by excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition and elevated tissue stiffness. While aberrant mechanotransduction is increasingly recognized as a key driver of fibrotic progression, the mechanisms by which mechanical cues orchestrate macrophage dysfunction remain poorly elucidated. Here, we identify the mechanosensitive ion channel PIEZO1 as a key mediator coupling matrix stiffening to macrophage inflammatory activation in pulmonary fibrosis. We demonstrate that PIEZO1 is substantially upregulated in fibrotic lungs, and that its activation drives intracellular calcium overload via the CISD1/IP3R signaling axis. This process elicits aberrant opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP), causing mitochondrial dysfunction and augmented pro-inflammatory macrophage polarization. Conversely, PIEZO1 inhibition suppresses the CISD1/IP3R signaling cascade, alleviates calcium dysregulation, prevents mitochondrial damage, and attenuates inflammatory activation. In vitro CISD1 inhibition ameliorates PIEZO1-driven mitochondrial abnormalities and pro-inflammatory signaling in macrophages. Furthermore, genetic knockdown of CISD1 mitigates mitochondrial abnormalities and attenuates bleomycin (BLM)-induced lung fibrosis in mice. Collectively, these findings identify a previously unrecognized PIEZO1/CISD1/IP3R mechanotransduction axis coupling tissue stiffening to macrophage-mediated inflammation and fibrosis. This study offers mechanistic insights into fibrosis-associated immune dysregulation, highlighting PIEZO1 and CISD1 as promising therapeutic targets for pulmonary fibrosis.

papers.title: Glutamate attenuates the ILC2 response and allergic airway inflammation via the kainate receptor GluK2.
papers.abstract: Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) play a critical role in initiating the type 2 immune response, particularly in allergic airway diseases. Although the effects of glutamate on the immune system have been reported previously, its role in modulating the function of ILC2s and lung inflammation remains unclear.In this study, we report that the glutamate levels increased in lung tissue following exposure to allergens. Consequently, glutamate was found to restrain ILC2 responses during lung inflammation in mice. Using Rag1 -/- mice, we demonstrated that the inhibitory effect of glutamate on type 2 inflammation was independent of T and B cells. Further ILC2 adoptive transfer experiments in Rag -/- Il2rg -/-  mice confirmed that glutamate likely exerted its effects by directly targeting ILC2s. In vitro experiments revealed that glutamate suppressed ILC2 function through ionic kainate receptor signaling. Genetic deletion of the kainate receptor subunit GluK2 enhanced ILC2 responses and exacerbated type 2 lung inflammation. Mechanistically, transcriptome and metabolic analyses revealed that glutamate reduced oxidative metabolism in ILC2s, thereby limiting their activation. Consistently, in vivo administration of BPAM344-a positive allosteric modulator that potentiates GluK2 signaling-effectively suppressed allergen-induced type 2 inflammation. Notably, ILC2-specific GluK2 deletion markedly attenuated the anti-inflammatory effects of BPAM344, indicating that its protective effects depend on ILC2-intrinsic GluK2 signaling.These findings demonstrate a novel role for glutamate in restraining ILC2 function, as it plays a protective role in alleviating airway inflammation. We propose that GluK2 activation may offer a promising therapeutic strategy for treating ILC2-driven allergic asthma.

papers.title: Glyoxalase 1 (GLO1) Deficiency Is Associated with Myeloid Skewing and Altered Inflammatory Responses.
papers.abstract: Glyoxalase 1 (GLO1) is involved in cellular adaptation to metabolic and oxidative stress, however, its role in regulating immune homeostasis remains poorly understood. Here, we used Glo1 knockout (Glo1-KO) mice to investigate the effects of GLO1 deficiency on bone marrow (BM) hematopoietic composition and the pulmonary inflammation environment. Flow cytometric analysis revealed alterations in BM myeloid-derived suppressor cell population, in Glo1-KO mice. In the lung GLO1 deficiency was accompanied by increased expression of inflammation and tissue-remodeling-associated genes, indicating an altered pulmonary inflammation milieu. Together, these findings demonstrate that GLO1 deficiency is associated with coordinated changes in hematopoietic immune environments and suggest that GLO1 may influence immune regulation across hematopoietic and peripheral tissue compartments.

papers.title: NUAK isoforms promote glucose and glutamine metabolic reprogramming driven colon cancer progression and migration through regulation of AMPK/mTOR signaling.
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) cells undergo significant alterations in glucose and glutamine metabolism to support rapid growth and migration. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying these metabolic changes remain incompletely understood. Although NUAK1 and NUAK2, members of the NUAK kinase family have been implicated in CRC tumorigenesis, their specific roles in metabolic reprogramming that drives CRC progression and metastasis have not been elucidated. In this study, we demonstrate that NUAK1 and NUAK2 are overexpressed in human CRC tissues and that their expression is associated with increased tumor metastasis and poorer patient survival. NUAK1/2 promotes CRC cell proliferation and migration, whereas their depletion markedly reduces cell growth and migratory capacity. Furthermore, knockout of NUAK1/2 disrupts key metabolic pathways, including aerobic glycolysis, pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), and glutamine metabolism. Mechanistically, NUAK1/2 facilitates mTOR-driven metabolic reprogramming and promotes CRC growth and migration by suppressing AMPK activity. Depletion of NUAK1/2 impairs metabolic function, cellular growth, and migration potential in CRC cells, effects that are further enhanced by pharmacological activation of AMPK with AICAR and inhibition of mTOR using Rapamycin. In conclusion, these findings identify NUAK1/2 as critical regulators of CRC progression and migration through AMPK/mTOR-mediated metabolic reprogramming, highlighting their potential as therapeutic targets in colorectal cancer.

papers.title: Matrix stiffness promotes colorectal cancer progression via Golgi-dependent cholesterol synthesis.
papers.abstract: Extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffening and metabolic reprogramming are hallmarks of colorectal cancer (CRC) progression; however, the mechanistic link between biomechanical cues and cholesterol metabolism remains poorly defined. Here, we delineate a mechano-metabolic pathway in which matrix stiffness activates the mechanosensitive Ca²⁺ channel Piezo1 to drive structural reorganization of the Golgi apparatus, promoting its close apposition with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). This organelle remodeling facilitates the proteolytic activation and nuclear translocation of SREBP2, thereby transcriptionally upregulating HMGCR, the rate-limiting enzyme for cholesterol synthesis, and elevating intracellular cholesterol. HMGCR upregulation is functionally essential for stiffness-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and CRC progression. Mechanistically, HMGCR-mediated cholesterol accumulation promotes phosphorylation of β-catenin at Ser552, which disrupts β-catenin/E-cadherin complexes at adherens junctions, leading to β-catenin nuclear accumulation and EMT execution. Therapeutically, combined pharmacological inhibition of matrix crosslinking and cholesterol synthesis synergistically suppresses tumor growth and invasion while restoring epithelial architecture in vivo. Collectively, these findings reveal that Piezo1-dependent Golgi-ER reorganization triggers SREBP2-driven cholesterol synthesis, ultimately fueling β-catenin-mediated junctional disassembly and metastasis, and highlight the therapeutic promise of co-targeting tumor mechanics and metabolism.

papers.title: Lipid metabolism: a potential checkpoint for cGAS-STING regulation in colorectal cancer.
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy for colorectal cancer (CRC) continues to face significant challenges, particularly in patients with microsatellite stable (MSS) tumors. The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway is a key regulator of innate immunity and has emerged as a promising target for enhancing anti-tumor immune responses. Meanwhile, lipid metabolic reprogramming is a defining hallmark of CRC and contributes to tumor progression, evasion, and therapeutic resistance. Although direct evidence linking lipid metabolism to cGAS-STING signaling in CRC remains limited, accumulating studies from diverse disease models suggest extensive interactions between these two processes. This review summarizes the major features of lipid metabolic reprogramming in CRC and discusses current understanding of cGAS-STING signaling in tumor immunity. We further examine potential mechanisms by which lipid metabolism may influence cGAS-STING activity, including the regulation of mitochondrial DNA release, intracellular trafficking of signaling components and lipid-associated post-translational modifications. Emerging evidence also indicates that cGAS-STING signaling can affect lipid metabolic pathways by regulating lipid metabolic homeostasis and inducing lipid peroxidation-driven ferroptosis. Importantly, microbiota-derived lipid metabolites exert context-dependent effects on cGAS-STING signaling to balance intestinal inflammation and anti-tumor immunity. Finally, we discuss therapeutic strategies targeting lipid metabolism and cGAS-STING signaling, with a particular focus on approaches that may enhance anti-tumor immunity through coordinated metabolic-immune modulation. By bridging metabolic reprogramming with innate immune sensing, we propose that modulating the lipid-cGAS-STING axis could break immune tolerance and offer a distinct therapeutic window for CRC.

papers.title: GART expression is associated with a proliferative and purine-metabolic ISC-like epithelial state in ulcerative colitis.
papers.abstract: To characterize the epithelial state associated with GART expression in ulcerative colitis (UC) and determine whether this association reflects a GART-specific program or a broader proliferative and purine-metabolic phenotype. Four independent bulk transcriptomic cohorts were analyzed and synthesized by random-effects meta-analysis. Human colonic scRNA-seq datasets (GSE214695 and SCP259) were integrated, with principal comparisons repeated using donor-aware pseudobulk or mixed-effects approaches and adjustment for sequencing depth, gene detection, and cell-cycle covariates. GART detection was defined from raw counts and tested using alternative thresholds. Pseudotime, scTenifoldKnk, CellChat/LIANA, and transcriptional-network analyses were used as exploratory analyses. Spatial transcriptomics (GSE189184), human colonic multiplex immunofluorescence, and acute DSS-induced colitis tissues were used for tissue-level localization. Across the four bulk cohorts, GART expression showed an overall increase in UC (pooled Hedges' g = 0.743, 95% CI 0.239-1.248; P = 0.0183). In the single-cell atlas, GART detection localized preferentially to an ISC-like epithelial compartment, although the magnitude of the UC-associated detection difference varied between cohorts. Within UC ISC-like cells, donor-paired pseudobulk analyses identified proliferative and nucleotide-metabolic transcriptional differences associated with GART detection. Across the broader ISC-like epithelial atlas, donor-aware module analyses showed positive associations of GART detection with purine-biosynthesis, DNA-replication, DNA-repair, and mitotic programs, and these associations remained positive within cell-cycle strata. Comparison with other de novo purine-synthesis enzymes did not support a uniquely GART-specific alteration. Exploratory network analyses linked the GART-associated state to proliferative and nucleotide-metabolic programs but did not establish functional dependence. In seven independent spatial donors, the single-cell-derived epithelial program was consistently higher in GART-detected than GART-undetected epithelial regions (mean within-donor difference = 0.0262, 95% CI 0.0140-0.0407; exact P = 0.0156). Human tissue immunofluorescence further showed co-enrichment of GART with OLFM4-positive ISC-like, MYBL2/Ki67-positive proliferative, and MIF/CD74-associated inflammatory regions across the corresponding panel-specific participant sets. GART identifies a proliferative and purine-metabolic ISC-like epithelial state in UC but is not established as a specific driver of epithelial regeneration. The findings support an association between GART detection, nucleotide-demand programs, proliferative epithelial activity, and the inflammatory tissue context, providing a framework for future direct functional studies.

papers.title: Gut microbiome-related plasma metabolites and risk of colorectal cancer.
papers.abstract: Perturbations in gut microbiome composition and altered levels of related metabolites may be related to colorectal cancer (CRC). This study assessed whether pre-diagnostic, circulating, microbiome-related metabolite concentrations were associated with CRC risk. We undertook a nested case-control study of 739 participants in the Colon Cancer Family Registry Cohort (312 cases, 427 controls). Median follow-up time from blood draw to diagnosis was 7 years. Pre-diagnostic plasma concentrations of 70 metabolites were quantified by targeted liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated for metabolite concentrations and CRC risk using multivariable conditional logistic regression models. Stratified analyses were conducted by sex, Lynch syndrome diagnosis, and age at tumor onset. The primary bile acids, cholate and chenodeoxycholate, were positively associated with CRC incidence, overall and among females. The odds of CRC were higher in individuals in the highest compared with the lowest quartiles of cholate (ORQ4vQ1=1.61, 95% CI=1.05-2.49) and chenodeoxycholate (ORQ4vQ1=1.60, 95% CI=1.03-2.50). Two short-chain fatty acids (caproate, valerate) and three metabolites involved in phenylalanine and tyrosine metabolism (cinnamoylglycine, phenylpropionate, 4-ethylphenylsulfate) were suggested to be associated, positively and negatively, respectively, with incident CRC but these associations did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons. In stratified analyses, some differences were observed according to sex, Lynch syndrome diagnosis, and age at tumor onset. Circulating microbiome-related metabolites, including bile acids and short-chain fatty acids, may be associated with CRC risk. These findings provide insight into potential pathways linking the gut microbiome to colorectal carcinogenesis.

papers.title: Impact of mixed nut consumption on faecal lipid content and gut microbiota composition in healthy adults.
papers.abstract: Nuts are a source of dietary fibre and are considered a nutritious snack despite their high fat content. The effects of nut consumption on the microbiota and the role of nut-derived lipids in altering the large intestinal microbial community remain poorly understood. This study examined changes in faecal characteristics and microbiota composition in 15 healthy volunteers consuming unrestricted diets during a cross-over dietary intervention consisting of three weeks of daily mixed-nut consumption (30 g almonds, macadamias and pistachios) and three weeks of nut abstinence. Microscopic examination of faecal samples revealed lipid-containing nut particles following nut consumption, which were not observed during the nut abstinence. Mixed nut consumption was associated with a significant increase in total faecal lipid content compared with nut abstinence ( P < 0.05), suggesting incomplete digestion and absorption of nut-derived lipids. In contrast, faecal pH, dry matter, ash content, short-chain fatty acids and ammonium concentrations were not significantly altered by the intervention. 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis demonstrated substantial inter-individual variation in gut microbial community composition, with only modest differences associated with nut consumption. Predicted functional profiling suggested variation in pathways related to lipid metabolism between intervention periods. Overall, the findings indicate that a portion of consumed nut cells likely reaches the large intestine intact. Upon degradation of the nut cell wall, encapsulated lipids may become available to the colonic microbiota, potentially contributing to microbial metabolism and community responses observed.

papers.title: 2'-Fucosyllactose enhances indole-3-lactic acid production by Bifidobacterium bifidum DNG-08 and alleviates colitis-associated bone loss: Associations with microbiota remodeling and intestinal AHR-related responses.
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease is frequently associated with an imbalance in bone remodeling and a decline in bone mass, however, there is a lack of systematic research on microbiome-based intervention strategies targeting colitis-associated bone loss. In this study, Bifidobacterium bifidum DNG-08 (DNG-08) was selected from four candidate strains based on its favorable 2'-fucosyllactose (2'-FL) utilization and indole-3-lactic acid (ILA) production. Genomic annotation revealed that DNG-08 harbors functional genes related to fucosylated oligosaccharide utilization and the conversion of tryptophan to ILA. In a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model, combined intervention with DNG-08 and 2'-FL significantly alleviated colitis-associated phenotypes, and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels by 13.33%-58.69%, while increasing IL-10-1.23 times that of the DSS group. Simultaneously, the combined intervention improved trabecular bone microstructure, increasing the bone formation marker procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (PINP) by 14.61%-56.37%, decreasing the bone resorption marker C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX-I) by 17.03%-21.77%, and upregulating the expression of Wnt3a, β-catenin, and Runx2. Gut microbiota analysis showed that combined intervention could partially reverse DSS-induced dysbiosis, enriching potentially beneficial bacterial taxa while reducing inflammation-associated genera. Notably, combined treatment group exhibited elevated serum ILA levels, increased colonic aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) fluorescence, and upregulatied CYP1A1 expression. Correlation analysis identified significant associations among serum ILA, AHR-related indicators, selected bacterial genera, and bone remodeling parameters. This study highlights that strain-substrate matching may serve as a precise synbiotic strategy to improve inflammation-related gut-bone axis dysfunction.

papers.title: Linking the fine structural characteristics of cereal β-glucans to their differential protective effects against colitis.
papers.abstract: Although cereal β-glucans exert protective effects against experimental colitis, the relationship between their fine structural and physicochemical properties and differential in vivo responses remains unclear. This study directly compared highland barley β-glucan (BBG) and oat β-glucan (OBG), two high-purity mixed-linkage β-(1 → 3)/(1 → 4)-D-glucans, under identical experimental conditions. BBG had a higher cellotriosyl-to-cellotetraosyl (DP3/DP4) ratio than OBG (2.33 vs. 1.51) and a lower weight-average molecular weight. In dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis mice, both β-glucans alleviated clinical signs of disease, while BBG showed greater protection at the tissue and biochemical levels. BBG preserved colon length at 4.88 cm, compared with 4.46 cm for OBG. It reduced myeloperoxidase activity, nitric oxide, and malondialdehyde levels to 1226 U g -1 , 0.42 μmol g -1 , and 78.8 nmol mg -1 , respectively, and fully restored Claudin-1 expression. BBG was also associated with enrichment of Ligilactobacillus , Limosilactobacillus , Romboutsia , and Turicibacter and suppression of Escherichia-Shigella . Fecal metabolomics showed higher levels of selected indole derivatives and taurine-conjugated bile acids, accompanied by lower uric acid and prostaglandin-related inflammatory metabolites. These in vivo differences were accompanied by distinct physicochemical behaviors. BBG showed faster self-aggregation, with a shorter lag time than OBG (112.9 vs . 256.0 min), accompanied by a markedly higher storage modulus (360 vs. 66 Pa). BBG also showed stronger intestinal-phase reassembly under simulated gastrointestinal conditions, approximately threefold greater bile acid retention during dynamic dialysis, and higher DPPH radical-scavenging activity (11.8% vs. 4.8%). Overall, the differential intestinal responses to BBG and OBG were accompanied by distinct physicochemical, microbial, and metabolic profiles, supporting a potential aggregation between cereal β-glucan fine structure, supramolecular behavior, and protective effects against colitis.

papers.title: Myrica rubra juice attenuates DSS-induced colitis and is associated with changes in the gut microbiota-metabolite-host axis.
papers.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is characterized by chronic intestinal inflammation and impaired mucosal barrier function. Myrica rubra contains polyphenols and flavonoids, but the mechanisms underlying its potential protective effects in colitis remain unclear. We evaluated Myrica rubra juice (MRJ) in a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model of colitis and a TNF-α-injured colonic organoid model. The study combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, untargeted serum and fecal metabolomics, and molecular docking. MRJ treatment attenuated disease severity and was associated with increased expression of occludin and MUC2 in DSS-treated mice. MRJ also altered microbial diversity and taxonomic composition in a taxon-specific manner. Serum and fecal metabolomic profiles differed after MRJ treatment, including pathways related to amino acid and bile acid metabolism. Integrated analyses identified associations among microbial taxa, putatively annotated metabolites, and host inflammatory and barrier-related variables. Direct exposure to 20% (v/v) whole MRJ increased occludin immunofluorescence in TNF-α-injured colonic organoids cultured without a gut microbial community. This single-marker result is consistent with an epithelial response to whole MRJ under the applied in vitro conditions. Molecular docking generated predicted poses and docking scores for selected parent compound-protein pairs. These calculations did not demonstrate physical binding, functional inhibition, or target engagement in vivo . Together, the findings support a direct epithelial response and identify concurrent microbiota-associated changes. However, the present design could not determine whether these microbial changes contributed to protection. It also could not separate or quantify the host-directed and microbiota-mediated contributions or identify the active chemical species.

papers.title: When do starch-polyphenol complexes qualify as type 5 resistant starch? A critical evidence framework from molecular assembly to colonic utilization.
papers.abstract: Starch-polyphenol complexes are increasingly explored for modulating starch digestibility, developing low-glycemic-index foods, and improving polyphenol stability and delivery. Some systems have been described as type 5 resistant starch (RS5) or RS5-like based on V-type crystalline signals, increased resistant starch content, or reduced glucose release. However, these outcomes alone are insufficient for RS5 assignment because they may also arise from surface adsorption, non-inclusion networks, substrate shielding, enzyme inhibition by free or released polyphenols, or food-matrix effects. This review critically assesses the evidence required to describe starch-polyphenol systems as V-type starch-polyphenol complexes with demonstrated enzymatic resistance and examines their relationship to the proposed non-lipid extension of RS5. Evidence from molecular assembly, structural characterization, processing-induced rearrangement, resistance to enzymatic digestion, polyphenol release, colonic fermentation, and physiological relevance is integrated. V-type or V-type-like inclusion provides the strongest structural basis for identifying a V-type starch-polyphenol complex, whereas surface-bound complexes, non-inclusion networks and covalent derivatives require different mechanistic descriptions. Mechanistic attribution should include removal and quantification of unbound polyphenols, physical-mixture and washed-complex controls, and enzyme-inhibition kinetics. A tiered evidence framework is proposed to classify these systems as putative RS5, RS5-like complexes, polyphenol-bound resistant starch candidates, enzyme-inhibition-dominated systems, or non-RS mixtures.
